rules.heading: Ordinal numbers
rules.text: Spell out all ordinal numbers in text.
rules.bad: 1st, 5th, 12th, 43rd
rules.good: first, fifth, twelfth, forty-third

rules.heading: Ordinal numbers
rules.text: Spell out all ordinal numbers in text.
rules.why: Ordinal numbers are spelled out in text.
rules.example: Select the 1st option in the list.

rules.heading: Numbers as words
rules.text: If it's important to have the number and associated noun together on the same line, use a nonbreaking space between the number and the noun.

rules.heading: Numbers as words
rules.text: Spell out numbers from zero through nine, except as noted in Numbers as numerals.
rules.good: four options

rules.heading: Numbers as words
rules.text: Spell out a number that starts a sentence; it's okay, but non-optimal, to begin a sentence with a four-digit year.
rules.good: Fifteen directories are created.

rules.heading: Numbers as words
rules.text: In some cases, rearrange the sentence so that the number appears later instead of starting the sentence.
rules.bad: 164 MB is generally considered too large a file to send as an attachment.
rules.good: In general, avoid sending files larger than 164 MB as attachments.

rules.heading: Numbers as words
rules.text: Spell out a number that is followed by a numeral, or rephrase so both are numerals.
rules.good: This procedure creates fifteen 100,000-byte files.

rules.heading: Numbers as words
rules.text: Use words like millions or billions only for approximate numbers; for precise numbers, use numerals.
rules.good: You can specify thousands of combinations.

rules.heading: Numbers as numerals
rules.text: Use numerals for numbers 10 and greater.

rules.heading: Numbers as numerals
rules.text: Use numerals for version numbers.
rules.good: version 3

rules.heading: Numbers as numerals
rules.text: Use numerals for technical quantities, such as amounts of memory, amounts of disk space, numbers of queries, or usage limits.
rules.good: 6 queries per second

rules.heading: Numbers as numerals
rules.text: Use numerals for page numbers, chapter numbers, sections, and so on.

rules.heading: Numbers as numerals
rules.text: Avoid referring to step numbers whenever possible, but when you must, use the numeral.

rules.heading: Numbers as numerals
rules.text: Use numerals for prices.

rules.heading: Numbers as numerals
rules.text: Use numerals for numbers without units, such as numbers used in mathematical expressions.

rules.heading: Numbers as numerals
rules.text: Use numerals for numbers less than 10 when they appear in the same sentence with numbers greater than 9.
rules.good: The menu contains 15 options but 6 of them are deselected.

rules.heading: Numbers as numerals
rules.text: Use numerals for negative numbers.

rules.heading: Numbers as numerals
rules.text: Use numerals for most fractions.

rules.heading: Numbers as numerals
rules.text: Use numerals for percentages.

rules.heading: Numbers as numerals
rules.text: Use numerals for numbers containing decimal points.

rules.heading: Numbers as numerals
rules.text: Treat decimal numbers as plural even when less than or equal to 1.0.
rules.good: 0.3 inches

rules.heading: Numbers as numerals
rules.text: For decimal numbers less than one, place a zero in front of the decimal point.
rules.good: 0.3 inches

rules.heading: Numbers as numerals
rules.text: Use numerals for measurements.
rules.good: 8 pixels

rules.heading: Numbers as numerals
rules.text: Use numerals for numbers in a range.

rules.heading: Numbers as numerals
rules.text: For decimal numbers less than one, place a zero in front of the decimal point.
rules.why: Decimals less than one need a leading zero.
rules.example: Set the margin to .3 inches.

rules.heading: Numbers as Roman numerals
rules.text: Avoid using Roman numerals when possible; instead, use Arabic numerals because they are easier to scan.
rules.why: Arabic numerals are easier to scan.

rules.heading: Numbers as Roman numerals
rules.text: You can use Roman numerals for sub-steps in numbered procedures.

rules.heading: Fractions
rules.text: Express fractions as decimal numbers, when possible.

rules.heading: Fractions
rules.text: If you must express fractions as words, connect the numerator and denominator with a hyphen unless one of them is already hyphenated.
rules.good: two-fifths

rules.heading: Percentages
rules.text: In general, use numerals and the percent sign (%), without a space between them.

rules.heading: Percentages
rules.text: If the percentage starts the sentence, then spell out both the number and the word percent.
rules.good: Forty percent of the files

rules.heading: Percentages
rules.text: Don't put a space between the numeral and the percent sign.
rules.why: No space between numeral and percent sign.
rules.example: Usage rose to 40 % this month.

rules.heading: Percentages
rules.text: Use the percent sign (%), not the word percent, after a numeral.
rules.why: Use numerals with the percent sign.
rules.example: Only 40 percent of the files were copied.

rules.heading: Ranges of numbers
rules.text: In ranges of numbers, use a hyphen with no space on either side of it; do not use an en dash.

rules.heading: Ranges of numbers
rules.text: Use a hyphen, not an en dash, in ranges of numbers.
rules.why: Ranges use a hyphen, not an en dash.
rules.example: The project ran from 2012–2016.

rules.heading: Suspended hyphens
rules.text: When two or more hyphenated compounds that start with numbers modify the same word, use suspended hyphens.
rules.good: You can set up the system to scan for new files at one-, two-, or three-hour intervals.

rules.heading: Currency
rules.text: Make sure that it's clear what country's currency you are describing.

rules.heading: Currency
rules.text: For US dollars, use a comma to delineate the thousands place of whole currency.
rules.bad: $10 000 in fees is out of reach for many developers.
rules.good: $10,000 in fees is out of reach for many developers.

rules.heading: Currency
rules.text: For US dollars, use a period to delineate whole currency and fractions of currency.

rules.heading: Currency
rules.text: For US dollars, always include the dollar sign ($) at the beginning of the currency.

rules.heading: Currency
rules.text: For US dollars, do not use any punctuation or spaces to the right of the decimal.
rules.bad: The price is $0.006,653 per vCPU hour.
rules.good: The price is $0.006653 per vCPU hour.

rules.heading: Currency
rules.text: For US dollars, use a comma, not a space, to delineate the thousands place of whole currency.
rules.why: Use commas to separate thousands in US dollars.
rules.example: $10 000 in fees is out of reach for many developers.

rules.heading: Currency
rules.text: Do not use any punctuation or spaces to the right of the decimal in currency.
rules.why: No digit separators right of the decimal point.
rules.example: The price is $0.006,653 per vCPU hour.

rules.heading: Commas and decimal points in numbers
rules.text: Use commas and decimal points in accordance with standard American number-formatting.

rules.heading: Commas and decimal points in numbers
rules.text: In numbers four or more digits long, use commas to set off groups of three digits, counting leftward from the decimal point.
rules.bad: The limit is 1532784 bytes per day.
rules.good: The limit is 1,532,784 bytes per day.

rules.heading: Commas and decimal points in numbers
rules.text: For long decimal numbers, do not use any digit-group separators to the right of the decimal point.
rules.bad: $0.031 611/vCPU hour
rules.good: $0.031611/vCPU hour

rules.heading: Commas and decimal points in numbers
rules.text: Use a period for a decimal point, in the standard American style.

rules.heading: Dimensions
rules.text: Use numerals for dimensions.

rules.heading: Dimensions
rules.text: Use a lowercase x between the numerals in the dimensions, with no space between the numerals and the x.

rules.heading: Dimensions
rules.text: Use a lowercase x between the numerals in the dimensions, with no space between the numerals and the x.
rules.why: Dimensions use a lowercase x with no spaces.
rules.example: The icon must be 192 x 192 pixels.

rules.heading: Exponents
rules.text: Use standard mathematical notation for exponents.

rules.heading: Exponents
rules.text: Don't put a space between the base and the exponent.
rules.good: 2³

rules.heading: Accompany numerical concepts with real-world practical implications
rules.text: Accompany numerical concepts with real-world practical implications to provide tangible meaning; for example, if using a feature incurs additional fees, add a link to pricing calculator.

rules.heading: Introductory sentences
rules.text: In most cases, introduce a procedure with an introductory sentence that provides context to the reader that isn't part of the section heading.
rules.why: Gives readers context beyond the heading.

rules.heading: Introductory sentences
rules.text: Don't simply repeat the heading: if the heading explains what the procedure is, and no additional context is needed, then don't include an introductory statement.

rules.heading: Introductory sentences
rules.text: End the introductory sentence with a colon if it immediately precedes the procedure.
rules.good: To customize the buttons, follow these steps:

rules.heading: Introductory sentences
rules.text: End the introductory sentence with a period if there's more material (such as a note paragraph) between the introduction and the procedure.

rules.heading: Introductory sentences
rules.text: Don't introduce a procedure with a partial sentence that's completed by the numbered steps; you can use an imperative statement or a complete sentence instead.
rules.bad: To customize the buttons:
rules.good: To customize the buttons, follow these steps:
rules.why: Steps shouldn't complete a partial sentence.

rules.heading: Single-step procedures
rules.text: When a procedure consists of only one step, write the step in one sentence and format it as a bulleted list.
rules.bad: To clear (flush) the entire log, follow this step: 1. Click Clear logcat.
rules.good: To clear (flush) the entire log, click Clear logcat.
rules.why: A single step isn't a numbered sequence.

rules.heading: Sub-steps in numbered procedures
rules.text: In a numbered procedure, label sub-steps with lowercase letters, and label sub-sub-steps with lowercase Roman numerals.

rules.heading: Sub-steps in numbered procedures
rules.text: When a step has sub-steps, treat the step like an introductory sentence: put a colon or a period at the end of the step, as appropriate.
rules.good: For Name, enter a name for the VM instance, and then do the following:

rules.heading: Order of multiple components in a step
rules.text: To document a complex procedural step, use the following order: describe the action to take; list a command, if necessary; explain any placeholders used in the command; explain the command in more detail, if necessary; list the output of the command, if necessary; in a separate paragraph, explain the result of an action, or any output, if necessary.

rules.heading: Multi-action procedures
rules.text: In general, use one step for each action.

rules.heading: Multi-action procedures
rules.text: You can combine small actions into one step by using angle brackets (>) for sequential menu selections.
rules.good: Click File > New > Document.

rules.heading: Multi-action procedures
rules.text: Don't make the steps too long; if they feel too long, consider splitting them into multiple steps.

rules.heading: Multiple procedures for the same task
rules.text: If there's more than one way to complete a task, then document one procedure that's accessible for all readers.

rules.heading: Multiple procedures for the same task
rules.text: Choose a procedure that lets readers do all the steps by using only a keyboard.
rules.why: Accessibility for keyboard-only readers.

rules.heading: Multiple procedures for the same task
rules.text: If all methods are accessible, pick the shortest and simplest approach if possible.

rules.heading: Multiple procedures for the same task
rules.text: Choose a procedure that uses a programming language that most of your audience is familiar with.

rules.heading: Multiple procedures for the same task
rules.text: If you need to document multiple ways to complete a task, then separate them in different pages, headings, or tabs.

rules.heading: Repetitive procedures
rules.text: Avoid repeating procedures; instead, reference those procedures and link to them.
rules.good: Create a user as you did in the previous step.

rules.heading: Optional steps
rules.text: For an optional step, at the beginning of the step, type Optional followed by a colon.
rules.bad: (Optional) Type an arbitrary string ...
rules.good: Optional: Type an arbitrary string ...

rules.heading: Optional steps
rules.why: Optional steps start with "Optional:".
rules.example: (Optional) Type an arbitrary string ...

rules.heading: Steps that say where to complete a task
rules.text: Tell the reader where to complete an action—for example, in a particular tool or UI field—before you state the action.
rules.bad: Go to the Monitoring page in the Google Cloud console.
rules.good: In the Google Cloud console, go to the Monitoring page.

rules.heading: Steps that say where to complete a task
rules.text: If a set of procedures is split across multiple headings, then in each procedure, restate where the reader completes the action, even if the context is the same as in the previous procedure.
rules.good: In the Google Cloud console, go to the BigQuery page.

rules.heading: Summary of guidelines for writing procedures
rules.text: Set the context (such as a tool or an environment) in which the reader performs a procedure.
rules.good: In Cloud Shell, connect to the development cluster.

rules.heading: Summary of guidelines for writing procedures
rules.text: Write in the order that the reader needs to follow.

rules.heading: Summary of guidelines for writing procedures
rules.text: Make sure that the first sentence in a procedural step includes an imperative verb.
rules.bad: You need the project ID later in this document. Retrieve the project ID.
rules.good: Clone the repository that contains the sample data.

rules.heading: Summary of guidelines for writing procedures
rules.text: Use complete sentences.

rules.heading: Summary of guidelines for writing procedures
rules.text: Use parallel structure and consistent verb form.
rules.bad: Download the service account key to your local machine by clicking More and then clicking Download file.
rules.good: Download the service account key to your local machine. Click More, and then click Download.

rules.heading: Summary of guidelines for writing procedures
rules.text: Don't use directional language to orient the reader, such as above, below, or right-hand side.
rules.bad: In the above diagram, ...
rules.good: In the preceding diagram,...
rules.why: Doesn't work well for accessibility or localization.

rules.heading: Summary of guidelines for writing procedures
rules.text: If a UI element is hard to find, provide a screenshot instead of describing its position or appearance.
rules.bad: Click the button with three lines.
rules.good: Click menu Menu.

rules.heading: Summary of guidelines for writing procedures
rules.text: Avoid using "run the following command" to introduce code; instead, focus on what the command does.
rules.bad: In Cloud Shell, deploy the load generator by running the following command:...
rules.good: In Cloud Shell, deploy the load generator:...

rules.heading: Summary of guidelines for writing procedures
rules.text: If the reader must press Enter after a step, then include that instruction as part of the step.
rules.bad: Click the search box and type custom function. Press Enter.
rules.good: Click the search box, type custom function, and then press Enter.

rules.heading: Summary of guidelines for writing procedures
rules.text: Don't include keyboard shortcuts.
rules.bad: Press Ctrl+C, and then press Ctrl+V...
rules.good: Copy the command, and then paste it...

rules.heading: Summary of guidelines for writing procedures
rules.text: When there's more than one way to do something, give only the best way.
rules.why: Giving alternate ways can confuse readers.

rules.heading: Summary of guidelines for writing procedures
rules.text: Ensure that the reader has the information that they need in order to prepare for the task ahead of time.
rules.good: The following hardware and software are required:...
rules.why: Supports task management, memory, and emotional regulation.

rules.heading: Summary of guidelines for writing procedures
rules.text: Include as few steps as possible to complete the task.

rules.heading: Summary of guidelines for writing procedures
rules.text: Limit interruptions in the path.

rules.heading: Summary of guidelines for writing procedures
rules.text: Focus on one reader decision at a time.

rules.heading: Summary of guidelines for writing procedures
rules.text: Separate each instruction by making each instruction a separate list item.

rules.heading: Summary of guidelines for writing procedures
rules.why: Don't use please in procedures.
rules.example: To open a document, please click File > Open.

rules.heading: Summary of guidelines for writing procedures
rules.why: Directional language fails accessibility and localization.
rules.example: In the diagram below, ...

rules.heading: Summary of guidelines for writing procedures
rules.why: Focus on what the command does.
rules.example: Run the following command:...

rules.heading: Summary of guidelines for writing procedures
rules.why: Don't include keyboard shortcuts in procedures.
rules.example: Press Ctrl+C, and then press Ctrl+V...

rules.heading: Steps with goals
rules.text: When a step includes a goal, state the goal before the action.
rules.bad: Click File > New > Document to start a new document.
rules.good: To start a new document, click File > New > Document.
rules.why: Helps readers understand and complete the step.

rules.heading: Steps with goals
rules.text: If the "To ..." format can imply that a required step is optional, state the goal followed by a colon and then the action; otherwise prefer the more natural "To ..." format.
rules.good: Start a new document: click File > New > Document.
rules.why: Clarifies that the step isn't optional.

rules.heading: Steps with results or justifications
rules.text: State the action first and the result second, and keep the result in the same paragraph as the action.
rules.good: Click Run. The query results appear after the query runs.

rules.heading: Steps with results or justifications
rules.text: Consider whether you can avoid repetitiveness and overwhelming the reader with too much bolding of UI elements when stating results.
rules.bad: Click Enter. The New file dialog appears. In the New file dialog, click Next.
rules.good: Click Enter. In the New file dialog that appears, click Next.

rules.heading: Steps with results or justifications
rules.text: When a step includes a justification for why the step is important, state the action first and the justification second.
rules.good: Store the private key in a secure location. You need it later.

rules.heading: Write prescriptive documentation
rules.text: Recommend a way to achieve tasks and tell the reader what to do instead of giving them a list of options to choose from; when a task involves multiple approaches or products, recommend a path.
rules.why: Prescriptive documentation tells readers what to do.

rules.heading: Write prescriptive documentation
rules.text: State a clear, specific purpose for the document, and write headings and content with that purpose in mind.

rules.heading: Write prescriptive documentation
rules.text: Make example scenarios and procedures reflect the use cases that are most likely relevant to the readers.

rules.heading: Write prescriptive documentation
rules.text: Provide sample commands and arguments that accomplish the task for the most common use case.

rules.heading: Word choice for recommendations and requirements
rules.text: To indicate required or optional user actions or the outcomes of a process, select an appropriate auxiliary verb such as must, can, or might, and generally avoid the word should.
rules.bad: The Classroom Share Button should conform to our min-max size guidelines and related color and button templates.
rules.good: Ensure that the Classroom Share Button conforms to our min-max size guidelines and related color/button templates.
rules.why: Should leaves readers unsure whether an action is optional.

rules.heading: Word choice for recommendations and requirements
rules.text: Determine whether an action is required versus optional, an outcome is expected versus possible, or a state is actual versus recommended.

rules.heading: Word choice for recommendations and requirements
rules.text: If an action is required, use must, or rephrase the sentence so that it's a clear imperative instruction such as "Do the following before you continue."
rules.bad: Whether it's a brand new project or an existing one, here's what you should do.
rules.good: Whether it's a brand new project or an existing one, perform the following steps.

rules.heading: Word choice for recommendations and requirements
rules.text: If an action is recommended, use "We recommend" or "Google recommends"; use should only if the recommended action is generally recognized, such as "You should use a strong password."

rules.heading: Word choice for recommendations and requirements
rules.text: If an action is optional, use can, as in "You can also use approach B to solve the same problem."
rules.good: You can also use approach B to solve the same problem.

rules.heading: Word choice for recommendations and requirements
rules.text: If an outcome is expected, describe the outcome in terms of what is expected, as in "The process returns 10 items."
rules.good: The process returns 10 items.

rules.heading: Word choice for recommendations and requirements
rules.text: If an outcome is possible, use might or can, as in "The process can take about 30 minutes."
rules.good: The process can take about 30 minutes.

rules.heading: Word choice for recommendations and requirements
rules.text: When you describe the state of something, such as the value of a variable, avoid writing "The value should be true"; instead clarify whether you mean "You must set the value to true," "The server sets the value to true," or "If the value is false, follow these steps to change it to true."
rules.bad: The column of the data table that the filter should operate on.
rules.good: The column of the data table that the filter operates on.

rules.heading: Ellipses
rules.text: In general, don't use ellipses.

rules.heading: Ellipses as suspension points
rules.text: Don't use ellipses as suspension points to indicate hesitation.
rules.bad: The answer is ... wait for it ... that you shouldn't do this.

rules.heading: Ellipses in a user interface
rules.text: When ellipses appear in a user interface, exclude them from the documentation describing the user interface unless their omission could cause confusion; for example, document a button labeled Save ... as click Save.

rules.heading: Ellipses in text
rules.text: Don't use ellipses in your written documentation; omit any unnecessary information and include all necessary information.

rules.heading: Ellipses in text
rules.text: In quoted text, use ellipses only to replace a portion of the quoted text, not at the beginning of the text.
rules.bad: My high school English teacher made me learn that Shakespeare quote about all the world being a stage and " ... all the men and women merely players."

rules.heading: Ellipses in text
rules.text: In quoted text, use ellipses only to replace a portion of the quoted text, not at the end of the text.
rules.bad: My high school English teacher made me learn that Shakespeare quote: "All the world's a stage, And all the men and women merely players ...."

rules.heading: Ellipses in text
rules.text: When the material that you're omitting contains one or more sentence boundaries, use four dots instead of three.
rules.good: My high school English teacher made me learn that Shakespeare quote: "All the world's a stage, .... And one man in his time plays many parts."
rules.why: The final ellipsis point is, in fact, a period.

rules.heading: Punctuation and spacing of ellipses
rules.text: Insert one space before and after the ellipsis unless a punctuation mark immediately follows the ellipsis.
rules.bad: You don't need to understand all the other Python code in there...we'll explain it all in class.
rules.good: You don't need to understand all the other Python code in there ... we'll explain it all in class.

rules.heading: Punctuation and spacing of ellipses
rules.text: When a punctuation mark immediately follows the ellipsis, don't insert a space after the ellipsis.
rules.good: You don't need to understand all the other Python code in there ...; we'll explain it all in class.

rules.heading: Punctuation and spacing of ellipses
rules.text: Instead of the ellipsis character, use three periods in a row.
rules.example: Click Save… to continue.

rules.heading: Punctuation and spacing of ellipses
rules.text: Keep all three ellipsis points together.
rules.example: The answer is . . . unclear.

rules.heading: Punctuation and spacing of ellipses
rules.text: Insert one space before and after the ellipsis.
rules.example: You don't need to understand all the other Python code in there...we'll explain it all in class.

rules.heading: Express times
rules.text: Use the 12-hour clock, except if required to use a 24-hour time, such as when documenting features that use 24-hour time.

rules.heading: Express times
rules.text: If the UI, a command, or a code sample uses the 24-hour format, use that format throughout the page for consistency.
rules.why: Consistency within the page.

rules.heading: Express times
rules.text: Use exact times when possible, but noon and midnight are OK.

rules.heading: Express times
rules.text: Use hyphens in time ranges, and don't add spaces before or after the hyphens.
rules.good: 5-10 minutes ago

rules.heading: Express times
rules.text: Capitalize AM and PM, and leave one space between it and the time.

rules.heading: Express times
rules.text: Remove the minutes from round hours.
rules.good: 3 PM

rules.heading: Express times
rules.text: Use hyphens in time ranges, and don't add spaces before or after the hyphens.
rules.example: Wait 5 - 10 minutes before you retry.

rules.heading: Express times
rules.text: Capitalize AM and PM.
rules.example: The backup runs at 3:45 pm.

rules.heading: Express times
rules.text: Leave one space between AM or PM and the time.
rules.example: The backup runs at 3:45PM.

rules.heading: Express times
rules.text: Remove the minutes from round hours.
rules.example: The job runs at 3:00 PM.

rules.heading: Express time zones
rules.text: Avoid using time zones unless absolutely necessary, such as when describing real events at real times.

rules.heading: Express time zones
rules.text: Let the reader know if the time is local to their time.
rules.good: 10 AM your local time

rules.heading: Express time zones
rules.text: If a time zone is necessary, use the timestamp format as seen in the user interface (if available).

rules.heading: Express time zones
rules.text: If using a specific time zone, spell out the region and include the UTC offset as a parenthetical.
rules.good: US and Canadian Pacific Standard Time (UTC-8)

rules.heading: Express time zones
rules.text: Don't abbreviate the name of the time zone.
rules.good: US and Canadian Pacific Daylight Time (UTC-7)

rules.heading: Express time zones
rules.text: In the rare event where the time of an event doesn't change for daylight saving time, use the specific time zone, without reference to UTC.

rules.heading: Express time zones
rules.text: Don't abbreviate the name of the time zone.
rules.example: Maintenance starts at 10 AM PST.

rules.heading: Express dates
rules.text: In general, spell out the names of months and days of the week in full.
rules.good: January 19, 2017

rules.heading: Express dates
rules.text: Give the full four-digit year, not a two-digit abbreviation.
rules.good: January 19, 2017

rules.heading: Express dates
rules.text: If including the day of the week, add it before the month as follows: DAY_OF_WEEK, MONTH DAY, YEAR.
rules.good: Tuesday, April 27, 2021

rules.heading: Partial dates and abbreviations
rules.text: When giving only the month and year, don't use a comma.
rules.good: She was hired in January 2017.

rules.heading: Partial dates and abbreviations
rules.text: In most cases, don't abbreviate the day of the week or the month; when conserving space, such as in a heading or table, it's okay to abbreviate them to their three-letter abbreviations.
rules.good: Mon, Sep 3, 2018

rules.heading: Partial dates and abbreviations
rules.text: When you abbreviate a month or day of the week, capitalize the first letter and do not add a period at the end of the abbreviation.
rules.good: Mon, Sep 3, 2018

rules.heading: Partial dates and abbreviations
rules.text: If you abbreviate, do so for the entire date; don't mix written-out forms with abbreviated forms in the same date.
rules.bad: Mon, September 3, 2018
rules.good: Mon, Sep 3, 2018

rules.heading: Partial dates and abbreviations
rules.text: Be consistent in where you apply abbreviations throughout your documentation; for example, if you choose to abbreviate in table cells, do so in all table cells.

rules.heading: Partial dates and abbreviations
rules.text: When giving only the month and year, don't use a comma.
rules.example: She was hired in January, 2017.

rules.heading: Partial dates and abbreviations
rules.text: Do not add a period at the end of a month or day-of-week abbreviation.
rules.example: Mon., Sep. 3, 2018

rules.heading: Partial dates and abbreviations
rules.text: Don't mix written-out forms with abbreviated forms in the same date.
rules.example: Mon, September 3, 2018

rules.heading: Dates in the middle of a sentence
rules.text: When a MONTH DAY, YEAR date appears in the middle of a sentence, add a comma after the year.
rules.good: The January 19, 2017, release of ...

rules.heading: Dates in the middle of a sentence
rules.text: If the date in the middle of the sentence consists of the month and year only, don't use a comma.
rules.good: The January 2017 release of ...

rules.heading: Dates in the middle of a sentence
rules.text: When a MONTH DAY, YEAR date appears in the middle of a sentence, add a comma after the year.
rules.example: The January 19, 2017 release of the API added new methods.

rules.heading: Why we prefer dates written out
rules.text: Use words to express dates; don't express months as numbers unless you don't have the option.
rules.good: February 12, 2017
rules.why: Numeric date order differs by region.

rules.heading: Why we prefer dates written out
rules.text: Don't express dates in numbers only with slashes, periods, or day-first or month-first hyphens.
rules.why: Numeric date order differs by region.
rules.example: The release shipped on 12/02/2017.

rules.heading: Numeric-only date format
rules.text: If you must express a date in numerical date format, use the format YYYY-MM-DD, and separate the elements by using hyphens.
rules.why: Conforms to ISO 8601.

rules.heading: Numeric-only date format
rules.text: If you have a choice of what date to write (such as in a fictional example), choose a calendar day greater than 12 to differentiate it from the month.

rules.heading: Express dates and times together
rules.text: If you must express a date and a time together, mention the date first and then the time.
rules.good: May 4, 2009, at 6 PM

rules.heading: Express divisions of the year
rules.text: Avoid referring to seasons; instead, use the month, quarter, or temperature (if relevant).
rules.bad: Changes are released in the Fall of each year.
rules.good: Changes are released in October of each year.
rules.why: Seasons differ between hemispheres.

rules.heading: Express divisions of the year
rules.text: Avoid referring to seasons; instead, use the month, quarter, or temperature (if relevant).
rules.why: Seasons differ between hemispheres.
rules.example: Changes are released in the Fall of each year.

rules.heading: Pronouns
rules.text: Ensure that a pronoun clearly refers to its antecedent (the noun that it's replacing).
rules.why: Unclear references confuse readers.

rules.heading: Ambiguous pronoun references
rules.text: Avoid vague and confusing references between a pronoun and its antecedent; repeat the noun when the pronoun could refer to more than one thing.
rules.bad: If you type text in the field, it doesn't change.
rules.good: If you type text in the field, the text doesn't change.
rules.why: Ambiguous pronouns make the meaning unclear.
rules.example: The name of the function to execute in the given script. It does not include parentheses or parameters.

rules.heading: Ambiguous pronoun references
rules.text: In many cases, follow a demonstrative pronoun (like this and these) with a noun.
rules.bad: Set this to true.
rules.good: Set this value to true.
rules.why: A following noun clarifies what this or these means.
rules.example: These are your best options.

rules.heading: Gender-neutral pronouns
rules.text: Don't use gender-specific pronouns unless the person you're referring to is actually that gender.

rules.heading: Gender-neutral pronouns
rules.text: Don't use he, him, his, she, or her as gender-neutral pronouns; instead, use the singular they.

rules.heading: Gender-neutral pronouns
rules.text: Don't use he/she or (s)he or other such punctuational approaches; use the singular they.
rules.why: Use the singular they instead.
rules.example: Each user must confirm that he/she agrees to the terms.

rules.heading: Optional pronouns
rules.text: To avoid ambiguity and clarify meaning in sentences, use optional pronouns such as that and which.
rules.bad: Right-click the link you want to open.
rules.good: Right-click the link that you want to open.
rules.why: Optional pronouns avoid ambiguity and clarify meaning.
rules.example: You can use other option parameters, described in the following section.

rules.heading: Personal pronouns
rules.text: Avoid first-person pronouns (I, we, us, our, and ours) except in the questions in FAQs, in a document whose author makes comments in the first person, or when using we to refer to your organization after using your organization's name.
rules.example: Example Pet Store recommends that you feed your aardvark Standardized Aardvark Treats. We cannot guarantee the happiness of your aardvark otherwise.

rules.heading: Personal pronouns
rules.text: Use the second-person pronoun (you) whenever possible.

rules.heading: Relative pronouns
rules.text: That and which don't mean exactly the same thing, so don't substitute one for the other.
rules.why: They introduce different kinds of clauses.

rules.heading: Relative pronouns
rules.text: Use that to introduce a restrictive clause, and don't precede it with a comma.
rules.good: The echidna that has a long snout is furry.

rules.heading: Relative pronouns
rules.text: Use which to introduce a nonrestrictive clause, and precede it with a comma.
rules.good: The echidna, which has a long snout, is furry.

rules.heading: Relative pronouns
rules.text: When you're referring to a person, you can use who instead of that; if you're not sure which pronoun is appropriate in your context, it's generally OK to use that.

rules.heading: Relative pronouns
rules.text: You can use whose, the possessive form of both who and which, to refer to people, animals, and things.
rules.good: Examine the variables whose values are set at compile time.

rules.heading: Sentence structure
rules.text: If you want to tell the reader to do something, mention the circumstance, conditions, or goal before you provide the instruction.
rules.bad: Click Delete if you want to delete the entire document.
rules.good: To delete the entire document, click Delete.
rules.why: Lets the reader skip the instruction if it doesn't apply.

rules.heading: Third-party content
rules.text: Don't copy content (text, images, code, logos, or speech) from another source; instead, paraphrase and link to their content.
rules.bad: Recovery Point Objective (RPO): "RPO is the maximum targeted period in which data (transactions) might be lost from an IT service due to a major incident" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disaster_recovery#Recovery_Point_Objective).
rules.good: A recovery point objective (RPO), which is the maximum acceptable length of time during which data might be lost from your app due to a major incident.
rules.why: Copying might violate copyright.

rules.heading: Avoid third-party content
rules.text: Unless you are sure that your company owns the assets, avoid copying from third-party sources, such as documentation, websites, books, blogs, videos, images, and podcasts.
rules.why: Copying might violate copyright.

rules.heading: Avoid third-party content
rules.text: Avoid copying from reference sources such as dictionaries, encyclopedias, and Wikipedia.
rules.why: Copying might violate copyright.

rules.heading: Avoid third-party content
rules.text: Don't assume that you can reuse open source product documentation freely; when in doubt, don't use their content.
rules.why: OSS licenses range from no reuse to complete freedom.

rules.heading: Avoid third-party content
rules.text: Don't assume that you can reuse GitHub content freely; when in doubt, don't use their content.
rules.why: GitHub users adopt different licenses for their content.

rules.heading: Verbs in reference documents
rules.text: When you're writing reference documentation for a method, phrase the main method description in terms of what the method does (gets, lists, creates, searches), rather than what the developer would use it to do (get, list, create, search).
rules.bad: tasks.insert: Create a new task on the specified task list.
rules.good: tasks.insert: Creates a new task on the specified task list.
rules.why: The initial verb describes what the method does.

rules.heading: Capitalize product names
rules.text: When you refer to a Google product, use title case except when you're matching a UI label.
rules.why: Google product names are in title case.

rules.heading: Capitalize product names
rules.text: Follow the official capitalization for the names of brands, companies, software, products, services, features, and terms defined by companies and open source communities.
rules.good: The Cloud Scheduler job publishes a message to a Pub/Sub topic at one-minute intervals.

rules.heading: Capitalize product names
rules.text: If an official name begins with a lowercase letter, then put it in lowercase even at the start of a sentence.

rules.heading: Capitalize product names
rules.text: If possible, revise the sentence to avoid putting a lowercase product name at the start.
rules.bad: macOS can run the app.
rules.good: You can use macOS to run the app.

rules.heading: Feature names
rules.text: When you write about a feature, don't capitalize it unless the name is officially capitalized; if you're unsure, follow the precedent that's set by other documents that describe the feature.
rules.why: In general, feature names are lowercase.

rules.heading: Feature names
rules.text: Match the capitalization of a UI label if you're referring to one.

rules.heading: Shorten Google product names
rules.text: Use the full trademarked product name; don't abbreviate product names, except in cases where you're matching a UI label.

rules.heading: Shorten Google product names
rules.text: When you match an abbreviated UI label, make it clear that you're referring to the Google product and not some other thing with a similar name.

rules.heading: Shorten Google product names
rules.text: Consider whether you need to refer to a product name throughout a document, or if you can use a more general term.

rules.heading: Articles before product names
rules.text: Don't use the before a product name unless you're using the name to modify something else.
rules.bad: Using the Cloud Datastore with Cloud Dataproc
rules.good: Using Cloud Datastore with Cloud Dataproc

rules.heading: Articles before product names
rules.text: Do use the before tool and API names.
rules.good: The Transcoder API

rules.heading: Articles before product names
rules.text: If you use a product name as a modifier with an indefinite article (a or an), pay close attention to which article precedes the product name.
rules.good: An Anthos Service Mesh environment

rules.heading: Use "service" to refer to multiple products
rules.text: It's OK to refer to Google products as services, but if the term services leads to ambiguity, use the product names.

rules.heading: Don't use product names as verbs
rules.text: Don't use product names or feature names as verbs.

rules.heading: Introductory phrase preceding colon
rules.text: When a colon introduces a list, make sure the text that precedes the colon can stand alone as a complete sentence.
rules.bad: The fields are:
rules.good: The fields are defined as follows:

rules.heading: Colons within sentences
rules.text: In general, put the first word in the text that follows a colon in lowercase.
rules.good: When you add or update content to an existing project, remember to take these steps: review the style guide, use checklists, enlist a fellow writer or an editor to copyedit your work, and request a developmental edit if you feel that it's warranted.
rules.why: Exceptions are covered in Capitalization and colons.
rules.example: Tone: concise, conversational, friendly, respectful

rules.heading: Use example phone numbers
rules.text: To show an example phone number, use a US number in the range 800‑555‑0100 through 800‑555‑0199.
rules.why: That range is reserved for use in examples and fiction.

rules.heading: Use example phone numbers
rules.text: Never use a real phone number in examples.
rules.why: Real numbers in examples reach real people.

rules.heading: Format phone numbers in HTML or Markdown
rules.text: To ensure that a phone number is displayed on the same line, use a nonbreaking hyphen (‑) where appropriate in HTML or Markdown.
rules.why: Keeps the phone number on one line.

rules.heading: Format phone numbers in HTML or Markdown
rules.text: Use a nonbreaking hyphen (‑), not a regular hyphen, in phone numbers.
rules.why: Keeps the phone number on one line.
rules.example: Call 800-555-0123 for support.

rules.heading: Format North American phone numbers
rules.text: To format a real phone number in the US, Canada, and other NANP countries, use a nonbreaking hyphen to separate the area code, three-digit exchange code, and four-digit number.

rules.heading: Format North American phone numbers
rules.text: Separate the area code with a nonbreaking hyphen, not parentheses.
rules.example: Call (415) 555-0132 for help.

rules.heading: Format international phone numbers
rules.text: To format a real phone number in non-NANP countries, include the country and area codes.

rules.heading: Format international phone numbers
rules.text: Insert a plus sign immediately before the country code (no space); the plus sign stands in for the exit code.
rules.why: Each country has a different exit code.

rules.heading: Format phone numbers that include an extension
rules.text: To specify a phone extension, follow the phone number with the word extension, and then specify the extension number.

rules.heading: Format phone numbers that include an extension
rules.text: Spell out the word extension after a phone number; don't abbreviate it.

rules.heading: Capitalization
rules.text: Follow the standard capitalization rules for American English.

rules.heading: Capitalization
rules.text: Don't use unnecessary capitalization; before you capitalize a word, think about why (and whether) it should be capitalized.

rules.heading: Capitalization
rules.text: Don't rely on a difference in capitalization to convey meaning.
rules.why: Casual or new readers likely miss the distinction.

rules.heading: Capitalization
rules.text: Don't use all-uppercase, except in official names, in abbreviations that are always written in all-caps, or when referring to code that uses all-caps.

rules.heading: Capitalization
rules.text: Don't use camel case, except in official names or when referring to code that uses camel case.

rules.heading: Capitalization in titles and headings
rules.text: In document titles and headings, use sentence case: capitalize only the first word in the title, the first word in a subheading after a colon, and any proper nouns or other terms that are always capitalized a certain way.

rules.heading: Capitalization in titles and headings
rules.text: Don't put a period at the end of a title or heading.

rules.heading: Capitalization in references to titles and headings
rules.text: In references to any title or heading from a document that follows this guide, use sentence case even if the title or heading itself uses title case.
rules.why: The reference will match once the heading is updated.

rules.heading: Capitalization in references to titles and headings
rules.text: When you reference the title of any work or source that doesn't follow this guide, retain the original capitalization.

rules.heading: Capitalization and colons
rules.text: Use a lowercase letter to begin the first word of the text immediately following a colon, unless the text is a proper noun, a heading, a quotation, or text that follows a label such as Caution or Note.

rules.heading: Capitalization and figures
rules.text: Use sentence case for captions.

rules.heading: Capitalization and figures
rules.text: Use sentence case for labels, callouts, and other text in images and diagrams.

rules.heading: Capitalization in glossaries and indexes
rules.text: Use lowercase for glossary and index terms unless the term is a proper noun or has another reason to require capitalization.

rules.heading: Capitalization in glossaries and indexes
rules.text: Use sentence case for glossary definitions.

rules.heading: Capitalization and hyphenated words
rules.text: When a hyphenated word is the first word in a sentence or in a heading, capitalize only the first element in the word, unless a subsequent element is a proper noun or proper adjective.

rules.heading: Capitalization in lists
rules.text: Use sentence case for items in all types of lists.

rules.heading: Capitalization for tables in text
rules.text: Use sentence case for all the elements in a table: contents, headings, labels, and captions.

rules.heading: Special capitalization style names
rules.text: Don't use a casing style name, such as camel case or snake case, to describe a casing style; instead, explain what the requirements are and provide an example.
rules.good: Enter the value for the attribute field in the format where there are no spaces between words and the first letter of each word is capitalized—for example, AssertionAccount.
rules.why: These names don't localize well and aren't standardized.

rules.heading: Special capitalization style names
rules.why: Casing style names don't localize well; explain and give example.
rules.example: Enter the attribute value in camel case.

rules.heading: Headings and titles
rules.text: Use sentence case for headings and titles.

rules.heading: Headings and titles
rules.text: Use descriptive headings and titles.
rules.why: They help a reader navigate their browser and the page.

rules.heading: Headings and titles
rules.text: Make headings and titles unique.
rules.why: Unique headings make it easier to jump between sections.

rules.heading: Heading and title text
rules.text: Write document titles based on the primary purpose of the document.

rules.heading: Heading and title text
rules.text: Write section headings based on the type of content that's in the section.

rules.heading: Heading and title text
rules.text: For a task-based heading, start with a bare infinitive.
rules.bad: Creating an instance
rules.good: Create an instance

rules.heading: Heading and title text
rules.text: For a conceptual or non-task-based heading, use a noun phrase that doesn't start with an -ing verb.
rules.bad: Migrating to Google Cloud
rules.good: Migration to Google Cloud

rules.heading: Heading and title text
rules.text: If a section is not required for all users or scenarios, use the Optional: prefix in the heading.
rules.bad: Customize your alias (optional)
rules.good: Optional: Customize your alias
rules.why: Signals the section applies only to a specific use case.

rules.heading: Title phrasing
rules.text: Use a unique level-1 heading (h1) for each page in a set of documents.

rules.heading: Title phrasing
rules.text: Only use a level-1 heading once on a page.

rules.heading: Title phrasing
rules.text: Avoid repeating the exact page title in a heading on the page.
rules.good: Create and start VM instances, with section headings Create a VM and Start a VM

rules.heading: Mixed heading styles
rules.text: If a single document includes both task-based and conceptual sections, use the appropriate phrasing for each section's heading.
rules.good:
Log serving requests by using AI Platform Prediction

ML model monitoring overview

Configure notebook settings
rules.why: It's OK to mix task-based and conceptual heading styles.

rules.heading: Use of -ing verb forms
rules.text: When possible, avoid using -ing verb forms as the first word in any heading or title.
rules.bad: Transferring data sets
rules.good: Transfer data sets
rules.why: Inconsistently translated and increases character count.

rules.heading: Use of -ing verb forms
rules.text: It's OK to use a gerund such as Billing or Pricing when there isn't a better alternative.
rules.good: Billing

rules.heading: Use of -ing verb forms
rules.text: It's OK to use an -ing verb form later in a heading or title.
rules.good: Introduction to BigQuery monitoring

rules.heading: Heading and title format
rules.text: Apply the guidance for standard text, such as contractions and articles, to headings.

rules.heading: Syntax and capitalization
rules.text: Keep punctuation in headings simple; if a heading needs complicated punctuation, consider rewriting it.
rules.why: Punctuation can signal the heading is too complicated.

rules.heading: Syntax and capitalization
rules.text: Only use an abbreviation of a word in a page title or heading if it's the more commonly known version of the word.

rules.heading: Syntax and capitalization
rules.text: If you use an abbreviation in a heading, define the abbreviation in the first instance of the word in a paragraph.

rules.heading: Syntax and capitalization
rules.text: For SEO, use the more prominent version of a term in headings.

rules.heading: Formatting and code
rules.text: Don't use numbers in headings to indicate a sequence of sections; rely on heading hierarchy and order instead.

rules.heading: Formatting and code
rules.text: Avoid code items in headings.

rules.heading: Formatting and code
rules.text: If you must mention a code item in a heading, add a descriptive noun to the item in code font.

rules.heading: Formatting and code
rules.text: Don't put links in headings.
rules.why: A link can be confused with heading styling.

rules.heading: Hierarchy and structure
rules.text: Don't use heading tags to change visual formatting; use CSS rather than a heading level that doesn't fit the hierarchy.

rules.heading: Hierarchy and structure
rules.text: Don't make up your own formatting for headings.

rules.heading: Hierarchy and structure
rules.text: Use heading tags to structure your content hierarchically.

rules.heading: Hierarchy and structure
rules.text: Don't skip levels of the heading hierarchy; for example, put an h3 tag only under an h2 tag.
rules.bad:
Transfer data sets

This document provides a high-level overview of ways to transfer your data to Google Cloud.

Estimate costs
rules.good:
Transfer data sets

This document provides a high-level overview of ways to transfer your data to Google Cloud.

Estimate costs

rules.heading: Hierarchy and structure
rules.text: Don't use empty headings; make sure headings are followed by content.
rules.bad:
Migrate VMs to Compute Engine

Design the migration
rules.good:
Migrate VMs to Compute Engine

Migration is not just a single step. The following sections describe the recommended steps.

Design the migration

rules.heading: Refer to a group of sections
rules.text: If you introduce a group of related H3 or lower sections within a larger H2 section, use the phrase the following sections.
rules.good: The following sections describe the views in the data preparation editor.

rules.heading: Refer to a group of sections
rules.text: Don't refer to a group of subsections using the phrases this section or these sections.
rules.why: Those phrases are ambiguous.

rules.heading: New terms
rules.text: When you introduce a new term that you're defining immediately, use italics on the first mention of the term; don't use bold or quotation marks.
rules.good: A Clos network is a kind of multistage circuit switching network.
rules.why: Italics mark a newly defined term consistently.

rules.heading: Words as words
rules.text: When you refer to a word, phrase, or letter in reference to the word, phrase, or letter itself (words as words), use italics; don't use bold or quotation marks.
rules.good: Don't use & (ampersand) as a conjunction. Use the word and instead.
rules.why: Italics distinguish words referred to as words.

rules.heading: Serial commas
rules.text: In a series of three or more items, use a comma before the final and or or.
rules.bad: Locations are divided into zones, regions and multi-regions.
rules.good: Locations are divided into zones, regions, and multi-regions.
rules.why: Avoids potentially changing the meaning of the sentence.

rules.heading: Commas after introductory words and phrases
rules.text: In general, place a comma after an introductory word or phrase.
rules.good: Finally, only groups that contain parameters appear in this list.

rules.heading: Commas separating two independent clauses
rules.text: When a coordinating conjunction (and, but, or, nor, for, so, or yet) separates two independent clauses, insert a comma after the first clause (before the conjunction).
rules.bad: The libraries make feed creation easier and they ensure that only valid feeds are produced.
rules.good: The libraries make feed creation easier, and they ensure that only valid feeds are produced.

rules.heading: Commas separating two independent clauses
rules.text: Don't insert a comma before the coordinating conjunction when both independent clauses are very short.
rules.bad: Type your ID, and click OK.
rules.good: Type your ID and click OK.

rules.heading: Commas separating independent from dependent clauses
rules.text: When an independent clause and a dependent clause are separated by a coordinating conjunction, insert a comma only if the sentence could be misunderstood without one.
rules.bad: Direct-access flags are plain variables, and can be read directly.
rules.good: Direct-access flags are plain variables and can be read directly.

rules.heading: Commas separating independent from dependent clauses
rules.text: When an independent clause and a dependent clause are separated by a coordinating conjunction, insert a comma if the sentence could be misunderstood without one.
rules.bad: The manager acknowledged the last team member who entered the room and started the meeting.
rules.good: The manager acknowledged the last team member who entered the room, and started the meeting.

rules.heading: Set off other kinds of clauses
rules.text: In general, put a comma before the word which at the start of a nonrestrictive clause.
rules.bad: Name of the group which has a maximum length of 200 characters.
rules.good: Name of the group, which has a maximum length of 200 characters.

rules.heading: Set off other kinds of clauses
rules.text: In general, put a semicolon or a period or a dash before a conjunctive adverb, such as otherwise, however, or therefore, and put a comma after the conjunctive adverb.
rules.bad: The variable must have a value otherwise the server returns an error.
rules.good: The variable must have a value; otherwise, the server returns an error.

rules.heading: Set off other kinds of clauses
rules.text: In general, don't use a comma before the causal conjunction because unless it starts a nonrestrictive clause.
rules.bad: You can use the same key name in multiple backend services and backend buckets because each set of keys is independent of the others.
rules.good: You can use the same key name in multiple backend services and backend buckets, because each set of keys is independent of the others.

rules.heading: Set off other kinds of clauses
rules.text: Put a comma after a conjunctive adverb that follows a semicolon.
rules.bad: The variable must have a value; otherwise the server returns an error.
rules.good: The variable must have a value; otherwise, the server returns an error.
rules.example: The variable must have a value; otherwise the server returns an error.

not_applicable.reason: Page introduction; content repeated in other units

rules.heading: Timeless documentation
rules.text: Document the current version of a product or feature.
rules.why: Time-anchored words make documentation inaccurate or outdated.

rules.heading: Timeless documentation
rules.text: Focus on how the product works right now, not on how it has changed from previous versions or how it might change in the future.
rules.why: Avoids assuming the reader knows earlier versions.

rules.heading: Timeless documentation
rules.text: Avoid time-based words in product documentation that refers to a product's features and capabilities; they're okay only in procedural or time-stamped content such as press releases, blog posts, or release notes.
rules.good: The VM goes offline soon after you send the shutdown command.
rules.why: Such words can become outdated or incorrect.

rules.heading: Words and phrases to avoid
rules.text: When describing product or feature capabilities, don't use words and phrases that make promises or project plans and strategies, such as at present, as of this writing, or eventually.
rules.why: They can prematurely disclose plans or imply change.

rules.heading: Words and phrases to avoid
rules.text: Don't use words and phrases that are implied by the existence of the documentation itself, such as currently and as of this writing.
rules.bad: The following command-line options aren't currently supported:
rules.good: The following command-line options aren't supported:
rules.why: Documentation is assumed current unless a release is specified.

rules.heading: Words and phrases to avoid
rules.text: Avoid words and phrases that become outdated soon after publication, such as soon and latest.
rules.why: They quickly become irrelevant.

rules.heading: Words and phrases to avoid
rules.text: If you must use words like new, give a reference point such as a date or version release number.
rules.good: The January 14, 2021 release of BigQuery includes a new resource panel.
rules.why: Avoids assuming prior knowledge of a product or feature.

rules.heading: Words and phrases to avoid
rules.text: When describing product or feature capabilities in product and reference documentation, avoid existing.
rules.why: Assumes prior knowledge of the product.

rules.heading: Words and phrases to avoid
rules.text: When describing product or feature capabilities in product and reference documentation, avoid future.
rules.why: Can prematurely disclose plans for a product.

rules.heading: Words and phrases to avoid
rules.text: When describing product or feature capabilities in product and reference documentation, avoid latest.
rules.why: Becomes outdated soon after publication.

rules.heading: Words and phrases to avoid
rules.text: When describing product or feature capabilities in product and reference documentation, avoid new and newer.
rules.bad: These new subcommands let you interact with HTTP load balancing.
rules.good: These subcommands let you interact with HTTP load balancing.
rules.why: Assumes prior knowledge and becomes outdated.

rules.heading: Words and phrases to avoid
rules.text: When describing product or feature capabilities in product and reference documentation, avoid now.
rules.bad: The emulator now supports the following filters:
rules.good: The emulator supports the following filters:
rules.why: Anchors documentation to a point in time.

rules.heading: Words and phrases to avoid
rules.text: When describing product or feature capabilities in product and reference documentation, avoid old and older.
rules.why: Assumes prior knowledge of earlier versions.

rules.heading: Words and phrases to avoid
rules.text: When describing product or feature capabilities in product and reference documentation, avoid soon.
rules.why: Becomes outdated soon after publication.

rules.heading: Words and phrases to avoid
rules.text: When describing product or feature capabilities, avoid as of this writing.
rules.why: Implied by the documentation itself.
rules.example: The API, as of this writing, supports JSON output.

rules.heading: Words and phrases to avoid
rules.text: When describing product or feature capabilities, avoid currently.
rules.why: Implied by the documentation itself.
rules.example: The following command-line options aren't currently supported:

rules.heading: Words and phrases to avoid
rules.text: When describing product or feature capabilities, avoid does not yet.
rules.why: Implies the product might change.
rules.example: The emulator does not yet support filters.

rules.heading: Words and phrases to avoid
rules.text: When describing product or feature capabilities, avoid eventually.
rules.why: Can prematurely disclose plans for a product.
rules.example: The service will eventually support more regions.

rules.heading: Words and phrases to avoid
rules.text: When describing product or feature capabilities, avoid in the future.
rules.why: Can prematurely disclose plans for a product.
rules.example: More formats will be supported in the future.

rules.heading: Words and phrases to avoid
rules.text: When describing product or feature capabilities, avoid presently and at present.
rules.why: Implies the product might change.
rules.example: At present, the tool supports only CSV files.

rules.heading: Contractions
rules.text: Use common two-word contractions such as you're, don't, and there's.
rules.why: Documentation uses an informal tone.

rules.heading: Negation contractions
rules.text: Use negation contractions such as isn't, don't, and can't.
rules.why: Scanning readers can miss not; don't is hard to misread.

rules.heading: Negation contractions
rules.text: If you need to emphasize the negative, use text formatting such as is not, but in most cases don't add emphasis to make your point clear.

rules.heading: Contractions to avoid
rules.text: Don't make up nonstandard contractions such as guides're or browser's (where 's means is).

rules.heading: Contractions to avoid
rules.text: Don't use three-word contractions such as mightn't've.

rules.heading: Contractions to avoid
rules.text: Don't make up nonstandard contractions such as guides're.
rules.example: The guides're available online.

rules.heading: Contractions to avoid
rules.text: Don't use three-word contractions such as mightn't've.
rules.example: You mightn't've seen the warning.

rules.heading: Periods and end punctuation
rules.text: End a complete sentence with a period, unless it's a question; lists have exceptions.

rules.heading: Periods with URLs
rules.text: Whenever possible, avoid putting URLs in text.
rules.why: A period after a URL may look like part of it.

rules.heading: Periods with URLs
rules.text: Rewrite the sentence so that the URL isn't at the end of the sentence.
rules.why: A period after a URL may look like part of it.

rules.heading: Periods with URLs
rules.text: Put the URL on a separate line from the text, omitting the final period.

rules.heading: Basic guidelines
rules.text: Follow the indentation guidelines in the relevant code style guide; for most programming languages, this means using spaces instead of tabs and using two spaces for each indentation level.

rules.heading: Basic guidelines
rules.text: Wrap lines in code samples at 80 characters.

rules.heading: Basic guidelines
rules.text: If you expect readers to have a relatively narrow browser window or to print out your document, consider wrapping code at a smaller number of characters for readability.

rules.heading: Basic guidelines
rules.text: Mark code blocks as preformatted text; in HTML, use a pre element.

rules.heading: Basic guidelines

rules.heading: Basic guidelines

rules.heading: Introductory statements

rules.heading: General dos and don'ts
rules.text: Don't use ableist language; avoid bias and harm when discussing disability and accessibility.
rules.why: Ableist language excludes and harms readers.

rules.heading: General dos and don'ts
rules.text: Ensure that readers can reach all parts of the document, including tabs, form-submission buttons, and interactive elements, by using only a keyboard.
rules.why: Some readers can't use a mouse or trackpad.

rules.heading: General dos and don'ts
rules.text: Use a screen reader to test your documentation.
rules.why: Testing finds accessibility issues in your content.

rules.heading: General dos and don'ts
rules.text: In HTML, use semantic tagging; for example, use the em element only to indicate emphasis, not to indicate italics.
rules.why: Screen readers rely on semantic markup.

rules.heading: General dos and don'ts
rules.text: In HTML, prefer native elements over custom styles.

rules.heading: General dos and don'ts
rules.text: Avoid unnecessary font formatting.
rules.why: Screen readers explicitly describe text modifications.

rules.heading: General dos and don'ts
rules.text: If you're documenting a product that includes specialized accessibility features, then explicitly document those features.

rules.heading: General dos and don'ts
rules.text: Don't force line breaks (hard returns) within sentences and paragraphs.
rules.why: Breaks fail in resized windows or enlarged text.

rules.heading: General dos and don'ts
rules.text: Avoid when possible camel case and all caps, and follow capitalization guidelines.
rules.why: Some screen readers read capitals letter by letter.

rules.heading: General dos and don'ts
rules.text: Make sure that the same meaning is conveyed without punctuation marks, and avoid when possible exclamation marks, question marks, and semicolons.
rules.why: Screen readers don't always read punctuation.

rules.heading: General dos and don'ts
rules.text: Don't use & instead of and in headings, text, navigation, or tables of contents; it's OK when referencing UI elements that use &, in space-constrained table headings and diagram labels, or in code.

rules.heading: Ease of reading
rules.text: Break up walls of text to aid in scannability; for example, separate paragraphs, create headings, and use lists.

rules.heading: Ease of reading
rules.text: Use shorter sentences; try to use fewer than 26 words per sentence.

rules.heading: Ease of reading
rules.text: Define acronyms and abbreviations on first usage and if they're used infrequently.

rules.heading: Ease of reading
rules.text: Use parallel writing structures for similar things; for example, start each list in the same format.

rules.heading: Ease of reading
rules.text: Place distinguishing and important information of a paragraph in the first sentence.
rules.why: Aids scannability.

rules.heading: Ease of reading
rules.text: Use clear and direct language; avoid double negatives and exceptions for exceptions.
rules.bad: A missing path won't prevent you from continuing.
rules.good: You can continue without a path.

rules.heading: Ease of reading
rules.text: Left-align text; don't center or full-justify text.
rules.why: Left-aligned text is easier to read.

rules.heading: Headings and titles
rules.text: Use descriptive and unique headings and titles.
rules.why: They help readers navigate the browser and page.

rules.heading: Headings and titles
rules.text: Use a heading hierarchy.

rules.heading: Headings and titles
rules.text: Don't skip levels of the heading hierarchy; for example, put an h3 element only after an h2 element.

rules.heading: Headings and titles
rules.text: To change the visual formatting of a heading, use CSS rather than using a heading level that doesn't fit the hierarchy.

rules.heading: Headings and titles
rules.text: Don't have empty headings or headings with no associated content.

rules.heading: Headings and titles
rules.text: Tag headings using heading elements (h1, h2, and so on).

rules.heading: Headings and titles
rules.text: Use a level-1 heading for the page title or main content heading.

rules.heading: Links
rules.text: Use meaningful link text; links should make sense when read out of context.
rules.why: Screen reader users jump from link to link.

rules.heading: Links
rules.text: Use see to refer to links and cross-references.

rules.heading: Links
rules.text: When a link does anything that the reader might not expect, such as downloading a file, opening in a new tab, or jumping to another section on the same page, explain that behavior when you link.

rules.heading: Links
rules.text: When possible, avoid adjacent links; instead, put a character in between to separate them.

rules.heading: Links
rules.text: Don't use click here or read this document as link text.
rules.why: Screen reader users need to know what a link contains.
rules.example: To download the SDK, click here.

rules.heading: Lists
rules.text: In a procedure, make each instruction a list item.
rules.why: Lists make steps easier to follow.

rules.heading: Images
rules.text: For every image, provide an alt attribute.

rules.heading: Images
rules.text: Use alt text that adequately summarizes the intent of each image.

rules.heading: Images
rules.text: If the image is purely decorative, use empty alt text.

rules.heading: Images
rules.text: Don't present new information in images; always provide an equivalent text explanation with the image.

rules.heading: Images
rules.text: Don't repeat images unless absolutely necessary.

rules.heading: Images
rules.text: Don't use images of text, code samples, or terminal output; use actual text.

rules.heading: Images
rules.text: Use SVG instead of PNG if available.
rules.why: SVGs stay sharp when zoomed.

rules.heading: Videos, recordings, and GIFs
rules.text: Provide captions, transcripts, or descriptions of audio and video content.

rules.heading: Videos, recordings, and GIFs
rules.text: Ensure that captions can be translated into major languages.

rules.heading: Videos, recordings, and GIFs
rules.text: Don't use flickering or flashing elements.
rules.why: They can cause motion sickness or seizures.

rules.heading: Buttons and icons
rules.text: For form-submission buttons, use the native HTML button element.

rules.heading: UI navigation
rules.text: When you use angle brackets (>) to document menu paths, add an aria-label attribute so screen readers interpret the brackets as "and then".
rules.why: Otherwise read as "greater than".

rules.heading: Tables
rules.text: Introduce tables in the text preceding the table.
rules.why: Not all screen readers preannounce tables.

rules.heading: Tables
rules.text: Use table headings for the first column and the first row only.

rules.heading: Tables
rules.text: Use the th element for table headings.

rules.heading: Tables
rules.text: If your tables include both row and column headings, then mark heading cells with the scope attribute.

rules.heading: Tables
rules.text: If your tables have more than one row containing column headings, then use the headers attribute and make sure that the headings have unique IDs.

rules.heading: Tables
rules.text: Avoid when possible tables in the middle of a numbered procedure.

rules.heading: Tables
rules.text: Don't merge cells; don't use colspan or rowspan attributes.

rules.heading: Tables
rules.text: Don't use tables unless it's the best method to present your information.
rules.why: Tables are challenging for screen readers.

rules.heading: Tables
rules.text: Don't present new information in tables through images or symbols alone; always provide a descriptive alt attribute for the image or symbol.

rules.heading: Interactive elements
rules.text: Introduce an interactive element, such as a button that expands and collapses, in the text preceding the element.
rules.good: To see a list of requirements, expand the Requirements section.

rules.heading: Forms
rules.text: Label every input field by using a label element.

rules.heading: Forms
rules.text: Place labels outside of fields.

rules.heading: Forms
rules.text: When you're creating an error message for form validation, clearly state what went wrong and how to fix it.
rules.good: Name is a required field.

rules.heading: Custom CSS and JavaScript
rules.text: Try to use your site's standard styles and standard JavaScript code as much as possible.

rules.heading: Custom CSS and JavaScript
rules.text: Pick colors that respect accessible color contrast ratios (4.5:1 for text).

rules.heading: Custom CSS and JavaScript
rules.text: Avoid when possible using mouseover events; if you do use them, add alternate focus and blur events for keyboard users.

rules.heading: Custom CSS and JavaScript
rules.text: Ensure that any ordering and positioning defined in styles reflects the DOM and the reading order of your page.

rules.heading: Custom CSS and JavaScript
rules.text: Don't use visibility:hidden or display:none.
rules.why: Both styles hide information from screen readers.
rules.example: Optional settings

rules.heading: Document rendering
rules.text: Make sure that your document conveys all the information that you intended when viewed without sound, using only sound, without images or animation, without color, using a keyboard, with screen magnification, and without punctuation.

rules.heading: Document rendering
rules.text: Don't use color, size, location, or other visual cues as the primary way of communicating information.

rules.heading: Document rendering
rules.text: If you're using color, an icon, or outline thickness to convey state, then also provide a secondary cue, such as a change in the text label.

rules.heading: Document rendering
rules.text: Refer to buttons and other elements by their label; for visual elements that have no text, don't describe the element but use its aria-label if possible.
rules.bad: Click the bell icon.
rules.good: Click Notifications.

rules.heading: Document rendering
rules.text: Don't use directional language, such as above, below, or right-hand side, to orient the reader or refer to a position in a document; instead, use earlier, preceding, or following.
rules.bad: In the diagram above, clients run jobs on multi-team or single-team clusters.
rules.good: In the preceding diagram, clients run jobs on multi-team or single-team clusters.
rules.why: Fails for screen readers and right-to-left languages.

rules.heading: Document rendering
rules.text: If a UI element is hard to find, provide a screenshot instead of describing its location.
rules.bad: In the left-side panel, click the button with three lines.
rules.good: Click Menu.

rules.heading: Voice and tone
rules.text: Aim for a voice and tone that's conversational, friendly, and respectful without using slang or being overly colloquial or frivolous.
rules.bad: Dude! This API is totally awesome!
rules.good: This API lets you collect data about what your users like.
rules.why: Sound like a knowledgeable friend, not pedantic or pushy.

rules.heading: Voice and tone
rules.text: Aim for a conversational tone rather than a formal one, without writing exactly the way you speak.
rules.bad: The API documented by this page may enable the acquisition of information pertaining to user preferences.
rules.good: This API lets you collect data about what your users like.
rules.why: Speech is more colloquial and verbose than good documentation.

rules.heading: Voice and tone
rules.text: Don't try to be super-entertaining, but also don't aim for super-dry; the primary purpose is to provide information to someone who may be in a hurry.
rules.why: Readers are looking for information and may be hurried.

rules.heading: Voice and tone
rules.text: As much as possible, avoid culturally specific references, and write simply and consistently.
rules.why: Readers come from many cultures; simple writing translates easier.

rules.heading: Some things to avoid where possible
rules.text: Avoid buzzwords or technical jargon.

rules.heading: Some things to avoid where possible
rules.text: Avoid being too cutesy.

rules.heading: Some things to avoid where possible
rules.text: Avoid figurative language, which includes metaphors and ableist language.

rules.heading: Some things to avoid where possible
rules.text: Avoid placeholder phrases like please note and at this time.
rules.bad: Please note that completion of the task requires the following prerequisite: executing an automated memory management function.
rules.good: To clean up, call the collectGarbage method.

rules.heading: Some things to avoid where possible
rules.text: Avoid choppy or long-winded sentences.

rules.heading: Some things to avoid where possible
rules.text: Avoid starting all sentences with the same phrase (such as You can or To do).

rules.heading: Some things to avoid where possible
rules.text: Avoid current pop-culture references.
rules.bad: Just like a certain pop star, this call gets your telephone number. The easy way to ask for someone's digits!
rules.good: To get the user's phone number, call user.phoneNumber.get.

rules.heading: Some things to avoid where possible
rules.text: In general, avoid exclamation points.
rules.bad: Dude! This API is totally awesome!
rules.good: This API lets you collect data about what your users like.

rules.heading: Some things to avoid where possible
rules.text: Avoid wackiness, zaniness, and goofiness.
rules.bad: Then—BOOM—just garbage-collect, and you're golden.
rules.good: To clean up, call the collectGarbage method.

rules.heading: Some things to avoid where possible
rules.text: Avoid phrasing that denigrates or insults any group of people.

rules.heading: Some things to avoid where possible
rules.text: Avoid phrasing in terms of let's do something.

rules.heading: Some things to avoid where possible
rules.text: Avoid using phrases like simply, It's that simple, It's easy, or quickly in a procedure.

rules.heading: Some things to avoid where possible
rules.text: Avoid internet slang, or other internet abbreviations such as tl;dr or ymmv.

rules.heading: Some things to avoid where possible
rules.text: Avoid placeholder phrases like at this time.
rules.avoid: at this time, At this time
rules.why: Placeholder phrase.
rules.example: This feature isn't available at this time.

rules.heading: Some things to avoid where possible
rules.text: Avoid phrasing in terms of let's do something.
rules.why: Avoid let's phrasing.
rules.example: Let's create a new project.

rules.heading: Some things to avoid where possible
rules.text: Avoid using phrases like simply, It's that simple, or It's easy in a procedure.
rules.avoid: simply, Simply, It's that simple, it's that simple, It's easy, it's easy
rules.why: Avoid in procedures.
rules.example: Simply click Save. It's that simple.

rules.heading: Some things to avoid where possible
