rules.text: Avoid internet abbreviations such as tl;dr or ymmv.
rules.why: Internet abbreviation.
rules.example: tl;dr: the API returns user data.

rules.heading: Some things to avoid where possible
rules.text: In general, avoid exclamation points.
rules.why: Avoid exclamation points in general.
rules.example: This API is totally awesome!

rules.heading: Some techniques and approaches to consider
rules.text: If a sentence is awkward or confusing when spoken, consider whether you can make it more conversational.

rules.heading: Some techniques and approaches to consider
rules.text: Use transitions between sentences, such as Though or This way, to make paragraphs less stilted.
rules.why: Some transitions like However can make paragraphs more stilted.

rules.heading: Some techniques and approaches to consider
rules.text: Make sure you're communicating useful information in a clear and direct way.
rules.why: That's the most important part.

rules.heading: Politeness and use of please
rules.text: Don't use please in a set of instructions.
rules.bad: To view the document, please click View.
rules.good: To view the document, click View.
rules.why: Using please in instructions overdoes the politeness.

rules.heading: Politeness and use of please
rules.text: Don't use please when referring readers to other documents.
rules.bad: For more information, please see [link to other document].
rules.good: For more information, see [link to other document].
rules.why: Overdoes the politeness.

rules.heading: Politeness and use of please
rules.text: Don't use please in instructions.
rules.why: Overdoes the politeness.
rules.example: For more information, please see [link to other document].

rules.heading: Semicolons
rules.text: If possible, avoid using semicolons.
rules.why: Semicolons are preferred only in a few cases.

rules.heading: Semicolons
rules.text: Use a semicolon when joining two closely related independent clauses where a period or a comma is not as effective.
rules.good: You can easily test compatibility by computing the centroid; if it is on the opposite side of the planet, reverse the order of your vertices.

rules.heading: Semicolons
rules.text: Use a semicolon before a conjunctive adverb (like therefore) or a phrase (like that is) that joins two independent clauses.
rules.good: This setup places the head-tracked node below the Main Camera; therefore, only the stereo cameras are affected by the user's head motion.

rules.heading: Semicolons
rules.text: Use semicolons to separate a series of long or complex items that contain their own punctuation.
rules.good: Review your document one more time, checking for the following: present tense and active voice; typos, punctuation, and grammar; and whether you can shorten anything.

rules.heading: Excessive claims
rules.text: Don't make statements about performance or cost that aren't easily verifiable with data that's available to the reader.
rules.bad: Our product is faster than ExampleCorp's product.
rules.good: Our product distributes datasets and computation in memory across a cluster, and therefore it can be faster for this scenario than ExampleCorporation's product. For more information, see Performance comparison.
rules.why: Unverifiable performance or cost claims are excessive claims.

rules.heading: Excessive claims
rules.text: If you make specific performance claims—how fast a product is, how much storage it requires, and so on—reference the source of your information.
rules.bad: Our product is faster than ExampleCorp's product.
rules.good: Our product distributes datasets and computation in memory across a cluster, and therefore it can be faster for this scenario than ExampleCorporation's product. For more information, see Performance comparison.
rules.why: Readers must be able to verify performance claims.

rules.heading: Excessive claims
rules.text: Don't make a statement about security that would be invalidated by a security incident; suggest that a feature "helps with security" or "is designed for security" instead of claiming that a product is secure.
rules.bad: Our security product prevents account takeovers from phishing attacks.
rules.good: Using our security product is part of an overall strategy that helps prevent account takeovers from phishing attacks.
rules.why: A security incident would make the documentation invalid and not credible.

rules.heading: Excessive claims
rules.text: Don't make statements that might be interpreted as subjective or even disparaging, especially about third-party products.
rules.why: Claims about competitors can be wrong or become untrue later.

rules.heading: Excessive claims
rules.text: When you describe products, avoid superlatives like best, simplest, fastest, never, and always.
rules.why: Superlatives about products are excessive claims.

rules.heading: Excessive claims
rules.text: Be careful about words like ensure and guarantee, and use them only when something can truly be ensured or guaranteed.
rules.why: Overpromising is an excessive claim.

rules.heading: Excessive claims
rules.text: Write factually and objectively, limiting what you say to verifiable information that will be true over the lifespan of your documentation, not just what's true today.
rules.why: Claims true today might become untrue in the future.

rules.heading: List or table?
rules.text: Don't use a list to show only one item; if you want to set a single item off from surrounding text, use some other formatting.
rules.why: A single item isn't really a list.

rules.heading: Types of lists
rules.text: Use a numbered list for a set of items where the sequence is significant, such as ordered steps, phases, or priorities.
rules.good: Here's a sequence of steps to follow: 1. Open the box. 2. Remove the bobcat from the box. 3. Feed the bobcat.

rules.heading: Types of lists
rules.text: Label nested sequential lists with lowercase letters or lowercase Roman numerals.
rules.good: Here's a list of things to do after breakfast, in order: 1. Go shopping. a. Buy groceries: Flour, Eggs, Sugar, Butter b. Go to mall: i. Buy dress. ii. Buy shoes. 2. Make cake. 3. Build birthday present out of spare parts. 4. Clean house.

rules.heading: Types of lists
rules.text: Use a bulleted list for a set of items that's not a sequence, such as a set of nonsequential options or examples.
rules.good: Here's a list of things that can go wrong, in no particular order: • Your bicycle might explode. • The sun might go out. • An ant might break its leg and require a tiny splint.

rules.heading: Types of lists
rules.text: In a bulleted list, make sure it's clear whether or not every item is required.

rules.heading: Types of lists
rules.text: Use a description list for a set of terms, each with a description, definition, or explanation, when you want to draw attention to two or more terms (such as a glossary).
rules.good: Here are some descriptions of types of birds: Emu: The best kind of bird. Crow: The other best kind of bird. Peacock: Also the best kind of bird. Phoenix: An even better kind of bird.

rules.heading: Types of lists
rules.text: Use a description list with bulleted run-in headings for a set of introductory terms or phrases, each followed by a description, when you want to highlight and explain several concepts or save space.
rules.good: Here are some descriptions of types of birds: • Emu: the best kind of bird • Crow: the other best kind of bird • Peacock: also the best kind of bird • Phoenix: an even better kind of bird

rules.heading: Multiple paragraph list items
rules.text: To create multiple paragraphs in a list item, use the p element rather than using the br element.

rules.heading: Introductory sentences for lists
rules.text: Introduce a list with the appropriate context; in most cases, precede a list with an introductory sentence.

rules.heading: Introductory sentences for lists
rules.text: End the introductory sentence with a colon if it immediately precedes the list, and usually with a period if there's more material (such as a note paragraph) between the introduction and the list.

rules.heading: Introductory sentences for lists
rules.text: If the list doesn't need any additional context other than the heading that immediately precedes the list, it's OK to not introduce the list with an introductory sentence.
rules.bad: Objectives In the following tutorial, you will complete the following tasks: Create an instance Snapshot an instance Delete an instance
rules.good: Objectives Create an instance Snapshot an instance Delete an instance

rules.heading: Introductory sentences for lists
rules.text: Introduce a list with a complete sentence, not a partial one that's completed by the list items; you can also use "the following" as a noun phrase.
rules.bad: Use the Submit button to: Submit the form. Indicate that you're done. Allow the next person to enter their data.
rules.good: Use the Submit button for any of the following purposes: To submit the form. To indicate that you're done. To allow the next person to enter their data.

rules.heading: Unusual list numbering
rules.text: To present a list in reverse-numerical order, use an ol element with a reversed attribute.

rules.heading: Unusual list numbering
rules.text: In most cases, don't manually number a list item in a numbered list with the value attribute, because if the number of items changes later, you'll have to manually change the value.
rules.why: Manual numbers must be updated when items change.

rules.heading: Parallel syntax
rules.text: Use the same syntax/structure for all list items in a given list, if possible.

rules.heading: Numbered, lettered, and bulleted lists
rules.text: Start each list item with a capital letter, unless case is an important part of the information conveyed by the list—such as in a list of glossary terms.

rules.heading: Numbered, lettered, and bulleted lists
rules.text: End each list item with a period or other appropriate sentence-ending punctuation, except for items that are a single word, have no verb, are entirely in code font, or are entirely link text or a document title.
rules.good: You can do any of the following by using the API: Create an item. Replace one item with another. Update an item. Delete an item.

rules.heading: Numbered, lettered, and bulleted lists
rules.text: If the list item consists of a single word, don't add end punctuation.
rules.good: The following words are adjectives: Big Small Gratuitous

rules.heading: Numbered, lettered, and bulleted lists
rules.text: If the list item doesn't include a verb, don't add end punctuation.
rules.good: The SDK supports the following UI elements: Text box Bulleted list Button

rules.heading: Numbered, lettered, and bulleted lists
rules.text: If the list item is entirely in code font, don't add end punctuation.

rules.heading: Numbered, lettered, and bulleted lists
rules.text: If the list item is entirely link text or a document title, don't add end punctuation.

rules.heading: Numbered, lettered, and bulleted lists
rules.text: If you end up with inconsistent punctuation in your list, either rewrite your list to use parallel construction or add end punctuation to every list item for consistency.

rules.heading: Description lists
rules.text: Don't add an explanatory phrase to only a single list item; instead, use a description list, and provide explanatory phrases for all items.
rules.bad: The following words are adjectives: Big Relevant Gratuitous Purple—this is a color.
rules.good: The following words are adjectives: Big: A short word. Relevant: A fancy word. Gratuitous: A long word. Purple: A vibrant color.

rules.heading: Description lists
rules.text: In most contexts, start each term (dt element) in a description list with a capital letter.

rules.heading: Description lists
rules.text: Don't end the term (dt element) in a description list with a period.

rules.heading: Description lists
rules.text: Generally put a period at the end of each dd (description) element.

rules.heading: Description lists that use run-in headings
rules.text: In most contexts, start the run-in heading with a capital letter.

rules.heading: Description lists that use run-in headings
rules.text: End the run-in heading with a period or a colon, but be consistent within the list.

rules.heading: Description lists that use run-in headings
rules.text: If the description text follows a period, start the text with a capital letter and end the description with a period.
rules.good: Budget Airlines reduces your ticket cost in several ways: • It increases fuel economy by reducing baggage weight. By charging astronomical prices for anything larger than a wallet.... • It carries more passengers per flight. By reducing leg room to industry and medical minimums, it fits more seats....

rules.heading: Description lists that use run-in headings
rules.text: If the description text follows a colon, start the text with a lowercase letter.
rules.good: The following words are adjectives: • Big: a short word • Relevant: a fancy word • Gratuitous: a long word • Purple: a vibrant color

rules.heading: Description lists that use run-in headings
rules.text: If the description follows a colon and is a list of items or short phrases without verbs, don't include a period.
rules.good: The coffee shop has several great choices: • Coffee: latte, mocha, cappuccino, espresso, macchiato • Tea: chai tea, chai latte, black tea, green tea, herbal tea

rules.heading: Description lists that use run-in headings
rules.text: If the description follows a colon and includes a verb or expresses a standalone thought, end the description with a period.

rules.heading: Description lists that use run-in headings
rules.text: Don't use a dash to set off a description from an item in a description list; use a colon instead.
rules.bad: Purple—this is a color.
rules.good: Purple: a vibrant color

rules.heading: Comma-separated lists
rules.text: When you write a list in a paragraph, use serial commas to separate the items.
rules.good: The service processes data like event logs, clickstream data, social network interactions, and e-commerce transactions.

rules.heading: Comma-separated lists
rules.text: Avoid ending a list with etc. or phrases like and so on; instead, introduce the list in a way that makes it clear that the list isn't all-inclusive.
rules.bad: The service processes event logs, clickstream data, social network interactions, e-commerce transactions, etc.
rules.good: The service processes data like event logs, clickstream data, social network interactions, and e-commerce transactions.

rules.heading: Comma-separated lists
rules.text: Avoid ending a list with etc. or phrases like and so on.
rules.why: Introduce the list as non-exhaustive instead.
rules.example: The service processes event logs, clickstream data, social network interactions, e-commerce transactions, etc.

rules.heading: Possessives
rules.text: For singular nouns, including those that end in s, add 's to the end of the word.
rules.good: Raise the storage class's quota.

rules.heading: Possessives
rules.text: For plural nouns that end in s, add only an apostrophe to the end of the word.
rules.bad: Extend the models's capabilities.
rules.good: Extend the models' capabilities.

rules.heading: Possessives
rules.text: For plural nouns that don't end in s, add 's to the end of the word.

rules.heading: Possessives
rules.text: If a possessive seems awkward, rewrite the sentence to omit the possessive.
rules.bad: Analyze the businesses' data.
rules.good: Analyze the business data.

rules.heading: Possessives
rules.text: Avoid using 's to form a plural noun.

rules.heading: Product, feature, and company names
rules.text: When describing function or performance, don't form a possessive from a feature name, product name, or trademark, regardless of who owns it; instead, use the name as a modifier or rewrite to use a word like of to indicate the relationship.
rules.bad: You can use this template to monitor Google Search's performance.
rules.good: You can use this template to monitor Google Search performance.

rules.heading: Product, feature, and company names
rules.text: To form the possessive of a company name, add 's to the end of the name.
rules.good: Google's new office is nearby.

rules.heading: Product, feature, and company names
rules.text: Don't form the possessive of a company name when using it as a trademark.
rules.bad: The capabilities of Google's Search are vast.

rules.heading: Code items
rules.text: Don't form the possessive of a code item; instead, form the possessive from the noun that follows the code item or rewrite to avoid the possessive form.
rules.bad: Compare the number to wordCount 's return value.
rules.good: Compare the number to the wordCount method's return value.

rules.heading: Future features
rules.text: Avoid documenting future features or products, even in innocuous ways.

rules.heading: Future features
rules.text: Don't pre-announce anything in documentation unless it has been approved by your legal counsel.
rules.why: Pre-announcements need legal approval.

rules.heading: Prepositions
rules.text: Place the preposition where it makes the most sense and makes the sentence easiest to read, even at the end of a sentence.
rules.bad: For details, see the client library documentation for the language with which you're interacting.
rules.good: For details, see the client library documentation for the language you're interacting with.
rules.why: There's no rule against ending a sentence with a preposition.

rules.heading: Prepositions
rules.text: Include prepositions that increase clarity.

rules.heading: Prepositions
rules.text: Omit unnecessary prepositions.

rules.heading: Prepositions
rules.text: Don't clutter the sentence with too many prepositions.
rules.good: The icon for the connector manager turns green within a few minutes, and the connector instance is displayed shortly after.

rules.heading: Present tense
rules.text: Use present tense for statements that describe general behavior that's not associated with a particular time.
rules.bad: Send a query to the service. The server will send an acknowledgment.
rules.good: Send a query to the service. The server sends an acknowledgment.

rules.heading: Present tense
rules.text: It's fine to use future tense (will) to distinguish an action that will occur in the future, such as one that happens asynchronously or later.
rules.bad: A message is sent that notifies any Pub/Sub subscribers.
rules.good: A message is sent that will notify any Pub/Sub subscribers.
rules.why: Future tense marks actions that don't happen immediately.

rules.heading: Present tense
rules.text: Don't use future tense to describe how a product or feature will work after the next release or update.

rules.heading: Present tense
rules.text: Avoid the hypothetical future would.
rules.bad: You can send an unsubscribe message. The server would then remove you from the mailing list.
rules.good: If you send an unsubscribe message, the server removes you from the mailing list.

rules.heading: Slashes
rules.text: Avoid using slashes, except in code.

rules.heading: Slashes with dates
rules.text: Don't use date formats that rely on slashes.

rules.heading: Slashes with dates
rules.text: Don't use date formats that rely on slashes.
rules.example: The release is scheduled for 03/15/2024.

rules.heading: Slashes with alternatives
rules.text: Don't use slashes to separate alternatives.
rules.bad: For example, a disaster relief map is not subject to the usage limits even if it has been developed/hosted by a commercial entity.
rules.good: For example, a disaster relief map is not subject to the usage limits even if it has been developed or is hosted by a commercial entity.

rules.heading: Slashes with alternatives
rules.text: Don't use slashes to separate alternatives.
rules.bad: Call this method 5/6 times.
rules.good: Call this method five or six times.

rules.heading: And/or
rules.text: Avoid writing and/or except when space is limited, such as in tables; often, and implies or, so you don't need to write both words.
rules.bad: You can view and/or edit your own data.
rules.good: You can view and edit your own data.
rules.why: And often implies or.

rules.heading: And/or
rules.text: If you need to specify both and and or, write it out instead of using and/or.
rules.bad: You can export raw and/or processed events.
rules.good: You can export raw events, processed events, or both.

rules.heading: And/or
rules.text: Avoid writing and/or except when space is limited, such as in tables.
rules.why: And often implies or.
rules.example: You can view and/or edit your own data.

rules.heading: Slashes with file paths and URLs
rules.text: Use forward slashes, as appropriate, in computer file paths and URLs.
rules.good: https://developers.google.com/cardboard/

rules.heading: Slashes with file paths and URLs
rules.text: Where very long URLs extend beyond a line, add a line break immediately after a slash.
rules.good: https://developers.google.com/ cardboard/

rules.heading: Slashes with file paths and URLs
rules.text: Don't ever insert an extraneous hyphen into a URL to break it between two lines.

rules.heading: Slashes with fractions
rules.text: Don't use slashes with fractions because they can be ambiguous.
rules.why: 3/4 could mean three-quarters or 4 as alternative.

rules.heading: Slashes with abbreviations
rules.text: Don't use abbreviations that rely on slashes; instead, spell the words out.
rules.bad: c/o, w/
rules.good: care of, with

rules.heading: Slashes with abbreviations
rules.text: Don't use abbreviations that rely on slashes; instead, spell the words out.
rules.example: Send the form c/o the site administrator.

rules.heading: Slashes with abbreviations
rules.text: Don't use abbreviations that rely on slashes; instead, spell the words out.
rules.example: Run the command w/ administrator rights.

rules.heading: Hyphens
rules.text: Use a hyphen when needed for clarity, to separate parts of words to avoid misreadings or to combine terms that should be read as a unit.
rules.why: Hyphens prevent misreadings and group terms read as units.

rules.heading: General guidelines
rules.text: If there's an established convention for hyphenating a term in the documentation set that you're working with, follow that convention.
rules.why: Consistency within a documentation set.

rules.heading: General guidelines
rules.text: If you're not sure whether to hyphenate a term, check the word list in this style guide, and then the Merriam-Webster dictionary.

rules.heading: Prefixes
rules.text: In general, don't use a hyphen between a prefix and the main noun.
rules.good: infrastructure, megabyte, metadata, preprocessing, pseudocode, semiconductor

rules.heading: Exceptions
rules.text: Add a hyphen after a prefix if the prefix is self or cross.
rules.good: self-managing, cross-region

rules.heading: Exceptions
rules.text: Add a hyphen after a prefix if the noun is capitalized or is a number.
rules.good: non-Google, post-2000

rules.heading: Exceptions
rules.text: Add a hyphen after a prefix to avoid confusion or difficulty in reading.
rules.good: de-energize, intra-index, re-mark, re-sign

rules.heading: Exceptions
rules.text: Add a hyphen after a prefix if the prefix is for a term that already has hyphens or spaces.
rules.good: un-Google-like, non-twentieth-century

rules.heading: Exceptions
rules.text: Add a hyphen after a prefix to be consistent within a document.
rules.good: pre-processing, post-processing

rules.heading: Exceptions
rules.text: Follow the word list for well-established terms that commonly use a hyphen or a space, such as multi-region and style sheet, including where noun, verb, and adjective versions are treated differently.
rules.good: multi-region, style sheet

rules.heading: Exceptions
rules.text: When the components of a unit of measurement are multiplied by each other, hyphenate them.
rules.good: 5 vCPU-hours

rules.heading: Exceptions
rules.text: Don't hyphenate adverbs that end in -ly except when needed for clarity.
rules.bad: Publicly-available implementations
rules.good: Publicly available implementations

rules.heading: Exceptions
rules.text: Don't use hyphens in compounds that are conventionally not hyphenated; follow the word list or the convention in the documentation that you're working with.
rules.good: A machine learning model

rules.heading: Exceptions
rules.text: Hyphenate compound terms that are always hyphenated even if they follow a verb, checking the word list, then the Merriam-Webster dictionary, and the convention in your documentation.
rules.good: You can deploy the app on-premises.

rules.heading: Exceptions
rules.text: Don't hyphenate adverbs that end in -ly except when needed for clarity.
rules.why: -ly adverbs don't need a hyphen.
rules.example: Publicly-available implementations

rules.heading: The non prefix
rules.text: For the non prefix, use your best judgment about hyphenating, because it can easily form words that are hard to parse, taking into account consistency within your documentation.
rules.good: noncurrent, nonempty, noninteractive, nonpublic; non-existence, non-integer, non-key, non-managed, non-negative
rules.why: Non- words are often hard to parse.

rules.heading: The non prefix
rules.text: When using non as a prefix, add a hyphen before hyphenated compound words.
rules.good: non-KSA-based, non-self-sustaining

rules.heading: Compound nouns
rules.text: In general, write compound nouns in their closed (one-word, unhyphenated) form, including when the closed form is the predominant convention in your context even if Merriam-Webster uses another form.
rules.good: webpage

rules.heading: Compound nouns
rules.text: Write these compound nouns in their closed form.
rules.avoid: web page, host name, trade-off, work-around
rules.why: Use the closed form of compound nouns.
rules.example: Open the web page in a browser.

rules.heading: Compound modifiers before a noun
rules.text: If needed for clarity, hyphenate compound modifiers that come before a noun.
rules.good: A well-designed app
rules.why: Almost never wrong to hyphenate before a noun for clarity.

rules.heading: Compound modifiers before a noun
rules.text: Use a hyphen after more or most if you need to clarify what those words modify.
rules.good: Edge locations with more-reliable internet links

rules.heading: Compound modifiers before a noun
rules.text: In general, avoid writing compound modifiers that have more than two words; instead, move some words after the noun.
rules.bad: edition-2023-specific test cases
rules.good: test cases that are specific to the 2023 edition

rules.heading: Compound modifiers before a noun
rules.text: If you must use a compound modifier of more than two words, use a hyphen between each word as needed for clarity.
rules.good: cross-data-center replication

rules.heading: Numbers and units of measurement
rules.text: Hyphenate a number and a spelled-out unit of measurement when they combine to modify a noun.
rules.good: a 64-bit system

rules.heading: Numbers and units of measurement
rules.text: Don't hyphenate if the unit of measurement is abbreviated unless the hyphen is needed for clarity; instead, use a nonbreaking space between the number and unit of measurement.
rules.good: 200 GB disk

rules.heading: Numbers and units of measurement
rules.text: Don't hyphenate a number and an abbreviated unit of measurement; use a nonbreaking space.
rules.why: Abbreviated units take a nonbreaking space, not a hyphen.
rules.example: Attach a 200-GB disk to the instance.

rules.heading: Compound terms after a verb
rules.text: In general, don't add a hyphen to a compound that follows a verb.
rules.good: The app is well designed.

rules.heading: Range of numbers
rules.text: Use a hyphen, not an en dash, to indicate a range of numbers.
rules.good: 8-20 files

rules.heading: Range of numbers
rules.text: If a hyphen in a range of numbers introduces ambiguity, use words such as from, to, and through for clarity.
rules.good: from 8 to 20 files

rules.heading: Range of numbers
rules.text: Use a hyphen, not an en dash, to indicate a range of numbers.
rules.why: Ranges of numbers use a hyphen.
rules.example: Upload 8–20 files.

rules.heading: Range of numbers
rules.text: Don't mix hyphens with words in a range of numbers.
rules.bad: from 8-20 files
rules.good: from 8 to 20 files
rules.why: Use from…to, not from with a hyphen.
rules.example: Upload from 8-20 files.

rules.heading: Spaces around hyphens
rules.text: Never place a space on either side of a hyphen except when using a suspended hyphen, in which case you can leave a space after (but not before) the hyphen.

rules.heading: Spaces around hyphens
rules.text: Never place a space on either side of a hyphen.
rules.why: Hyphens never have spaces on both sides.
rules.example: The app is fast - and secure.

rules.heading: Suspended hyphens
rules.text: When two or more compound modifiers have a common base, you can keep the hyphens but leave out the base for all except the last modifier.
rules.good: You can set up the system to scan for new files at one- or two-hour intervals.

rules.heading: Examples
rules.text: Introduce a short-to-medium-length example at the end of a sentence.
rules.good: Choose a strong encryption algorithm, such as AES-256.

rules.heading: Examples
rules.text: For clarity, consider setting off an example at the end of a sentence using a comma, parentheses, or an em dash as appropriate.
rules.good: Enter a name for the instance, for example, my-instance-99.
rules.why: For clarity.

rules.heading: Examples
rules.text: Avoid using a semicolon to set off an example at the end of a sentence.
rules.bad: Specify the region for deployment; for example, us-central1.
rules.good: Enter a name for the instance (for example, my-instance-99).

rules.heading: Examples
rules.text: Keep an example in the middle of a sentence relatively short and consider setting it off with dashes, commas, or parentheses as appropriate.
rules.bad: Enter a six-digit hex number (for example, if you want the color forest green, enter 228B22), and then click OK.
rules.good: Enter a six-digit hex number (for example, 228B22), and then click OK.

rules.heading: Examples
rules.text: For a longer example, introduce it as a separate sentence using for example as an adverb in that sentence.
rules.good: You can assign tags to your virtual machine instances to categorize them. For example, you could tag instances by environment with env:prod or env:dev.

rules.heading: List or table?
rules.text: When each item is a single unit, such as a programming language name or a step to follow, use a numbered list, lettered list, or bulleted list.
rules.why: Single-unit items don't need rows and columns.

rules.heading: List or table?
rules.text: When each item is a pair of pieces of related data, such as term/definition pairs, use a description list (or, in some contexts, a table).

rules.heading: List or table?
rules.text: When each item is three or more pieces of related data, such as parameters with a name, a data type, and a description, use a table.

rules.heading: Places not to use tables
rules.text: Don't use tables to lay out a page; use your site's standard CSS instead.

rules.heading: Places not to use tables
rules.text: If you have only one row of material, usually don't use a table, except in some contexts such as consistency of layout in reference documentation.

rules.heading: Places not to use tables
rules.text: If you have only one column in your table, turn the table into a list.

rules.heading: Places not to use tables
rules.text: Don't use tables to lay out code snippets.

rules.heading: Places not to use tables
rules.text: Don't use tables to lay out long one-dimensional lists in multiple columns; use tables only to present two-dimensional data that semantically makes sense to display in rows and columns.

rules.heading: Places not to use tables
rules.text: Avoid tables in the middle of a numbered procedure.

rules.heading: Multi-paragraph table cells
rules.text: To create multiple paragraphs in a table cell, use the p element rather than the br element.

rules.heading: Introductory sentences for tables
rules.text: Introduce tables with a complete sentence that describes the purpose of the table.
rules.good: Change the environment variables to values for your deployment, as listed in the following table:
rules.why: Not all screen readers preannounce tables.

rules.heading: Introductory sentences for tables
rules.text: End the introductory sentence with a colon if it immediately precedes the table, and usually with a period if there's more material (such as a note paragraph) between the introduction and the table.

rules.heading: Table placement
rules.text: When introducing a table, try to refer to the table's position, using a phrase like the following table or the preceding table.

rules.heading: Table placement
rules.text: Don't put a table in the middle of a sentence.

rules.heading: Table placement
rules.text: Avoid using footnotes in tables when possible.

rules.heading: Table placement
rules.text: If your table refers to footnotes, place them immediately following the table.

rules.heading: Table captions
rules.text: Place the table adjacent to the text that refers to it.

rules.heading: Table captions
rules.text: If your document contains more than one table in fairly close proximity to each other, include a caption for each one, using a caption element as the first child of the table element.
rules.good:
...
Table 1. Prehistoric birds

rules.heading: Table captions
rules.text: Start the caption with a number, in the form "Table NUMBER. DESCRIPTION", and use sentence case for the caption.
rules.good:
...
Table 1. Prehistoric birds

rules.heading: Table captions
rules.text: When referring to a captioned table from text, refer to it by its number—for example, as shown in table 2.
rules.good: ... as shown in table 2.

rules.heading: Table captions
rules.text: Don't place a period at the end of a table caption.
rules.example: Table 1. Prehistoric birds.

rules.heading: Table captions
rules.text: Do not capitalize table unless it starts a sentence.
rules.example: The results are shown in Table 2.

rules.heading: Table formatting
rules.text: Don't add styling to the table element.

rules.heading: Table formatting
rules.text: Don't apply a visual style such as a different font, font color, or background color to convey a header row or column by itself; use the th element to semantically mark up headers in tables.

rules.heading: Table formatting
rules.text: Sort rows in a logical order, or alphabetically if there is no logical order.

rules.heading: Table formatting
rules.text: If the table is long or complicated—for example, with multiple header rows or columns—consider splitting it into multiple tables.

rules.heading: Table formatting
rules.text: Don't present new information in tables through images or symbols alone; always provide a descriptive alt attribute for the image or symbol.

rules.heading: Table formatting
rules.text: Don't merge cells. Don't use colspan or rowspan attributes.
rules.example: Value

rules.heading: Table formatting
rules.text: Always provide a descriptive alt attribute for an image or symbol in a table.

rules.heading: Table column heads
rules.text: Use sentence case for table column heads.

rules.heading: Table column heads
rules.text: Write concise table column headings.

rules.heading: Table column heads
rules.text: Use table headings for the first column and the first row only.

rules.heading: Table column heads
rules.text: Include the scope attribute on table headings as appropriate for accessibility.
rules.why: Helps screen readers associate headers with cells.

rules.heading: Table column heads
rules.text: Don't end table column heads with punctuation, including a period, an ellipsis, or a colon.
rules.example: <th>Description:</th>

rules.heading: Responsive tables
rules.text: Where possible, use table CSS that adapts to different viewport sizes.

rules.heading: Link to tables
rules.text: Where possible, avoid linking to tables; instead, refer to them by table number.

rules.heading: Address the reader as you
rules.text: Address the reader in the second person: use you or your instead of we, our, or us.
rules.bad: The following sections describe how we can create a website.
rules.good: The following sections describe how you can create a website.

rules.heading: Address the reader as you
rules.text: Address the reader as you instead of using first-person plural constructions such as Let's and our.
rules.bad: Let's add a description to our table.
rules.good: Consider adding a description to your table.

rules.heading: Address the reader as you
rules.text: Assume that the reader is the person who's doing the tasks or making the decisions.

rules.heading: Address the reader as you
rules.text: Use the word user only to refer to the user of the software that your reader is developing.
rules.bad: This document shows the user how to develop an app for their organization.
rules.good: This document shows you how to develop an app for your organization.

rules.heading: Address the reader as you
rules.text: If you're telling the reader to do something, then use the imperative (the you is implied).
rules.good: Click Submit.

rules.heading: Address the reader as you
rules.text: Use the imperative in running text only after you establish who is being addressed.
rules.good: You can obtain the IP address for the appliance from your network administrator. Store the address in a variable for future use in the runbook.

rules.heading: Address the reader as you
rules.text: Consider whether imperative text in running text needs to be formatted as a procedure.
rules.bad: To hold the backup data, create a storage bucket. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Buckets page. Click Create bucket.

rules.heading: Address the reader as you
rules.text: Use the second person to address what the reader does, but use the third person for what the software or an end user does.
rules.why: Using you might not be accurate or appropriate.

rules.heading: Address the reader as you
rules.text: In API documentation, use the third person to state facts about programming elements, but address the reader as you when you tell them what to do with them.

rules.heading: Use first-person plural pronouns carefully
rules.text: Use first-person plural pronouns (such as we, our, or us) only to refer to the organization that's represented as the author of the document.
rules.good: For more information, contact our sales organization.

rules.heading: Use first-person plural pronouns carefully
rules.text: When you use we, our, or us for the authoring organization, ensure that the antecedent for the pronoun is clear.
rules.good: Example Organization provides A and B, but we don't provide C and D.

rules.heading: Address your audience consistently
rules.text: Identify who the you is that you're addressing (a developer, a sysadmin, someone else) and be consistent about that.

rules.heading: Address your audience consistently
rules.text: Make it clear to the reader who you expect them to be, sometimes with an explicit audience sentence near the beginning of the document.

rules.heading: Long and short versions of a word
rules.text: Don't put a period after the short version of a word, such as app, demo, or sync; if you speak the short version as a word, treat it as a word and not an abbreviation.
rules.good: This is a demo version of the product
rules.why: Short versions of words aren't abbreviations.

rules.heading: General dos and don'ts
rules.text: Use standard acronyms and initialisms that will save the reader time.
rules.why: Abbreviations the reader must think about slow comprehension.

rules.heading: General dos and don'ts
rules.text: Avoid using abbreviations for terms that aren't related to the main topic of the document.
rules.bad: The IoT (internet of things) service can even be used for connecting to sensors in LEO (low Earth orbit).
rules.good: The internet of things (IoT) service can even be used for connecting to sensors in low Earth orbit.

rules.heading: General dos and don'ts
rules.text: Be wary of using specialized abbreviations that your readers might not understand.

rules.heading: When to spell out a term
rules.text: Spell out abbreviations on first reference: when an abbreviation is likely to be unfamiliar to the audience, spell it out upon first mention and include the abbreviation in parentheses immediately following.
rules.good: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)

rules.heading: When to spell out a term
rules.text: For all subsequent mentions of the abbreviation, use the abbreviation by itself.

rules.heading: When to spell out a term
rules.text: If you use an abbreviation only once, include it only if you think the abbreviation is as commonly used as the spelled-out term; otherwise, don't include the abbreviation.

rules.heading: When to spell out a term
rules.text: If the first mention of a term occurs in a heading or title, you can use the abbreviation and then spell out the abbreviation in the first paragraph that follows the heading or title.

rules.heading: When to spell out a term
rules.text: When deciding to spell out a term, consider your audience: if the majority of your audience is likely to recognize and understand the term, you don't need to spell it out.
rules.why: Spelling out helps translation and non-native readers.

rules.heading: When to spell out a term
rules.text: Don't spell out a term when spelling it out doesn't help the reader understand it; abbreviations such as API, DVD, file formats like PDF or XML, HTML, RAM, REST, units of measurement like MB, MiB, GB, or GiB, URL, and USB rarely need to be spelled out.

rules.heading: Format abbreviation introductions
rules.text: When you spell out a term and include its abbreviation in parentheses, italicize both the spelled-out term and its abbreviation.

rules.heading: Format abbreviation introductions
rules.text: Capitalize the spelled-out version of the abbreviation only if the long form is a proper noun or is conventionally capitalized; don't capitalize the term only because the abbreviation includes capital letters.
rules.bad: Data Manipulation Language (DML)
rules.good: data manipulation language (DML)

rules.heading: Format abbreviation introductions
rules.text: Include the abbreviation in link text.

rules.heading: Abbreviations not to use
rules.text: It's okay to use etc. in some circumstances, but it's best to use different phrasing in most lists.

rules.heading: Abbreviations not to use
rules.text: Don't use internet slang abbreviations; write out what you mean in a non-figurative way.

rules.heading: Abbreviations not to use
rules.text: Use the most common form of a word: if the spelled-out word is common and easily understandable, use that rather than abbreviating.

rules.heading: Abbreviations not to use
rules.text: Spell out shortened words or common symbols that are substitutions for words.
rules.bad: Updating the software made throughput 10x faster.
rules.good: Updating the software made throughput 10 times faster.

rules.heading: Abbreviations not to use
rules.text: Don't use i.e. or e.g.; instead, use that is or for example, respectively.
rules.example: Use a short name, e.g. myapp.

rules.heading: Abbreviations not to use
rules.text: Don't use internet slang abbreviations such as tl;dr, ymmv, or RTFM.
rules.why: Write out what you mean in a non-figurative way.
rules.example: tl;dr: restart the server.

rules.heading: Abbreviations not to use
rules.text: Write approximately instead of approx.
rules.example: The job takes approx. 10 minutes.

rules.heading: Abbreviations not to use
rules.text: Spell out symbols that substitute for words, such as 10x for 10 times.
rules.example: Updating the software made throughput 10x faster.

rules.heading: Periods with abbreviations
rules.text: Don't use periods with acronyms or initialisms.

rules.heading: Periods with abbreviations
rules.text: Put a period at the end of a shortened word, except for date and time abbreviations.

rules.heading: Periods with abbreviations
rules.text: Don't use a period with an abbreviation for the name of a country, US state, or the District of Columbia (DC).
rules.example: The service is available in the U.S. only.

rules.heading: Periods with abbreviations
rules.text: Don't use periods with acronyms or initialisms.
rules.example: Contact the I.T. team for access.

rules.heading: Abbreviations as verbs
rules.text: Don't use acronyms, initialisms, or shortened words as verbs.
rules.bad: Then ssh into your remote shell.
rules.good: Use SSH to log in to your remote shell.

rules.heading: Indefinite articles before abbreviations
rules.text: Use a before any consonant sound and an before any vowel sound, basing your decision on the pronunciation of the abbreviation that's most common for your audience.

rules.heading: Indefinite articles before abbreviations
rules.text: Write a SQL, a FHIR, and an SAP.
rules.avoid: an SQL, An SQL, an FHIR, An FHIR, a SAP, A SAP
rules.use: a SQL, A SQL, a FHIR, A FHIR, an SAP, An SAP
rules.why: Word list preference.
rules.example: Run an SQL query against the table.

rules.heading: Mathematical notation
rules.text: If you're using a third-party tool to display complex math, follow that tool's formatting guidance to ensure that your mathematical markup displays correctly.
rules.why: Ensures complex math markup renders correctly.

rules.heading: Use HTML entities for mathematical symbols
rules.text: In general, use HTML entities for mathematical symbols instead of keyboard symbols; for the plus sign (+), equals sign (=), and division sign (/), you can use their keyboard equivalents.
rules.why: Supports assistive technologies and accurate rendering.

rules.heading: Use HTML entities for mathematical symbols
rules.text: Use the listed HTML entity for each symbol: − (−), × (×), ≠ (≠), ± (±), ∓ (∓), < (<), > (>), ≈ (≈), ≉ (≉), ≅ (≅), ≤ (≤), ≥ (≥), ≡ (≡), ≢ (≢), √ (√), and ∑ (∑).
rules.why: Supports assistive technologies and accurate rendering.

rules.heading: Use HTML entities for mathematical symbols
rules.text: For multiplication, use the multiplication sign × (×); alternatively, you can use the dot operator ∙ (∙) or asterisk operator * (*) to match the UI, or omit the multiplication symbol if doing so doesn't create ambiguity.

rules.heading: Use HTML entities for mathematical symbols
rules.text: Don't use an asterisk (*) to indicate multiplication in text.

rules.heading: Operators
rules.text: To ensure accessibility and accurate HTML syntax, use HTML entities instead of keyboard symbols for operators—for example, use − instead of a hyphen (-).
rules.good: a − b
rules.why: Ensures accessibility and accurate HTML syntax.

rules.heading: Operators
rules.text: Include a non-breaking space ( ) on both sides of operators within a single expression, equation, or statement.
rules.good: a − b
rules.why: Keeps the expression on one line.

rules.heading: Operators
rules.text: Don't italicize operators.
rules.good: a − b

rules.heading: Variables
rules.text: Italicize variables.
rules.good: x ≠ y

rules.heading: Expressions and equations
rules.text: Include short expressions and equations inline with your text.
rules.good: The equation that describes a linear trend line is y = a + bx.

rules.heading: Expressions and equations
rules.text: Include a non-breaking space ( ) between components such as operators and variables so that the expression or equation renders on the same line.
rules.good: y = a + bx
rules.why: Keeps the expression or equation on one line.

rules.heading: Expressions and equations
rules.text: When an expression or equation creates an awkward line break, consider placing it on its own line.
rules.good: The equation that describes a polynomial trend line, where the order is o, is the following: y = a + b × x + ... + k × x^o

rules.heading: Fractions
rules.text: Express fractions as decimal numbers, when possible.

rules.heading: Fractions
rules.text: If you must express fractions as words, connect the numerator and denominator with a hyphen unless one of them is already hyphenated.
rules.good: three-sevenths

rules.heading: Exponents and subscripts
rules.text: Use standard mathematical notation, and don't put a space between the base and the exponent.
rules.good: 2³

rules.heading: Exponents and subscripts
rules.text: To render exponents, use the HTML <sup> tag; don't use the keyboard caret symbol (^) to indicate an exponent.
rules.good: 2³

rules.heading: Exponents and subscripts
rules.text: To render subscripts, use the HTML <sub> tag.
rules.good: yᵢ

rules.heading: Exponents and subscripts
rules.text: Don't use the keyboard caret symbol (^) to indicate an exponent; use the HTML <sup> tag.
rules.good: 2³
rules.why: Use the <sup> tag for exponents.
rules.example: The result is 2^3.

rules.heading: Notation as words
rules.text: In general, you can use mathematical notation in place of words in running text.
rules.bad: Check whether a is greater than b.
rules.good: Check whether a > b.

rules.heading: Notation as words
rules.text: If the use of notation instead of words creates ambiguous, grammatically incorrect, or difficult-to-read text, then use words to convey the mathematical concept.
rules.bad: The area is calculated by multiplying l × w.
rules.good: The area is calculated by multiplying the length by the width.

rules.heading: Tools for complex or multiline equations
rules.text: For complex, multiline equations, or formulas that are difficult to represent clearly with standard HTML, consider using diagrams, other images, or a dedicated math rendering tool to support comprehension.
rules.why: Supports comprehension of complex formulas.

rules.heading: Parentheses
rules.text: Don't put important information in parentheses if you can help it.
rules.why: Some readers ignore anything that appears in parentheses.

rules.heading: Parentheses
rules.text: Whenever you're inclined to use parentheses, consider whether they're necessary; remove them and set off the phrase or sentence by using commas, dashes, semicolons, or periods if that works just as well.
rules.bad: Enter a name for the instance (for example, my-instance-99).
rules.good: Enter a name for the instance—for example, my-instance-99.

rules.heading: Parentheses
rules.text: If you need to include parentheses in the middle of a sentence, keep the parenthetical thought short; otherwise, consider using two sentences.
rules.bad: Enter a six-digit hex number (for example, if you want the color forest green, enter 228B22), and then click OK.
rules.good: Enter a six-digit hex number, and then click OK. For example, if you want the color forest green, enter 228B22.

rules.heading: Parentheses
rules.text: Don't use parentheses to indicate optional plurals.
rules.example: Select the file(s) that you want to upload.

rules.heading: Active voice
rules.text: In general, use active voice instead of passive voice.
rules.bad: The service is queried, and an acknowledgment is sent.
rules.good: Send a query to the service. The server sends an acknowledgment.
rules.why: Passive voice often hides who performs the action.

rules.heading: Active voice
rules.text: Make clear who's performing the action.
rules.bad: The service is queried, and an acknowledgment is sent.
rules.good: Send a query to the service. The server sends an acknowledgment.
rules.why: Readers must know who is supposed to do something.

rules.heading: Active voice
rules.text: Whenever possible, make the doer the subject of the sentence instead of indicating it with "by" in passive voice.
rules.bad: The service is queried by you, and an acknowledgment is sent by the server.
rules.good: Send a query to the service. The server sends an acknowledgment.
rules.why: Passive with "by" reads worse than active voice.

rules.heading: Exceptions
rules.text: It's okay to use passive voice to emphasize an object over an action.
rules.good: The file is saved.

rules.heading: Exceptions
rules.text: It's okay to use passive voice to de-emphasize a subject or actor.
rules.bad: You created over 50 conflicts in the file.
rules.good: Over 50 conflicts were found in the file.

rules.heading: Exceptions
rules.text: It's okay to use passive voice if your readers don't need to know who's responsible for the action.
rules.good: The database was purged in January.

rules.heading: Use clear, concise, and unambiguous language
rules.text: Consider global audiences and translation and write in a way that's clear, concise, and unambiguous.
rules.why: Docs are translated and read by non-native English speakers.

rules.heading: Use simpler words and shorter sentences
rules.text: Use a simple word: don't use commence when you mean start or begin, consequently when you mean so, or utilize or leverage when you mean use.
rules.why: Fine when conveying a special sense, such as resource utilization.
rules.example: Cloud Spanner utilizes up to 100% of the available CPU resources.

rules.heading: Use simpler words and shorter sentences
rules.text: Use a single word when it conveys the same idea as a phrase; for example, don't use a number of when you can use some or many.

rules.heading: Use simpler words and shorter sentences
rules.text: Write shorter sentences.
rules.why: Shorter sentences are easier and cheaper to translate.

rules.heading: Avoid phrasal verbs
rules.text: Avoid phrasal verbs when possible; try to substitute a simpler verb first (exceptions include set up, log in, and sign in).
rules.bad: This document makes use of the following terms:
rules.good: This document uses the following terms:

rules.heading: Use modifiers appropriately
rules.text: Don't use too many modifiers; in particular, don't use more than two nouns as modifiers of another noun.
rules.bad: A hybrid cloud-native DevSecOps pipeline
rules.good: A cloud-native DevSecOps pipeline in a hybrid environment

rules.heading: Use modifiers appropriately
rules.text: Don't misplace modifiers; place a word like only immediately before the word or phrase that it relates to, and rephrase if the meaning is still ambiguous.
rules.bad: Only request one token.
rules.good: Request only one token.

rules.heading: Use modifiers appropriately
rules.text: Describe technical details in precise, technical terms, and avoid subjective modifiers such as simply, properly, or carefully.
rules.why: Subjective words can be vague.

rules.heading: Use active voice and present tense
rules.text: Use present tense.

rules.heading: Use active voice and present tense
rules.text: Avoid complex or uncommon verb forms.

rules.heading: Use active voice and present tense
rules.text: Use active voice, where the subject of the sentence is the person or thing performing the action.
rules.why: Passive voice hides who's supposed to do something.

rules.heading: Use active voice and present tense
rules.text: Avoid participles and gerunds (verbing) when possible; consider replacing using with by using, that use, or you use as appropriate.
rules.bad: Configuring the VPC firewall rules is required before deploying the VM instance.
rules.good: You must configure the VPC firewall rules before you deploy the VM instance.
rules.why: Verbing can be less direct and ambiguous.

rules.heading: Use words in their primary sense
rules.text: Don't use the same word to mean different things; in particular, avoid using the same word as both a noun and a verb in close proximity.
rules.why: Words like once, while, as, and since have multiple meanings.

rules.heading: Use words in their primary sense
rules.text: Avoid directional language (for example, above or below) in procedural documentation.

rules.heading: Use helper words and optional words
rules.text: Use qualifying nouns for technical keywords; for example, call a file the example.yaml file and not example.yaml by itself.

rules.heading: Use helper words and optional words
rules.text: Repeat a word if the redundancy improves comprehension.
rules.bad: If the VM has started and you're able to connect...
rules.good: If the VM has started and if you're able to connect...

rules.heading: Use helper words and optional words
rules.text: Use helper words such as then, that, and of to avoid ambiguity.
rules.bad: If the attribute key is not found, the default value is returned.
rules.good: If the attribute key is not found, then the default value is returned.
rules.why: Conversational English often omits them, creating ambiguity.

rules.heading: Use helper words and optional words
rules.text: Don't omit relative pronouns; use relative pronouns such as that and which.
rules.bad: You can programmatically update the rules you previously defined.
rules.good: You can programmatically update the rules that you previously defined.
rules.why: Provides clarity and avoids ambiguity.

rules.heading: Clarify abbreviations and pronouns
rules.text: Define abbreviations: spell things out whenever possible, at least the first time that you use a given term.
rules.why: Abbreviations confuse out of context and don't translate well.

rules.heading: Clarify abbreviations and pronouns
rules.text: Clarify antecedents: if a pronoun is ambiguous, then replace it with the appropriate noun.
rules.bad: If you use the term green beer in an ad, then make sure that it's targeted.
rules.good: If you use the term green beer in an ad, then make sure that the ad is targeted.
rules.why: Translators often work with small, unconnected strings.

rules.heading: Use apostrophes appropriately
rules.text: Don't form a plural with 's.

rules.heading: Use apostrophes appropriately
rules.text: Don't use the plural or possessive form with trademarks of company, product, and feature names.

rules.heading: Use apostrophes appropriately
rules.text: Don't use uncommon contractions.

rules.heading: Address users and their needs directly
rules.text: Address the user and their needs directly and avoid providing unnecessary information.

rules.heading: Address users and their needs directly
rules.text: Address the reader directly: use you instead of the user or they, unless you're referring to someone who uses the software that the reader is developing.

rules.heading: Address users and their needs directly
rules.text: Provide context; don't assume that the reader already knows what you're talking about.

rules.heading: Address users and their needs directly
rules.text: Avoid negative constructions when possible; consider whether it's necessary to tell the reader what they can't do instead of what they can.

rules.heading: Be consistent
rules.text: Use standard sentence structures, consistent terminology, and appropriate punctuation to avoid creating barriers to understanding, ambiguity, and mistranslations.

rules.heading: Use consistent terminology
rules.text: If you use a particular term for a concept in one place, then use that exact same term elsewhere, including the same capitalization.
rules.why: Translators might treat different names as different concepts.

rules.heading: Use standard sentence structures and formatting
rules.text: Use standardized phrases for frequently used sentences, introductory phrases, and other common tasks, such as introducing links, output, and code samples.

rules.heading: Use standard sentence structures and formatting
rules.text: Use standard English word order: subject + verb + object.

rules.heading: Use standard sentence structures and formatting
rules.text: Try to keep the main subject and verb as close to the beginning of the sentence as possible.

rules.heading: Use standard sentence structures and formatting
rules.text: Use the conditional clause first: mention the circumstance before you provide the instruction.

rules.heading: Use standard sentence structures and formatting
rules.text: Make list items parallel in structure.

rules.heading: Use standard sentence structures and formatting
rules.text: Be consistent in the capitalization and punctuation of list items.

rules.heading: Use consistent text formatting
rules.text: Use consistent typographic formats: use bold and italics consistently, and don't switch from using italics for emphasis to underlining.

rules.heading: Use consistent text formatting
rules.text: Use consistent capitalization.

rules.heading: Be inclusive
rules.text: You're not writing for your culture; write with inclusivity in mind.

rules.heading: Be inclusive
rules.text: Write dates and times in unambiguous and clear ways.

rules.heading: Be inclusive
rules.text: Don't be too culturally specific; don't refer to specific holidays, cultural practices, or sports unless you're certain they're known worldwide.

rules.heading: Be inclusive
rules.text: If you need to use people's names (for example, as email addresses), use a diverse set of names.

rules.heading: Be inclusive
rules.text: Avoid colloquialisms, idioms, or slang.
rules.why: Confusing and difficult to translate.

rules.heading: Be inclusive
rules.text: Avoid humor.
rules.why: Humor is hard to translate and culturally specific.

rules.heading: Be inclusive
rules.text: Avoid geographically specific references, like the seasons.
rules.why: August isn't summer in the southern hemisphere.

rules.heading: Be inclusive
rules.text: Avoid idioms such as ballpark figure, back burner, or hang in there.
rules.avoid: ballpark figure, back burner, hang in there
rules.why: Idioms are confusing and difficult to translate.
rules.example: Put this task on the back burner until the release.

rules.heading: Consider accessibility for images
rules.text: Use screenshots and text in figures sparingly.
rules.why: Images don't get translated.

rules.heading: Consider accessibility for images
rules.text: Convey any new information through text, not by introducing it in a figure or image.
rules.why: Images don't get translated.

rules.heading: Anthropomorphism
rules.text: Don't attribute human qualities to software or hardware.
rules.bad: A Delimiter object tells the splitter where a string should be broken.
rules.good: A Delimiter object specifies where to split a string.
rules.why: Figurative language is less precise and harder to translate.

rules.heading: Anthropomorphism
rules.text: Don't attribute human qualities to software or hardware.
rules.bad: The PC sees a new device.
rules.good: The PC detects a new device.
rules.why: Figurative language is less precise and harder to translate.

rules.heading: Best practices
rules.text: Provide an inline link to the command reference, for example in the text that introduces the command or a series of steps.
rules.good: To connect to the instance, use the gcloud compute ssh command: gcloud compute ssh
rules.why: Readers find the complete list of arguments there.

rules.heading: Best practices
rules.text: Determine which arguments are needed to complete each task in the recommended way, and use as few optional arguments as possible.
rules.why: Rely on the command reference for the complete list.

rules.heading: Best practices
rules.text: Provide a click-to-copy command example that the reader doesn't need to edit after they copy it, including only runnable code and placeholder variables if possible.

rules.heading: Optional arguments in click-to-copy commands
rules.text: Avoid using optional arguments, mutually exclusive arguments, or repeated arguments (square brackets, curly braces, pipes, and ellipses) in click-to-copy commands.
rules.why: These characters can break commands if not removed.

rules.heading: Optional arguments in click-to-copy commands
rules.text: Remove optional arguments from click-to-copy commands if possible, using only the arguments necessary to complete the task for the most common use case, and always provide a link to the command reference.
rules.good: To get an aggregate list of all virtual machine (VM) instances in all zones for a project, use the gcloud compute instances list command: gcloud compute instances list If you want to narrow the list of VMs to a specific zone, use the previous command with the --zones flag.

rules.heading: Optional arguments in click-to-copy commands
rules.text: Use separate code blocks for each option instead of optional-argument syntax in a click-to-copy command.
rules.good: To create a bootable Compute Engine image, use the gcloud compute images import command: gcloud compute images import IMAGE_NAME \ --source-file=SOURCE_FILE If you're importing an image with an existing license, specify the --byol flag: gcloud compute images import IMAGE_NAME \ --source-file=SOURCE_FILE \ --byol

rules.heading: Optional arguments in click-to-copy commands
rules.text: Document optional arguments in separate tasks when it's best to treat different options in separate sections.
rules.good: Import a bootable virtual disk: If your virtual disk has a bootable operating system installed on it, run the following command: gcloud compute images import IMAGE_NAME \ --source-file=SOURCE_FILE Import a non-bootable virtual disk: If your virtual disk doesn't have a bootable operating system installed on it, include the --data-disk flag: gcloud compute images import IMAGE_NAME \ --source-file=SOURCE_FILE \ --data-disk

rules.heading: Optional arguments in click-to-copy commands
rules.text: If you must include special characters to indicate optional arguments, let the reader know that the command contains optional arguments when you introduce the command.
rules.good: In the following example, you optionally specify the auto-delete subflag to keep or discard each disk when the VM is permanently deleted: gcloud compute instance-groups managed create-instance NAME \ --instance=VM_NAME \ --stateful-disk=device-name=DEVICE_NAME,source=DISK[,auto-delete=DELETE_RULE]

rules.heading: Format a command
rules.text: To mark a block of code such as a lengthy command or a code sample, use the pre element.

rules.heading: Format a command
rules.text: When a command line exceeds 80 characters, add a line break before a character such as a single hyphen, double hyphen, underscore, or quotation marks.

rules.heading: Format a command
rules.text: After the first line of a split command, indent each line by four spaces to vertically align each line that follows a line break.

rules.heading: Format a command
rules.text: When you split a command line with a line break, end each line except the last line with the command-continuation character: a backslash preceded by a space ( \) for Linux or Cloud Shell, or a caret preceded by a space ( ^) for Windows.
rules.good: gcloud compute images import IMAGE_NAME \ --source-file=SOURCE_FILE
rules.why: Commands without the continuation character don't work.

rules.heading: Format a command
rules.text: Format placeholder text in a command with placeholders.

rules.heading: Format a command
rules.text: Follow the command line with a descriptive list of the placeholders used in the command line.

rules.heading: Format a command
rules.text: When documenting a command-line option or argument, use end punctuation for complete sentences.

rules.heading: Format a command
rules.text: Don't use end punctuation for single words or noun phrases that document a command-line option or argument, unless there is a mix of sentences and noun phrases.

rules.heading: Format a command
rules.text: When you're documenting a bash or sh command, follow the quotation mark style in Google's shell style guide.

rules.heading: Command prompt
rules.text: If your command-line instructions show multiple lines of input in one block, start each line of input with the prompt symbol.
rules.good: $ adb shell shell@ $ screencap /sdcard/screen.png shell@ $ exit $ adb pull /sdcard/screen.png

rules.heading: Command prompt
rules.text: If you don't want users to copy the prompt symbol when they copy the command, turn off text selection for the symbol if you can, for example by using CSS.

rules.heading: Command prompt
rules.text: Don't show the current directory path before the prompt, even if part of the instruction includes changing directories.

rules.heading: Command prompt
rules.text: If the overall context of the command interface changes, such as from the local machine to a remote machine, add an additional prompt indicator for the new context.
rules.good: $ adb shell shell@ $ screencap /sdcard/screen.png shell@ $ exit $ adb pull /sdcard/screen.png

rules.heading: Command prompt
rules.text: If your document includes both multi-line and one-line commands, use the command prompt ($) for all of the commands in the document for consistency.
rules.why: For a one-line command alone, the prompt is optional.

rules.heading: Command prompt
rules.text: If your command-line instructions include a combination of input and output lines, use separate code blocks for input and output.
rules.good: $ cat ~/.ssh/my-ssh-key.pub The output is similar to the following: ssh-rsa KEY_VALUE USERNAME

rules.heading: Optional arguments
rules.text: Use square brackets around an argument to indicate that it's optional.
rules.good: gcloud dns GROUP [GLOBAL_FLAG] [FILENAME]

rules.heading: Optional arguments
rules.text: If there's more than one optional argument, enclose each item in its own set of square brackets.
rules.good: gcloud dns GROUP [GLOBAL_FLAG] [FILENAME]

rules.heading: Mutually exclusive arguments
rules.text: Use curly braces to indicate that the reader must choose one and only one of the items inside the braces, and use a pipe ( | ) to separate each choice.
rules.good: {FILE_1 | FILE_2}

rules.heading: Arguments that can repeat
rules.text: Use three dots and no spaces ( ... ) to indicate that the reader can specify multiple values for the argument.
rules.good: gcloud dns GROUP [GLOBAL_FLAG ...]

rules.heading: Output from commands
rules.text: Add output only if it adds value, for example if the reader needs to copy a value from the output or verify a value in the output.
rules.why: You don't have to show output for every command.

rules.heading: Output from commands
rules.text: If you are showing output, separate the command from the output with an introductory phrase such as "The output is similar to the following:" or "The output is the following:", customized if you want to call out something about the output.
rules.good: The output is similar to the following, in which the IP column shows the IP address for each resource:

rules.heading: Output from commands
rules.text: To indicate that one or more lines of output are omitted from sample output, use three dots and no spaces ( ... ) on a separate line.
rules.good: Reading file status Upload done, resetting board... ... Wakeup reason: 0

rules.heading: Output from commands
rules.text: Do not use the ellipsis character ( … ) to indicate omitted lines of output; use three dots ( ... ).

rules.heading: Command-line terminology
rules.text: Avoid mapping nomenclature of the gcloud CLI's commands to Linux commands; Linux commands use options, parameters, arguments, and specialized syntax elements rather than the gcloud catchall terms flag and option.

rules.heading: Command-line terminology
rules.text: Describe what the entire command does rather than what its individual elements are called, unless the reader must know the name of the command-line element.
rules.why: Linux commands can be complicated.

rules.heading: gcloud commands
rules.text: In docs, refer to gcloud command-line contents generally as commands, even though the gcloud CLI's syntax distinguishes between a command and a command group.

rules.heading: gcloud commands
rules.text: In the gcloud CLI, call any element other than the command or group name itself a flag, and call a value that a command or flag takes, such as a region value, an argument.
rules.why: Flag is a Google Cloud-specific term.

rules.heading: Example command with multiple elements
rules.text: Use option as a catchall term, in addition to flag, when you don't want to mire the reader in specialized nomenclature.

rules.heading: Linux commands
rules.text: Refer to an argument that specifies a path in a Linux command as only a path.

rules.heading: Linux signals
rules.text: Use the vocabulary of Linux signals, such as kill, only in the context of process control.
rules.why: These terms are generally discouraged elsewhere in documentation.

rules.heading: Linux signals
rules.text: When describing SIGKILL, a signal sent to kill a process, do not substitute cancel, end, exit, quit, stop, or terminate.

rules.heading: Linux signals
rules.text: When describing SIGTERM, a signal sent as a request to terminate a process, do not substitute cancel, end, exit, quit, or stop.

rules.heading: Linux signals
rules.text: When describing SIGQUIT, a signal sent from a keyboard to quit a process, do not substitute cancel, end, exit, quit, or stop.

rules.heading: Linux signals
rules.text: When describing SIGINT, a signal sent to interrupt a process immediately, do not substitute suspend, end, exit, pause, or terminate.

rules.heading: Linux signals
rules.text: When describing SIGPAUSE, a signal that tells a process to pause, or sleep, do not substitute cancel or interrupt.

rules.heading: Linux signals
rules.text: When describing SIGSUSPEND, a signal sent to temporarily suspend execution of a process, do not substitute pause or exit.

rules.heading: Linux signals
rules.text: When describing SIGSTOP, a signal sent to stop execution of a process for later continuation, do not substitute cancel, end, exit, interrupt, quit, or terminate.

not_applicable.reason: Markdown not used in Flare topics

rules.heading: Notes and other notices
rules.text: Use a notice only to offset important or useful information that isn't part of the flow of the text; if you're not sure, write it as regular text first.
rules.why: Readers often skip notices outside their focus of interest.

rules.heading: Notes and other notices
rules.text: Don't use too many notices; see if you can convey the information in a different way.
rules.why: Multiple notices lose their visual distinctiveness.

rules.heading: Notes and other notices
rules.text: Where possible, avoid grouping two or more notices together, such as a note with a caution inside it or several warnings one after another; consider reorganizing the content.
rules.why: Grouped notices lose their visual distinctiveness.

rules.heading: Pick a notice type
rules.text: Use a Note for an ordinary aside or tip that provides information that is useful but not critical to the reader.

rules.heading: Pick a notice type
rules.text: Use a Caution to tell the reader to proceed carefully.

rules.heading: Pick a notice type
rules.text: Use a Warning, which is stronger than a caution, when it means "Don't do this" or that a step might be irreversible, such as leading to permanent data loss, lost money, lost work, or a security breach.

rules.heading: Pick a notice type
rules.text: Use a Success notice only in interactive or dynamic content to describe a successful action or an error-free status; don't use this notice type in ordinary static pages.

rules.heading: When to use a note notice type
rules.text: Create a note only when the information is relevant but not necessary to what the reader is doing right now, so that a reader who skips it still succeeds.

rules.heading: When to use a note notice type
rules.text: Create a note only when interrupting the reader at this point is not an obstacle; for example, don't use a note to suggest an alternative that leads the reader down a different path.

rules.heading: When to use a note notice type
rules.text: Create a note only when the information is not part of the flow of what you're writing—not just a continuation, a result, or a pointer to additional information.

rules.heading: When not to use a note notice type
rules.text: Don't use notes for cross-references.

rules.heading: When not to use a note notice type
rules.text: Don't use notes to tell the reader about prerequisites or about steps they should have taken earlier; put that information before the step.

rules.heading: When not to use a note notice type
rules.text: Don't make a full procedural step into a note.

rules.heading: When not to use a note notice type
rules.text: Don't use notes to provide information that's necessary for the reader to succeed.

rules.heading: When not to use a note notice type
rules.text: Don't use notes for information that's in flow with the preceding text, such as expected results or information that simply describes what precedes.

rules.heading: Examples
rules.text: Use whatever visual presentation for notices is standard for your site.

rules.heading: Articles (a, an, the)
rules.text: Include definite and indefinite articles (a, an, and the) in your writing, and don't skip articles for brevity, including in headings and titles.
rules.bad: Create VM instance
rules.good: Create a VM instance
rules.why: For ease of comprehension and translation.
