Pointer to Articles before product names
Pointer to Indefinite articles before abbreviations

rules.heading: Guidelines for names
rules.text: Make file and directory names lowercase, with the occasional exception for consistency.
rules.bad: avoidingCliches.jd
rules.good: avoiding-cliches.jd
rules.why: Case-sensitive systems treat differently cased names as distinct files.

rules.heading: Guidelines for names
rules.text: Use hyphens, not underscores, to separate words in file and directory names.
rules.bad: avoidingcliches.jd
rules.good: avoiding-cliches.jd
rules.why: Search engines read hyphens as spaces; underscores can hurt SEO.

rules.heading: Guidelines for names
rules.text: Use only standard ASCII alphanumeric characters in file and directory names.
rules.bad: avoiding-clichés.jd
rules.good: avoiding-cliches.jd

rules.heading: Guidelines for names
rules.text: Don't use generic page names such as document1.html.

rules.heading: Exceptions for consistency
rules.text: If you're adding to a directory where everything else already uses underscores, and it's not feasible to change everything to hyphens, it's okay to use underscores to stay consistent; in all other situations, use hyphens.
rules.why: Consistency within a directory can outweigh the hyphen rule.

rules.heading: Other exceptions
rules.text: Accept inconsistent filenames when they can't otherwise be avoided, such as files that reference-documentation tools generate based on other style requirements or the product's or API's naming conventions.

rules.heading: Refer to filenames
rules.text: When referring to a specific file, use code font for the filename.

rules.heading: Refer to filenames
rules.text: When referring to a specific file, include the word file after the filename.
rules.good: In the following build.sh file, modify the default values for all parameters:

rules.heading: Refer to filenames
rules.text: Use the exact spelling of the filename even if it doesn't follow naming guidelines.
rules.why: Readers must be able to find the actual file.

rules.heading: Refer to filenames
rules.text: If a sample of the file is included on the page, precede the code sample with an introductory sentence or paragraph that includes the filename.
rules.good: In the following build.sh file, modify the default values for all parameters:

rules.heading: Refer to file interactions
rules.text: When interacting with files and file types, don't use the file types as a verb.
rules.bad: Unzip a zip file.
rules.good: Extract a zip file.

rules.heading: Refer to file types
rules.text: When you're discussing a file type, use the formal name of the type, not the filename extension.
rules.bad: a .png file
rules.good: a PNG file

rules.heading: Refer to file types
rules.text: Use these file type names for these extensions: .adoc AsciiDoc file, .csv CSV file, .exe executable file, .gif GIF file, .img disk image file, .ipynb IPYNB file, .jar JAR file, .jpg/.jpeg JPEG file, .json JSON file, .md Markdown file, .pdf PDF file, .png PNG file, .ps PowerShell file, .py Python file, .sh Bash file, .sql SQL file, .svg SVG file, .tar tar file, .tf Terraform file, .tiff TIFF file, .txt text file, .wasm Wasm file, .yaml YAML file, .zip zip file.
rules.bad: an .sh file
rules.good: a Bash file

rules.heading: Refer to file types
rules.text: Do not use the filename extension to refer generically to the file type; use the file type name.
rules.why: Use the formal file type name, such as PNG file.
rules.example: Save the screenshot as a .png file.

rules.heading: Spaces in units of measurement
rules.text: For most units of measurement, when you specify a number with the unit, use a nonbreaking space between the number and the unit.
rules.bad: 64GB
rules.good: 64 GB (64 GB)
rules.why: Keeps the number and unit together on one line.

rules.heading: Spaces in units of measurement
rules.text: When the unit of measure is money or percent or degrees of an angle, don't use a space.

rules.heading: Spaces in units of measurement
rules.text: For degrees of temperature, include a nonbreaking space between the number and the degree symbol, and don't use a space between the degree symbol and the temperature scale (F or C).

rules.heading: Spaces in units of measurement
rules.text: Use a nonbreaking space between the number and the unit, not no space.
rules.bad: 64GB
rules.good: 64 GB (64 GB)
rules.why: Number and unit need a nonbreaking space.
rules.example: The disk has 64GB of storage.

rules.heading: Spaces in units of measurement
rules.text: Use a nonbreaking space, not a regular space, between the number and the unit.
rules.bad: 64 GB
rules.good: 64 GB (64 GB)
rules.why: A regular space lets the unit wrap to the next line.
rules.example: The disk has 64 GB of storage.

rules.heading: Spaces in units of measurement
rules.text: Don't use a space between a number and the percent sign.
rules.example: Usage reached 65 % of the quota.

rules.heading: Spaces in units of measurement
rules.text: Don't use a space between the currency symbol and the amount.
rules.example: The plan costs $ 10 per month.

rules.heading: Spaces in units of measurement
rules.text: For degrees of temperature, include a nonbreaking space between the number and the degree symbol.
rules.example: The device operates at 50°C.

rules.heading: Spaces in units of measurement
rules.text: Don't use a space between the degree symbol and the temperature scale (F or C).
rules.example: The device operates at 50 ° C.

rules.heading: Markdown
rules.text: For Kelvin temperatures, leave out the degree symbol but use a nonbreaking space before the K.

rules.heading: Markdown
rules.text: When a number and unit of measurement combine to modify a noun, don't hyphenate unless the hyphen is needed for clarity.
rules.good: 200 GB disk (200 GB disk)

rules.heading: Markdown
rules.text: For Kelvin temperatures, leave out the degree symbol.
rules.why: Kelvin temperatures don't use a degree symbol.
rules.example: The sample is cooled to 300 °K.

rules.heading: Ranges of numbers with units
rules.text: In a range of numbers, repeat the unit for each number; unit includes symbols and abbreviations but not nouns.

rules.heading: Ranges of numbers with units
rules.text: Use the word to between the numbers in a range, rather than a hyphen.
rules.why: A hyphen can be misinterpreted as a subtraction sign.

rules.heading: Ranges of numbers with units
rules.text: Use the word to between the numbers in a range with units, rather than a hyphen, and repeat the unit.
rules.why: A hyphen can be misinterpreted as a subtraction sign.
rules.example: The operating range is -40-85 °C.

rules.heading: Hyphens with multiplied units
rules.text: When the components of a unit of measurement are multiplied by each other, hyphenate them.
rules.good: 5 vCPU-hours

rules.heading: Use k to indicate thousands
rules.text: If you indicate thousands with a lowercase k, add a noun to indicate what the number measures, to make clear that you're not using k as an abbreviation for kilobytes.
rules.good: On this plan, you are limited to 55k download operations and 20k upload operations per day.
rules.why: Prevents confusing k with kilobytes.

rules.heading: Use k to indicate thousands
rules.text: Don't put a space between the number and k.
rules.good: 55k download operations
rules.example: You are limited to 55 k download operations.

rules.heading: Currency
rules.text: If you're writing about monetary amounts, make sure that the reader knows what currency you're referring to.
rules.why: The $ symbol can refer to several currencies.

rules.heading: Currency
rules.text: If there's any possibility of ambiguity, use a currency indicator before the amount.
rules.good: US$10

rules.heading: Rates
rules.text: Use per instead of the division slash (/) when space permits; it's OK to use the slash when space is limited, such as in a table with small cells.
rules.bad: requests/day
rules.good: requests per day

rules.heading: Rates
rules.text: Shorten per to p only for well-established abbreviations for rate units, such as Gbps for gigabits per second or MBps for megabytes per second.
rules.bad: Gb/s
rules.good: Gbps

rules.heading: Rates
rules.text: Use Gbps, not Gb/s.
rules.example: The link supports 10 Gb/s.

rules.heading: Decimal and binary units
rules.text: Use the same system to measure bytes as the technology that you're documenting; don't use MB if you mean MiB, or GB if you mean GiB.
rules.why: Decimal and binary units differ in size.

rules.heading: Placeholders
rules.text: In general, don't use a single x or a series of x's as placeholders; use a more informative placeholder, except in contexts (such as HTTP status codes) where a series of x's is the standard.
rules.why: Descriptive placeholders tell readers what value to supply.

rules.heading: Placeholders in inline text
rules.text: If your sample code and command placeholders occur in a sentence, wrap them by using the var element inside a code element, like this: PLACEHOLDER_NAME.
rules.good: PLACEHOLDER_NAME

rules.heading: Placeholders in inline text
rules.text: If your placeholder does not represent a code sample or command, wrap it by using the var element, like this: <var>PLACEHOLDER_NAME</var>.
rules.good: <var>PLACEHOLDER_NAME</var>

rules.heading: Placeholders in code blocks
rules.text: If your placeholders are in a block of code, wrap the code block in a pre element, and tag placeholders with var elements.
rules.good: gcloud compute forwarding-rules create FORWARDING_RULE_NAME \ --global | --region=REGION \ --load-balancing-scheme=LOAD_BALANCING_SCHEME \ --network=NETWORK \ ...

rules.heading: Placeholder text
rules.text: Use uppercase characters with underscore delimiters in placeholder text.
rules.bad: .../<var>API-name</var>
rules.good: .../<var>API_NAME</var>

rules.heading: Placeholder text
rules.text: If the context in which your placeholders appear makes using uppercase characters with underscore delimiters a bad idea, use something else that makes sense to you, but be internally consistent.

rules.heading: Placeholder text
rules.text: Don't include possessive adjectives in placeholders.
rules.bad: .../<var>MY_API_NAME</var>
rules.good: .../<var>API_NAME</var>

rules.heading: Placeholder text
rules.text: Use uppercase characters with underscore delimiters in placeholder text.
rules.why: Placeholders use uppercase with underscore delimiters.
rules.example: .../<var>apiName</var>

rules.heading: Placeholder text
rules.text: Don't include possessive adjectives in placeholders.
rules.why: Placeholders shouldn't contain possessive adjectives.
rules.example: .../<var>YOUR_API_NAME</var>

rules.heading: Explain placeholders
rules.text: When you use a placeholder in text or code, explain the placeholder the first time you use it.
rules.good: gcloud compute instances create INSTANCE_NAME --metadata enable-guest-attributes=TRUE Replace INSTANCE_NAME with the name that you want your new VM instance to have.
rules.why: Readers must know what value to supply.

rules.heading: Explain placeholders
rules.text: Repeat a placeholder explanation only when doing so might benefit the reader—for example, when your document is lengthy, you've introduced several other placeholders in a long procedure, or your document isn't intended to be read from beginning to end.

rules.heading: Single placeholder
rules.text: For a single placeholder, use the format "Replace PLACEHOLDER with a description of what the placeholder represents."
rules.good: Replace BUILD_ID with the ID of the WORKING build that you copied in the preceding step.

rules.heading: Two or more placeholders
rules.text: For two or more placeholders, follow the command line with a descriptive list of the placeholders used in the command line.

rules.heading: Two or more placeholders
rules.text: Explain what each placeholder represents even if the placeholder value is intuitive to you.

rules.heading: Two or more placeholders
rules.text: Introduce the list of command-line placeholders with "Replace the following:".
rules.good: Replace the following:

rules.heading: Two or more placeholders
rules.text: List the placeholders in the order in which they appear in the command line.

rules.heading: Two or more placeholders
rules.text: Tag each placeholder in a code sample or command with code and var elements; for non-code samples, remove the code elements.
rules.good: • INSTANCE_NAME: description

rules.heading: Two or more placeholders
rules.text: Follow each listed placeholder with a colon and a description that starts with a lowercase letter.
rules.good: ADMIN_PROJECT_ID: the project that owns the reservation

rules.heading: Two or more placeholders
rules.text: If the placeholder description contains an example, introduce it with an em dash or "such as".
rules.good: ZONE: a Google Cloud zone that's close to your location—for example, us-east1.

rules.heading: Two or more placeholders
rules.text: Make each item in the placeholder list follow the list style.

rules.heading: Placeholders in output
rules.text: If you provide a code output example, explain any placeholders that appear in sample output.

rules.heading: Placeholders in output
rules.text: Use var elements to identify the placeholder text in the output.

rules.heading: Placeholders in output
rules.text: Follow the example output with a list of the placeholders used in the example.

rules.heading: Placeholders in output
rules.text: Introduce the list of output placeholders with "This output includes the following values:".
rules.good: This output includes the following values:

rules.heading: Placeholders in output
rules.text: List the output placeholders in the order in which they appear in the example.

rules.heading: Placeholders in output
rules.text: Tag each output placeholder with a var element, followed by a colon and a description that starts with a lowercase letter.
rules.good: OPERATION_ID: the ID of the import operation

rules.heading: Placeholders in output
rules.text: If an output placeholder description contains an example, introduce it with an em dash or "such as".
rules.good: SOURCE_FILE: the URI for the image in Cloud Storage—for example, gs://my-bucket/my-image.vmdk

rules.heading: Label trademarked terms
rules.text: For trademark marking or attribution in documentation, follow any usage guidelines provided by the owners of the respective marks.
rules.why: Trademark owners set the rules for marking their marks.

rules.heading: Use trademarks only as modifiers
rules.text: When you use a trademarked term, always use it to modify a noun, not as a noun by itself.
rules.bad: Another option is to use a Chromebook.
rules.good: Another option is to use a Chromebook notebook computer.
rules.why: Trademarks must be used as modifiers.

rules.heading: Use trademarks only as modifiers
rules.text: Don't use a trademark as a verb.
rules.bad: For information about Chromebook computers, google "notebook computers"
rules.why: Using a trademark as a verb misuses the mark.

rules.heading: Use trademarks only as modifiers
rules.text: Never form a possessive from a trademark.
rules.bad: Chromebook's features rely on an internet connection.
rules.why: Trademarks must not be changed in any way.

rules.heading: Use trademarks only as modifiers
rules.text: Never form a plural from a trademark.
rules.why: Trademarks must not be changed in any way.

rules.heading: Use trademarks only as modifiers
rules.text: Never change a trademark in any way.

rules.heading: Figures and other images
rules.text: Use images only when they provide useful visual explanations of information that is otherwise difficult to express with words.

rules.heading: Figures and other images
rules.text: For screenshots, be discreet: only capture UIs that are important to the discussion.

rules.heading: Create and save images
rules.text: Don't use images of text, code samples, or terminal output; use actual text.

rules.heading: Create and save images
rules.text: For diagrams, use SVG files if possible because SVGs stay sharp when you zoom in on the image.
rules.why: SVGs stay sharp when zoomed.

rules.heading: Create and save images
rules.text: If you don't have an SVG file, save your diagram as a PNG file unless you have a good reason to use a different format.

rules.heading: Create and save images
rules.text: Regardless of the format, don't use a transparent background for diagrams.
rules.why: Transparent backgrounds can cause display issues.

rules.heading: Create and save images
rules.text: For animations and videos, don't use animated GIF; use a more resource-efficient format such as MP4.

rules.heading: Create and save images
rules.text: Be consistent for a given document or doc set in what operating system you use for screenshots.

rules.heading: Create and save images
rules.text: Be consistent in how your screenshots look; for example, if some screenshots include drop shadows of the main window, make similar screenshots consistent.

rules.heading: Create and save images
rules.text: Crop screenshots to show the relevant information; don't include the full window if you just want to show a single button or menu item.
rules.why: Helps reader focus and future-proofs the screenshot.

rules.heading: Create and save images
rules.text: Don't include personally identifying information (PII) in screenshots.

rules.heading: Create and save images
rules.text: If a source screenshot includes PII, hide it with a solid-color overlay with 100% opacity, not blurs, mosaic effects, or similar image-processing effects.
rules.why: Blurs and mosaics can be reversed to reveal information.

rules.heading: Create and save images
rules.text: If you're exporting an image to a format that can include information on separate layers (for example, PDF or TIFF), flatten the image on export.

rules.heading: Create and save images
rules.text: Don't use image maps; instead, provide a list of text references following the image.
rules.why: Image maps hurt accessibility and fail on mobile.

rules.heading: Create and save images
rules.text: Use descriptive filenames for your image files.

rules.heading: Text associated with images
rules.text: Always introduce an image with a complete sentence, except for screenshots that immediately follow procedural text that describes a UI.
rules.good: The following diagram shows how you can apply bounded contexts to an existing ecommerce application:

rules.heading: Text associated with images
rules.text: End the sentence that introduces an image with a colon if it immediately precedes the image, or usually with a period if there's more material (such as a note paragraph) between the introduction and the image.

rules.heading: Alt text
rules.text: Write alt text as a concise description of the image that can replace the image in situations where the image isn't visible.
rules.why: Supports screen readers, text-only browsers, low bandwidth.

rules.heading: Alt text
rules.text: If the image is decorative or it's provided only as a visual aid for information that is already expressed in text, provide empty alternative text (alt="") so it's ignored by assistive technologies.

rules.heading: Alt text
rules.text: When using the img element, always include the alt attribute, even if its assigned value is an empty string (alt="").
rules.why: Without alt, screen readers might read the filename aloud.

rules.heading: Alt text
rules.text: If the alternative text is redundant with surrounding text or it's not useful to visually impaired readers, use the empty tag (alt="").
rules.why: Replacing images with alt text shouldn't change meaning.

rules.heading: Alt text
rules.text: Don't include phrases like Image of or Photo of in alt text.

rules.heading: Alt text
rules.text: Include punctuation in alt text.
rules.why: Screen readers pause at punctuation.

rules.heading: Alt text
rules.text: Use consistent alt text for repeated instances of an image, such as controls, status indicators, or icons that appear multiple times in your document.

rules.heading: Alt text
rules.text: When possible, avoid using all-caps in alt text.
rules.why: Some screen readers read capitals letter by letter.

rules.heading: Alt text
rules.text: Introduce diagrams in the text, not in the alt text.

rules.heading: Alt text
rules.text: Don't use figure captions to replace alt text.

rules.heading: Alt text
rules.text: Use full sentences or a noun phrase in alt text.
rules.good: alt="Architecture of an app that's built with Apps Script."

rules.heading: Alt text
rules.text: Write short, descriptive alt text in 155 characters or less.

rules.heading: Alt text
rules.text: If the image presents more useful information than you can fit in 155 characters, include a brief summary in the alt attribute and a more extensive description of the image in the text.

rules.heading: Alt text
rules.text: Write alt text that considers the context of the image, not just its content.

rules.heading: Figure captions
rules.text: When using the figcaption element, wrap both the figcaption and img elements in the figure element.
rules.why: Properly associates the caption with the image.

rules.heading: Figure captions
rules.text: If you use figure numbers, use the form "Figure NUMBER. DESCRIPTION." with the figure label in bold.
rules.good: Figure 1. Application capabilities are separated into bounded contexts that migrate to services.

rules.heading: Figure captions
rules.text: Use complete sentences in figure captions.
rules.bad: Bounded contexts
rules.good: Application capabilities are separated into bounded contexts that migrate to services.

rules.heading: Figure captions
rules.text: Always use end punctuation for captions.

rules.heading: Figure captions
rules.text: When you refer to a figure, don't use spatial descriptions such as "the image above."

rules.heading: Figure captions
rules.text: If you used figure numbers, consistently refer to the figure by number, for example "... as shown in figure 1."
rules.good: ... as shown in figure 1.

rules.heading: Figure captions
rules.text: If you can't use figure numbers, show the figure again instead of referring back to it.
rules.why: For accessibility and user experience.

rules.heading: Figure captions
rules.text: Don't include the figure caption in a sentence referencing the figure.

rules.heading: Figure captions
rules.text: Don't use spatial descriptions to refer to a figure.
rules.avoid: the image above, the image below, the figure above, the figure below, the diagram above, the diagram below, the screenshot above, the screenshot below
rules.example: As shown in the image above, the app has three services.

rules.heading: Figure captions
rules.text: Don't capitalize the word figure in a reference to a figure, except at the start of a sentence.
rules.example: The services are as shown in Figure 1.

rules.heading: Figure descriptions
rules.text: Convey any new information through text; don't introduce it in a figure or image.

rules.heading: Figure descriptions
rules.text: In a figure description, create text that conveys the same information as the figure.

rules.heading: Figure descriptions
rules.text: Use a figure description when a figure caption doesn't convey the purpose or complete information of the figure.

rules.heading: Figure descriptions
rules.text: Use punctuation in figure descriptions.

rules.heading: Text in figures
rules.text: In most cases, avoid embedding explanatory text in screenshot graphics.
rules.why: Hurts accessibility, searchability, and localization costs.

rules.heading: Text in figures
rules.text: If you must embed text in an image, also provide the same information in a form that people with visual disabilities can use, such as a figure description.

rules.heading: Text in figures
rules.text: Keep text in figures and images brief.

rules.heading: Text in figures
rules.text: In text in figures and images, avoid complete sentences and punctuation when possible.

rules.heading: Text in figures
rules.text: Don't embed figure descriptions or captions in the figure or image; put them in text following the figure.

rules.heading: Text in figures
rules.text: Don't create new abbreviations to condense text in figures and images.

rules.heading: Text in figures
rules.text: Use sentence case for text in figures and images, following the guidelines for capitalization for titles and headings.

rules.heading: Text in figures
rules.text: Use numbered callouts in figures to help you write a figure description, but don't use callouts for detailed annotations in the image.

rules.heading: Text in figures
rules.text: Use full trademarked product names in text in figures and images.

rules.heading: High-resolution images
rules.text: To provide a high-resolution image, use the img element's srcset attribute in addition to the standard src attribute.

rules.heading: High-resolution images
rules.text: When you use the srcset attribute, always still include the src attribute.
rules.why: Browsers without srcset support use src.

rules.heading: High-resolution images
rules.text: Set the width attribute to the CSS pixel size used for the page dimensions, and don't state the height explicitly.
rules.why: Height is calculated from width and proportions.

rules.heading: High-resolution images
rules.text: Set the src attribute to point to the standard-resolution (1x) image, not the 2x version.
rules.why: Low-resolution readers shouldn't download larger images.

rules.heading: High-resolution images
rules.text: Use a filename of the form BASENAME_2x.EXTENSION for the double-resolution image.
rules.good: skateboard_2x.png
rules.why: Makes the double-resolution version clear to humans.

rules.heading: High-resolution images
rules.text: Make the double-resolution image exactly twice the width and height of the standard image, give or take a pixel.

rules.heading: High-resolution images
rules.text: Don't scale up an existing 1x image to make the 2x version; if all you have is the 1x version, use it alone.

rules.heading: High-resolution images
rules.text: Specify all available image resolutions in the srcset attribute.
rules.why: Browsers supporting srcset ignore the src attribute.

rules.heading: Layout of images on a page
rules.text: Don't try to place an image manually, for example with a style attribute; use your site's standard CSS image styles.

rules.heading: Layout of images on a page
rules.text: Don't make your image too small; it's fine for an image to take up the full width of a page.

rules.heading: Layout of images on a page
rules.text: Consider how the image will look when printed out.

rules.heading: Layout of images on a page
rules.text: In general, don't use an image that's wider than the column it appears in.

rules.heading: Layout of images on a page
rules.text: Resize screenshots at full resolution if they take up too much space on the page.

rules.heading: Layout of images on a page
rules.text: Don't link to the figure from within the same page unless it's a very long page and you're linking to it from quite far away on the page.

rules.heading: Layout of images on a page
rules.text: Don't center the image on the page.

rules.heading: Layout of images on a page
rules.text: Don't put an img element inside a p element.

not_applicable.reason: Tool choice is free; no writing rule
Tool choice is free; no writing rule
Workflow advice about designers, site-specific sizes

rules.heading: Choose links selectively
rules.text: Be selective about which links you include on a page.
rules.why: Each link adds cognitive load and a chance to leave.

rules.heading: Provide context on the page
rules.text: When possible, provide help in context rather than linking elsewhere, such as to define a term, briefly explain a concept, or provide a couple of steps.
rules.why: Saves readers the trip away from the page.

rules.heading: Link to third-party sites
rules.text: When the reader needs to know about third-party standards or software, provide a link rather than attempt to thoroughly document someone else's standards, but provide brief information on the page instead when possible.

rules.heading: Avoid duplicate links
rules.text: Within a given page, don't provide duplicate links to the same destination; provide the link once where it's most useful, unless you're linking to a particular section, the page is very long and the links are far apart, or the page has multiple entry points such as procedure and troubleshooting sections.

rules.heading: Provide the most relevant link
rules.text: Link to the most relevant page on a site and to the most relevant heading on a page.

rules.heading: Provide the most relevant link
rules.text: Avoid providing multiple links that do the same job.

rules.heading: Write descriptive link text
rules.text: For the link text itself, use short, unique, descriptive phrases that provide context for the material that you're linking to.
rules.bad: See this blog post.
rules.good: You can use Cloud Scheduler and Cloud Functions to manage task scheduling on Compute Engine.
rules.why: Improves accessibility and scannability; screen readers jump between links.

rules.heading: Write descriptive link text
rules.text: Rework a sentence when needed to include a phrase that makes good link text.

rules.heading: Two options for effective link text
rules.text: For your link text, use either the exact page title or heading that you're referencing, or a descriptive phrase.
rules.good: For more information, see Load balancing and scaling.

rules.heading: Descriptive phrases as link text
rules.text: When you use a description of the destination page as link text, capitalize it as if it's part of the sentence.

rules.heading: Descriptive phrases as link text
rules.text: Place important words at the beginning of the link text.
rules.why: Helps readers quickly judge whether the link is relevant.

rules.heading: Descriptive phrases as link text
rules.text: Don't use the same link text in the same document for different target pages.

rules.heading: Descriptive phrases as link text
rules.text: Keep link text short where possible; don't write lengthy link text such as a sentence or short paragraph.

rules.heading: Avoid vague link text
rules.text: Write link text that makes sense without the surrounding text; don't use phrases such as this document, this article, or click here.
rules.bad: For more information, see this document.
rules.good: For more information, see Make headings into link targets.

rules.heading: Avoid vague link text
rules.text: Don't use click here as link text.
rules.why: Link text must make sense without surrounding text.
rules.example: Want more? Click here!

rules.heading: Avoid URLs as link text
rules.text: In general, don't use a URL as link text; instead, use the page title or a description of the page (in some legal documents, such as some Terms of Service documents, URLs as link text are okay).
rules.bad: See the HTTP/1.1 RFC at http://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616.html.
rules.good: For more information about protocols, see HTTP/1.1 RFC.

rules.heading: Include abbreviations in link text
rules.text: If the text includes an abbreviation in parentheses, include the long form and the abbreviation in the link text.

rules.heading: Link to commands
rules.text: If the text includes a command or another element usually conveyed with code font, include the description of the code element with the link text, unless doing so is awkward or redundant.
rules.bad: This service supports the GET method, HEAD method, and OPTIONS method.
rules.good: This service supports the GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS methods.

rules.heading: Write link introductions ("For more information")
rules.text: When you dedicate a separate sentence to a cross-reference, introduce it with "For more information, see..." or "For more information about..., see... ."
rules.good: For more information, see Load balancing and scaling.
rules.why: Consistent language for cross-references.

rules.heading: Write link introductions ("For more information")
rules.text: Include the "about..." clause when the link text or surrounding context doesn't clearly indicate why you're referring the reader to this information.
rules.good: For more information about task scheduling, see Reliable task scheduling on Google Compute Engine.

rules.heading: Write link introductions ("For more information")
rules.text: Use see to refer to links and cross-references.

rules.heading: Write link introductions ("For more information")
rules.text: Don't use on instead of about.
rules.example: For more information on indexes, see Manage indexes.

rules.heading: Clarify the purpose of a link
rules.text: Make sure that the surrounding context or the link text itself clearly indicates why you're referring the reader to this information; make the explanation specific, but don't repeat the link text.
rules.good: For more information about authentication and authorization, see Using OAuth 2.0 to access Google APIs.

rules.heading: Explain unexpected link behavior
rules.text: If a link goes to an unexpected destination or behaves in an unexpected way, then provide that context.

rules.heading: Explain unexpected link behavior
rules.text: If a link downloads a file or opens an email, then make that clear in the link text, and mention the file type.
rules.good: For more information, download the security features PDF.

rules.heading: Explain unexpected link behavior
rules.text: When you're linking to another section on the same page, use a standard phrase to let the reader know that the link takes them to a different section of the same page.

rules.heading: Explain unexpected link behavior
rules.text: When you're linking to a section heading on another page, use the same wording and formatting as you do in a regular cross-reference.
rules.good: For more information, see Create a table.

rules.heading: Explain unexpected link behavior
rules.text: If the title of the section that you're linking to is identical to a title on the source page, add context to the cross-reference.
rules.good: For more information, see Install libraries in "Building new audiences based on existing customer lifetime value."

rules.heading: Open links in the current tab
rules.text: Don't force links to open in a new tab or window; let the reader decide how to open links.

rules.heading: Open links in the current tab
rules.text: In the rare situation that a link needs to open in a new tab or window, let the reader know that the link opens differently than expected.
rules.bad: Accessible content
rules.good: Accessible content (opens in a new tab)

rules.heading: Footnotes
rules.text: Avoid footnotes because they aren't accessible and can present challenges for localization efforts.
rules.why: Footnotes aren't accessible and complicate localization.

rules.heading: Footnotes
rules.text: Instead of a footnote, consider adding a cross-reference, using a note, or putting the information in a parenthetical.
rules.why: These formats convey information without footnote drawbacks.

rules.heading: Footnotes
rules.text: If the only way to convey this information is to use a footnote, then use a superscript number (for example, <sup>1</sup>) and put the footnote at the bottom of the page.
rules.good:
You want to add a footnote to this sentence. 1
1 Put this footnote at the bottom of the page.

rules.heading: Paragraphs
rules.text: Break up your paragraphs to aid in the scannability of the page and to avoid walls of text.
rules.why: Readers scan, on devices with different screen sizes.

rules.heading: Paragraphs
rules.text: Make each paragraph address a single idea in the fewest words and in the fewest sentences possible.
rules.why: Readers scan for information.

rules.heading: Paragraphs
rules.text: Don't make sentences longer in order to limit the number of sentences in a paragraph; use shorter sentences and paragraphs.

rules.heading: Paragraphs
rules.text: If a paragraph longer than 5 or 6 sentences is trying to convey too much information, break the paragraph into smaller paragraphs or remove some content.
rules.why: Long paragraphs often convey too much information.

rules.heading: Paragraphs
rules.text: Don't break paragraphs up if they contain a single idea; a one-sentence paragraph, or one longer than 6 sentences about one idea, is OK.

rules.heading: Put critical information first
rules.text: Put the most important information first in a paragraph; don't hide the key point of a paragraph at the end of the paragraph.
rules.why: Readers don't read every word.

rules.heading: Format paragraphs
rules.text: Left-align text for readability; don't center, full-justify, or right-align text.
rules.why: Left-aligned text is more readable.

rules.heading: Format paragraphs
rules.text: Don't force line breaks (hard returns) within sentences and paragraphs.
rules.why: Breaks fail in resized windows, devices, or enlarged text.

rules.heading: Add a custom anchor
rules.text: To add an anchor to a heading in HTML, add a section element with an id attribute, or use an a element with a name attribute.
rules.good:
Introduction to everything

...
rules.why: Custom anchors keep links working if the heading text changes.

rules.heading: Add a custom anchor
rules.text: For anchor text, use lowercase letters, and put hyphens between words.
rules.good: introduction-to-everything

rules.heading: Revise a heading
rules.text: If you revise a heading where anchors are automatically created, create a custom anchor that uses the older ID string for the heading.
rules.good:
Introduction to everything

...
rules.why: Avoids breaking existing links to the heading.

rules.heading: Revise a heading
rules.text: If the heading already has a custom anchor, don't change the anchor unless it contains a term that you want to remove (such as a disrespectful term).
rules.why: Changing anchors breaks inbound links to the section.

rules.heading: Revise a heading
rules.text: If you need to change an existing custom anchor, update any links that use the old anchor.
rules.why: Old-anchor links reach the page but not the section.

rules.heading: Avoid unnecessarily gendered language
rules.text: Be mindful of the pronouns that are used in narrative examples, and be aware of other possible sources of gendered language.
rules.bad: Equipment installation takes around 16 man-hours to complete.
rules.good: Equipment installation takes around 16 person-hours to complete.
rules.why: Gendered language excludes readers.

rules.heading: Avoid unnecessarily gendered language
rules.why: Unnecessarily gendered language.
rules.example: Equipment installation takes around 16 man-hours to complete.

rules.heading: Avoid figurative language
rules.text: Use simple language and terminology that's precise and clear for all of your audiences.
rules.bad: You can allowlist a range of IP addresses by entering a CIDR block instead of a single address in the field.
rules.good: You can allow requests from a range of IP addresses by entering a CIDR block instead of a single address in the field.

rules.heading: Avoid figurative language
rules.text: Avoid idiomatic or figurative language that can be misunderstood, distracting, or difficult for translation.
rules.why: Idioms can be misinterpreted or hard to translate.

rules.heading: Avoid figurative language
rules.text: Avoid jargon.

rules.heading: Avoid figurative language
rules.text: Use terms that are established industry standards and widely understood by the target audience.

rules.heading: Avoid figurative language
rules.text: Be attentive to your word choice, especially when you aim for an informal tone, so that you don't use figures of speech and other turns of phrase.
rules.why: Conversational tone invites figurative language.

rules.heading: Avoid figurative language
rules.text: Don't use metaphors, and don't use a term in a metaphorical sense; use words in their primary sense (for example, avoid the metaphor of pets versus cattle).

rules.heading: Avoid ableist language
rules.text: Avoid ableist language such as crazy, insane, blind to or blind eye to, cripple, and dumb; choose a more accurate or alternative word, depending on the context.
rules.bad: There are some crazy outliers in the data.
rules.good: There are some baffling outliers in the data.
rules.why: Ableist language is exclusionary.

rules.heading: Avoid ableist language
rules.avoid: crazy, insane, cripple, cripples, crippled, dumb, blind eye, blind to, sanity check, sanity-check, dummy
rules.why: Ableist language; choose a more accurate word.
rules.example: Before launch, give everything a final sanity-check.

rules.heading: Avoid graphic or metaphorical language
rules.text: Avoid unnecessarily graphic or metaphorical language, when you can use a more precise term.
rules.bad: If the connection hangs, check for errors.
rules.good: If the connection doesn't respond, check for errors.

rules.heading: Avoid graphic or metaphorical language
rules.text: Instead of STONITH, use specific terms to describe the process that's used to stop an errant node.
rules.good: This approach might require you to fence failed nodes.

rules.heading: Avoid graphic or metaphorical language
rules.text: If you need to mention a term such as STONITH, mention it once when you first explain the relevant feature, and phrase it in a way that de-emphasizes the term.
rules.good: This approach might require you to fence failed nodes (sometimes referred to as STONITH).

rules.heading: Avoid graphic or metaphorical language
rules.text: Always use the most precise and well-understood terms for your context, keeping an industry-established term when it has a specific technical meaning without an accurate synonym.

rules.heading: Avoid graphic or metaphorical language
rules.example: Hover over File, and hit New.

rules.heading: Use precise, objective language
rules.text: Use precise, objective language so that all readers can gather the same information from your writing; don't use vague or subjective language.
rules.why: What's simple for experts might be complex for newcomers.

rules.heading: Use precise, objective language
rules.text: Avoid words like simple, simply, easy, easily, quick, and quickly, which introduce an opinion that might not reflect the user's experience.
rules.bad: Simply open the configuration file to quickly add your custom key.
rules.good: Open the configuration file and add your custom key.
rules.why: Introduces an opinion that might not reflect experience.

rules.heading: Use precise, objective language
rules.text: Avoid words like careful, carefully, thorough, and thoroughly, which provide unclear instruction or imply that the user is usually careless or inattentive.
rules.bad: Make sure that you carefully and thoroughly review all of the audit logs for potential security issues.
rules.good: Review the audit logs for security issues. For example, ensure that the user accounts have multi-factor authentication enabled.
rules.why: Unclear instruction; implies the user is careless.

rules.heading: Use precise, objective language
rules.text: Avoid words like proper and properly, which are unclear and can assert opinions of superiority.
rules.bad: Ensure the daemon is properly installed and running.
rules.good: To verify that the daemon is running, run systemctl status DAEMON_NAME and confirm that the output shows Active: active (running).
rules.why: Unclear and can assert opinions of superiority.

rules.heading: Use precise, objective language
rules.avoid: simply, easily, quickly, carefully, thoroughly, properly
rules.why: Subjective or unclear wording.
rules.example: Simply open the configuration file to quickly add your custom key.

rules.heading: Write diverse and inclusive examples
rules.text: Write documentation for a global audience, and use diverse names, genders, ages, and locations in examples.

rules.heading: Write diverse and inclusive examples
rules.text: Follow the gender-neutral pronoun guidance in examples.

rules.heading: Write diverse and inclusive examples
rules.text: Avoid being too culturally specific to the US, and be mindful when referring to specific holidays, cultural practices, sports, and figures of speech.

rules.heading: Write diverse and inclusive examples
rules.text: In examples, choose a diverse set of names to help reflect our global audience.

rules.heading: Write diverse and inclusive examples
rules.text: When writing about older adults, avoid terms and figures of speech such as the elderly, the aged, seniors, senior citizens, or 80 years young; use terms such as older adults or aging population, or mention relative age or relationship when relevant.

rules.heading: Write diverse and inclusive examples
rules.avoid: the elderly, the aged, senior citizens, seniors
rules.example: This feature helps the elderly read small text.

rules.heading: Write about features and users in inclusive ways
rules.text: Avoid referring to people in divisive ways, such as native speakers or non-native speakers of English; discuss the feature in terms that are relevant to anyone.

rules.heading: Write about features and users in inclusive ways
rules.text: Avoid using socially charged terms for technical concepts where possible, such as blacklist, native feature, and first-class citizen.

rules.heading: Write about features and users in inclusive ways
rules.why: Socially charged term for a technical concept.
rules.example: Add the address to the blacklist.

rules.heading: Replace established terms
rules.text: If replacing an established non-inclusive term could cause confusion, refer to the non-inclusive term on the first use only, and put it in parentheses.
rules.good: To make sure that administrators get the notification, add them to an allowlist (sometimes called a whitelist). Anyone who isn't on the allowlist is blocked ...

rules.heading: Replace established terms
rules.text: After the first use, use the inclusive, replacement term throughout the rest of the document.
rules.good: In this model, a Jenkins controller (master) handles HTTP requests. The Jenkins controller is designed to ...

rules.heading: Write around non-inclusive code terms
rules.text: Don't use a non-inclusive name or keyword unless it's in code font.

rules.heading: Write around non-inclusive code terms
rules.text: Minimize your use of a non-inclusive term embedded in code, while still providing clear documentation to your readers.
rules.why: Avoid propagating it as a term of art.

rules.heading: Write around non-inclusive code terms
rules.text: The first time that you refer to a code item that uses a non-inclusive term, format the term in code font, and put it in parentheses if possible.
rules.good: The configuration file helps you create a parent node (which is named master in the file).

rules.heading: Write around non-inclusive code terms
rules.text: In subsequent mentions, use the preferred term, and if it's necessary to refer to the entity name or keyword, do so only with code formatting.
rules.good: Start the replica by using the START SLAVE statement.

rules.heading: Avoid bias and harm when discussing disability and accessibility
rules.text: When writing about people with disabilities or about accessibility, work to eliminate unintentional bias and harm.

rules.heading: Avoid bias and harm when discussing disability and accessibility
rules.text: Don't describe people without disabilities as normal or healthy; use terms such as nondisabled person, sighted person, hearing person, person without disabilities, or neurotypical person.
rules.why: Implies people with disabilities are abnormal or sick.

rules.heading: Avoid bias and harm when discussing disability and accessibility
rules.text: Use the terms that the communities you're writing about prefer, and in many cases avoid terms that remove personhood or define people by their disability, such as the disabled or a quadriplegic.
rules.why: Some communities prefer identity-first language.

rules.heading: Avoid bias and harm when discussing disability and accessibility
rules.text: Use see to refer to links and cross-references.

rules.heading: Avoid bias and harm when discussing disability and accessibility
rules.text: Avoid terms that reflect or project feelings and judgments about a person's disability, such as victim of, suffering from, or wheelchair-bound; use neutral terms such as experiencing, living with, or uses a wheelchair.

rules.heading: Avoid bias and harm when discussing disability and accessibility
rules.text: Avoid euphemisms or patronizing terms such as physically challenged, special, differently abled, or handi-capable.

rules.heading: Avoid bias and harm when discussing disability and accessibility
rules.why: Projects judgment about a person's disability.
rules.example: The app helps users who are wheelchair-bound find accessible routes.

rules.heading: Avoid bias and harm when discussing disability and accessibility
rules.why: Euphemistic or patronizing term.
rules.example: These settings help users who are differently abled.

rules.heading: Jargon
rules.text: If you don't need a jargon term for search engine optimization (SEO), try writing around it.
rules.bad: Hold a post-mortem.
rules.good: When the project is finished, review what processes worked or didn't work.
rules.why: Jargon hampers clarity, translation, and inclusivity.

rules.heading: Jargon
rules.text: Replace a jargon term with a different, more specific term when you can.
rules.why: Specific terms are clearer for a global audience.

rules.heading: Jargon
rules.text: When a term on the word list is marked as "Don't use", replace that term or write around it.
rules.why: Some jargon is offensive, violent, or not inclusive.

rules.heading: Jargon
rules.text: If you use a jargon term only once in your document, describe the term in plain language and refer to it in parentheses, or link to a trusted definition.
rules.good: You then move the task to an earlier part of the process (also known as shifting left).
rules.why: Readers might not know the term.

rules.heading: Jargon
rules.text: If you use a jargon term throughout your document, briefly describe the term in parentheses on first reference, or link to a trusted definition.
rules.good: The application is in the same state as a cold standby (a backup or redundant system that's identical to a primary system).
rules.why: Readers might not know the term.

rules.heading: Jargon
rules.text: If a jargon term is used in a command or code sample, use the words only in direct reference to the code items, formatted as code, and make it clear what you're referring to.
rules.bad: Add a user to the whitelist by entering the following: whitelist adduser EMAIL_ADDRESS.
rules.good: Add a user to the allowlist (whitelist) by entering the following: whitelist adduser EMAIL_ADDRESS.

rules.heading: Jargon
rules.text: Replace blast radius with affected area or spatial impact.
rules.why: Use affected area or spatial impact instead.
rules.example: Check the blast radius of the change.

rules.heading: Jargon
rules.text: Replace ingest with import or load.
rules.why: Use import or load instead.
rules.example: The pipeline can ingest the data.

rules.heading: Jargon
rules.text: Replace off-the-shelf with ready-made or pre-built.
rules.why: Use ready-made or pre-built instead.
rules.example: Use an off-the-shelf template.

not_applicable.reason: Background and pointer to inclusive guide

rules.heading: Documentation basics
rules.text: Provide a description for every class, interface, struct, and any other similar member of the API (such as union types in C++).
rules.why: A complete API reference describes all public members.

rules.heading: Documentation basics
rules.text: Provide a description for every constant, field, enum, and typedef.
rules.why: A complete API reference describes all public members.

rules.heading: Documentation basics
rules.text: Provide a description for every method, with a description for each parameter, the return value, and any exceptions thrown.
rules.why: A complete API reference describes all public members.

rules.heading: Documentation basics
rules.text: On each unique page (for a class, interface, etc.), include a code sample (~5-20 lines) at the top.

rules.heading: Documentation basics
rules.text: Put all API names, classes, methods, constants, and parameters in code font.

rules.heading: Documentation basics
rules.text: Link each API name, class, method, constant, and parameter to the corresponding reference page.

rules.heading: Documentation basics
rules.text: Put string literals in code font, and enclose them in double quotation marks.
rules.good: "wrap_content"

rules.heading: Documentation basics
rules.text: Make sure that the spelling of a class name in documentation matches the spelling in code, with capital letters and no spaces.
rules.good: ActionBar

rules.heading: Documentation basics
rules.text: Don't make class names plural; instead, add a plural noun.
rules.bad: Intents, Activities
rules.good: Intent objects, Activity instances
rules.why: Class names must match the code.

rules.heading: Documentation basics
rules.text: If a class has a name that's a common term, you can refer to it with the corresponding English word, in lowercase and not in code font.
rules.good: activities, action bar

rules.heading: Classes, interfaces, structs
rules.text: In the first sentence of a class description, briefly state the intended purpose or function of the class or interface with information that can't be deduced from the class name and signature.
rules.good: A primary toolbar within the activity that may display the activity title, application-level navigation affordances, and other interactive items.

rules.heading: Classes, interfaces, structs
rules.text: In additional class documentation, elaborate on how to use the API, including how to invoke or instantiate it, what some of the key features are, and any best practices or pitfalls.

rules.heading: Classes, interfaces, structs
rules.text: Make the first sentence of each class description unique and descriptive, yet short.
rules.why: Tools extract the first sentence for class lists.

rules.heading: Classes, interfaces, structs
rules.text: Don't repeat the class name in the first sentence.

rules.heading: Classes, interfaces, structs
rules.text: Don't say "this class will/does ..." in a class description.

rules.heading: Classes, interfaces, structs
rules.text: Don't use a period before the actual end of the first sentence, because some document generators naively terminate the short description at the first period.
rules.why: Generators may truncate the short description.

rules.heading: Classes, interfaces, structs
rules.text: Use "for example" instead of "e.g.", because some generators terminate the sentence at its period.
rules.why: Generators may truncate the short description.
rules.example: Returns a resource, e.g. a bird.

rules.heading: Members
rules.text: Make descriptions for members (constants and fields) as brief as possible.
rules.good: Show 'home' elements in this action bar, leaving more space for other navigation elements. This includes logo and icon.

rules.heading: Members
rules.text: In member descriptions, be sure to link to relevant methods that use the constant or field.
rules.good: See also: setDisplayOptions(int), setDisplayOptions(int, int)

rules.heading: Methods
rules.text: In the first sentence for a method description, briefly state what action the method performs.
rules.good: Checks whether this activity is in the process of being destroyed in order to be recreated with a new configuration.

rules.heading: Methods
rules.text: In subsequent sentences of a method description, explain why and how to use the method, state any prerequisites that must be met before calling it, give details about exceptions that may occur, and specify any related APIs.

rules.heading: Methods
rules.text: Document any dependencies (such as Android permissions) that are needed to call the method, and how the method behaves if such a dependency is missing.
rules.good: the method throws a SecurityException

rules.heading: Methods
rules.text: Use present tense for all descriptions.
rules.good: Adds a new bird to the ornithology list.

rules.heading: Description
rules.text: If a method performs an operation and returns some data, start the description with a verb describing the operation.
rules.good: Adds a new bird to the ornithology list and returns the ID of the new entry.

rules.heading: Description
rules.text: If it's a "getter" method and it returns a boolean, start with "Checks whether ...."

rules.heading: Description
rules.text: If it's a "getter" method and it returns something other than a boolean, start with "Gets the ...."

rules.heading: Description
rules.text: If a method has no return value, start with a verb such as "Sets the ...." (turning on an ability or setting), "Updates the ...." (updating a property), "Deletes the ...." (deleting something), or "Registers ...." (registering a callback or other element for later reference).

rules.heading: Description
rules.text: For a callback, start with "Called by ...." (for example, "Called by Android when ....").
rules.good: Called by Android when ....

rules.heading: Description
rules.text: For a callback, later in the description say "Subclasses implement this method to ...."

rules.heading: Description
rules.text: If it's a convenience method that constructs the class object, start with "Creates a ...."

rules.heading: Parameters
rules.text: Capitalize the first word of a parameter description.

rules.heading: Parameters
rules.text: End a parameter description sentence or phrase with a period.

rules.heading: Parameters
rules.text: Begin descriptions of non-boolean parameters with "The" or "A" if possible.
rules.good: The ID of the bird you want to get.

rules.heading: Parameters
rules.text: For boolean parameters that tell the API to do or not do something, state what the API does if the parameter is true and if it's false.
rules.good: enableCertificateValidation: If true, validates the SSL certificate before proceeding. If false, trusts the certificate without validating it.

rules.heading: Parameters
rules.text: For boolean parameters that declare the already-established state of something, use the format "True if ...; false otherwise."
rules.good: True if the zoom is set; false otherwise.

rules.heading: Parameters
rules.text: In boolean parameter and return value descriptions, don't put the words "true" and "false" in code font or quotation marks.

rules.heading: Parameters
rules.text: For parameters with default behavior, explain what the behavior is for each value or range of values, and then say what the default value is.

rules.heading: Parameters
rules.text: Use the format Default: to explain the default value of a parameter.

rules.heading: Return values
rules.text: Be as brief as possible in the return value's description; put any detailed information in the class description.

rules.heading: Return values
rules.text: If the return value is anything other than a boolean, start with "The ...".
rules.good: The bird specified by the given ID.

rules.heading: Return values
rules.text: If the return value is a boolean, use the format "True if ...; false otherwise."
rules.good: True if the bird is in the sanctuary; false otherwise.

rules.heading: Exceptions
rules.text: In languages where the reference generator automatically inserts the word "Throws", begin your exception description with "If ...".
rules.good: If no key is assigned.

rules.heading: Exceptions
rules.text: Where the reference generator doesn't insert "Throws", begin your exception description with "Thrown when ...".
rules.good: Thrown when no key is assigned.

rules.heading: Deprecations
rules.text: When something is deprecated, tell the user what to use as a replacement.
rules.good: Deprecated. Use #CameraPose instead.

rules.heading: Deprecations
rules.text: If you track your API with version numbers, mention which version something was first deprecated in.

rules.heading: Deprecations
rules.text: Put the most important deprecation information in the first sentence of the description; use subsequent sentences to explain why something is deprecated and any other useful information.
rules.why: Only the first sentence appears in summaries and index.

rules.heading: Deprecations
rules.text: If a method is deprecated, tell the reader what to do to make their code work.
rules.good: Deprecated. Access this field using the getField method.

rules.heading: Focus on the task
rules.text: When practical, state instructions in terms of what the reader should accomplish, rather than focusing on the widgets and gestures.
rules.good: Refresh the page.
rules.why: Clarifies purpose and helps future-proof procedures.

rules.heading: Focus on the task
rules.text: Know the audience and provide the level of detail about UI elements and gestures that seems useful for the intended audience.
rules.good: To expand the Advanced options section, click the arrow_right expander arrow.
rules.why: Non-obvious UI may need explicit gestures.

rules.heading: Format names of UI elements
rules.text: When referring to any UI element by name, put its name in bold.
rules.bad: In the New Project window, select "New Activity", and then click the "Next" button.
rules.good: In the New project window, select the New activity checkbox, and then click Next.

rules.heading: Format names of UI elements
rules.text: Don't use code font for UI elements, unless it's an element that meets the requirements for code font; in that case, use both code font and bold.

rules.heading: Format names of UI elements
rules.text: Don't make an official feature name or product name bold, except when it directly refers to an element on the page that uses the name, such as a window title or button name.

rules.heading: Format names of UI elements
rules.text: If you document a UI element outside the context of a procedure, try to provide context for the element.
rules.bad: The service lets you check the status of all jobs in the Current jobs section.
rules.good: The service lets you check the status of all jobs in the Current jobs section of the service console.

rules.heading: Use appropriate capitalization
rules.text: In most cases, follow the capitalization of UI labels as it appears on the page.

rules.heading: Use appropriate capitalization
rules.text: When a label is all uppercase, use sentence case.
rules.bad: Click REFRESH.
rules.good: Click Refresh.

rules.heading: Use appropriate capitalization
rules.text: When referring to multiple labels that are inconsistently cased, use sentence case for all of the labels.
rules.bad: Click NEW PROJECT, and then click New Activity.
rules.good: Click New project, and then click New activity.

rules.heading: Refer to UI elements
rules.text: Don't use UI elements as if they were English verbs or nouns.
rules.bad: Save the settings.
rules.good: To save the settings, click Save.

rules.heading: Terminology and usage
rules.text: In general, focus on the feature and its functionality, not the UI element; use the name of the UI element only if it adds clarity for the reader.
rules.good: Go to File > Tools.

rules.heading: Terminology and usage
rules.text: Don't use slang terms for UI elements—for example, hamburger icon or zippy.
rules.bad: To expand the Advanced options section, click the zippy.
rules.good: Expand Advanced options.

rules.heading: Terminology and usage
rules.text: Don't use slang terms for UI elements.
rules.why: Slang terms for UI elements aren't clear.
rules.example: To expand the Advanced options section, click the zippy.

rules.heading: Windows, pages, dialogs, panes, and sections
rules.text: Use window for the entire application window in a desktop environment or for modular application elements that you can open and close, not page.
rules.bad: In the MyApp page, click Edit.
rules.good: In the MyApp window, click Edit.

rules.heading: Windows, pages, dialogs, panes, and sections
rules.text: Use page when referring to a web page in general and to a subpage of a console in particular.
rules.bad: In the Google Cloud console, go to the Deployments window.
rules.good: In the Google Cloud console, go to the Deployments page.

rules.heading: Windows, pages, dialogs, panes, and sections
rules.text: Use dialog for a smaller window that is usually detached from the main application window and appears in front of it.
rules.bad: In the Welcome pop-up window, click OK.
rules.good: In the Welcome dialog, click OK.

rules.heading: Windows, pages, dialogs, panes, and sections
rules.text: Do not use terms such as window, section, area, or column to refer to a pane or panel.
rules.bad: In the Create service account section, click New.
rules.good: In the Create service account pane, click New.

rules.heading: Menus and menu bars
rules.text: To refer to an item in a menu, use the term command, not choice, menu item, or option, unless you're documenting how to build an interface.

rules.heading: Menus and menu bars
rules.text: To refer to a menu, use the form the LABEL_NAME menu.

rules.heading: Menus and menu bars
rules.text: To tell the reader where to find a command in a menu or submenu, use a phrase like In the File menu, select Open.
rules.good: In the File menu, select Open.

rules.heading: Menus and menu bars
rules.text: Don't use drop-down as a synonym for menu.

rules.heading: Use angle brackets
rules.text: If you use angle brackets (>) for a menu sequence, put a nonbreaking space ( ) before each angle bracket.

rules.heading: Use angle brackets
rules.text: Don't bold each menu name separately; instead, enclose the entire angle-bracket sequence in a single bold tag.

rules.heading: Use angle brackets
rules.text: Wrap each angle bracket with a span tag and add an aria-label attribute with and then text, for example >.
rules.why: Some screen readers read > as "greater than."

rules.heading: Markdown
rules.text: Use angle-bracket notation only for menu items; don't use it to describe a combination of different UI elements.
rules.bad: Select MyApp > Preferences > Languages > + > CSS.
rules.good: Select MyApp > Preferences, and then select the Languages preference pane.

rules.heading: Navigation menu
rules.text: Use navigation menu for a control that contains a list of items to go to pages in an application or website; don't use the terms navigation bar, navigation pane, navigation panel, or navigation window for such a control.
rules.good: In the BigQuery navigation menu, click Scheduled queries.

rules.heading: Toolbar
rules.text: Refer to the toolbar by name if you think that the user needs help finding a button.
rules.good: On the Google Cloud console toolbar, click notifications_none Notifications.

rules.heading: Toolbar
rules.text: Call a toolbar button that includes a menu a menu button.

rules.heading: Buttons and icons
rules.text: To refer to a button, use the button's label.
rules.bad: Click the "OK" button.
rules.good: Click OK.

rules.heading: Buttons and icons
rules.text: If the button includes an icon, write the name of the button as shown in the tooltip, and add the button icon before the name.
rules.bad: Click more_vert.
rules.good: Click more_vert Settings and utilities.

rules.heading: Buttons and icons
rules.text: If you need to use a space between the icon and the button name for readability, use a nonbreaking space.

rules.heading: Buttons and icons
rules.text: If the icon tooltip is identical to the name of the icon, use an empty alt attribute.

rules.heading: Buttons and icons
rules.text: If a UI element name ends with an ellipsis (...), leave out the ellipsis.
rules.bad: Click Browse....
rules.good: Click Browse.

rules.heading: Buttons and icons
rules.text: Don't use directional language to orient the reader, such as above, below, or right-hand side.
rules.bad: In the left-side panel, click the button with three lines.
rules.good: Click menu Menu.
rules.why: Doesn't work well for accessibility or localization.

rules.heading: Difficult-to-find UI elements
rules.text: If a UI element is hard to find, provide a screenshot.
rules.good: In the list of services, click view_column Column display options.

rules.heading: Difficult-to-find UI elements
rules.text: For difficult-to-find UI elements, use the button icon along with its name as shown in the button tooltip instead of directional language.
rules.good: Click refresh Refresh.

rules.heading: Difficult-to-find UI elements
rules.text: Add context to help the user find a difficult-to-find element.
rules.good: On the Cloud Run toolbar, click refresh Refresh.

rules.heading: Tab
rules.text: To refer to a tab, use the form the LABEL_NAME tab.
rules.good: Select Tools > Options, and then click the Edit tab.

rules.heading: Text box
rules.text: To refer to a text box, use box and the form the LABEL_NAME box.
rules.good: In the Owner box, enter your name.

rules.heading: Text box
rules.text: Format the text that the user types by using the code element in HTML, or by using code formatting (monospace) in other markup.
rules.good: In the Name box, enter wsfc-1.

rules.heading: Text box
rules.text: In Google Cloud and Google Workspace documentation, use field instead of box.
rules.good: In the Instance field, specify a value less than 64 characters long.

rules.heading: List box, combo box, and spin box
rules.text: To refer to a list box, use the form the LABEL_NAME list or the LABEL_NAME box, whichever is clearer.
rules.good: In the Item list, select Desktop.

rules.heading: List box, combo box, and spin box
rules.text: To refer to a combo box, use the form the LABEL_NAME box.
rules.good: In the Font box, type or select the font that you want to use.

rules.heading: List box, combo box, and spin box
rules.text: To refer to entering a value into a combo box, use the verbs type or select or enter.
rules.good: In the Font box, type or select the font that you want to use.

rules.heading: List box, combo box, and spin box
rules.text: To refer to a spin box, use the form the LABEL_NAME box.
rules.good: In the Font Size box, enter a font size.

rules.heading: List box, combo box, and spin box
rules.text: To refer to entering a value into a spin box, use the verb enter.
rules.good: In the Font Size box, enter a font size.

rules.heading: Checkbox
rules.text: To refer to a checkbox, use the form the LABEL_NAME checkbox.
rules.good: Select the Automatically check for updates checkbox.

rules.heading: Checkbox
rules.text: Be wary of using the verbs check and uncheck for checkboxes; it's often best to use select and clear instead.
rules.good: Clear the Bookmarks checkbox.
rules.why: Check and uncheck can be ambiguous.

rules.heading: Checkbox
rules.text: If you need to refer to the state of a checkbox, refer to it as selected or not selected.
rules.good: Make sure that the Bookmarks checkbox isn't selected.

rules.heading: Radio button
rules.text: To refer to a radio button, use the radio button's label, or refer to the group of buttons by its label.
rules.good: For Startup mode, select an option.

rules.heading: Expander arrow
rules.text: Avoid referring to expander arrows explicitly, but when you do, use the terms expander arrow and expandable section rather than terms like expando or zippy.
rules.bad: To expand the Advanced options section, click the zippy.
rules.good: To expand the Advanced options section, click the arrow_right expander arrow.

rules.heading: Toggle
rules.text: Don't use the word toggle as a verb; describe the action that you want the user to take.
rules.good: To turn on the setting, click the Wi-Fi toggle.

rules.heading: Toggle
rules.text: If you might not know what state the toggle is in before the user interacts with it, be clear what position the toggle should be in.
rules.good: In Settings, click the Magic mode toggle to the on position.

rules.heading: Toggle
rules.text: Don't use the word toggle as a verb.
rules.why: Describe the action the user takes instead.
rules.example: Toggling the setting turns on Wi-Fi.

rules.heading: Press and type keyboard keys
rules.text: To indicate that the user should press a given keyboard key or combination, use the kbd element.
rules.good: Press <kbd>Control+C</kbd>.

rules.heading: Press and type keyboard keys
rules.text: If you're working with non-HTML markup, use monospace formatting for keys, which is how the kbd element renders.

rules.heading: Press and type keyboard keys
rules.text: To refer to a letter key, use uppercase instead of lowercase.
rules.bad: To save, press Control+s.
rules.good: To save, press Control+S.

rules.heading: Press and type keyboard keys
rules.text: To refer to a key that the user types to enter that key's value as text input, use the code element, not the kbd element.

rules.heading: Press and type keyboard keys
rules.text: To refer to a keyboard key, use the key's name; if that's ambiguous, use the form the KEY_NAME key.
rules.good: Press the Esc key.

rules.heading: Press and type keyboard keys
rules.text: Spell out the names of modifier keys such as Command, Control, Option, and Shift, and don't use symbols for those keys.
rules.bad: To copy, press Ctrl+C (⌘+C).
rules.good: To copy, press Control+C (or Command+C on macOS).

rules.heading: Press and type keyboard keys
rules.text: To refer to a key combination, use the form MODIFIER+KEY_NAME.
rules.good: Press Control+V.

rules.heading: Press and type keyboard keys
rules.text: When you provide shortcuts for multiple operating systems, put the macOS shortcut in parentheses after the Windows and Linux shortcut.
rules.bad: To copy, press Ctrl+C (⌘+C).
rules.good: To copy, press Control+C (or Command+C on macOS).

rules.heading: Press and type keyboard keys
rules.text: To refer to a key or combination that uses the Shift key, use the form MODIFIER+Shift+KEY_NAME.
rules.good: Press Control+Shift+?.

rules.heading: Press and type keyboard keys
rules.text: Spell out the names of characters that could be confusing in a keyboard shortcut, such as comma, hyphen, period, and plus.

rules.heading: Press and type keyboard keys
rules.text: To refer to a keyboard shortcut, use either keyboard shortcut or key combination.

rules.heading: Press and type keyboard keys
rules.text: To refer to pressing a key or combination to cause an action to occur, use the verb press.
rules.good: Press Esc.

rules.heading: Press and type keyboard keys
rules.text: To refer to typing a key or combination as part of text, use the verbs enter or type.

rules.heading: Press and type keyboard keys
rules.text: Spell out the names of modifier keys.
rules.why: Spell out modifier key names.
rules.example: To copy, press Ctrl+C.

rules.heading: Press and type keyboard keys
rules.text: To refer to a letter key, use uppercase instead of lowercase.
rules.why: Letter keys are written in uppercase.
rules.example: To save, press Control+s.

rules.heading: Press and type keyboard keys
rules.text: Don't use symbols for modifier keys.
rules.why: Spell out modifier key names.
rules.example: To copy, press Ctrl+C (⌘+C).

rules.heading: Press and type keyboard keys
rules.text: To refer to a key combination, use the form MODIFIER+KEY_NAME, without spaces.
rules.why: Key combinations use the form MODIFIER+KEY_NAME.
rules.example: Press Control + V.

rules.heading: Press and type keyboard keys
rules.text: Use the form MODIFIER+Shift+KEY_NAME, with Shift after the other modifier.
rules.why: Shift goes after the other modifier.
rules.example: Press Shift+Control+?.

rules.heading: Prepositions
rules.text: Use the preposition in with dialogs, fields, lists, menus, panes, and windows.
rules.good: In the Alert dialog, click OK.

rules.heading: Prepositions
rules.text: Use the preposition on with pages, tabs, and toolbars.
rules.good: On the Create an instance page, click Add.

rules.heading: Verbs in procedures
rules.text: To describe an action on the page, use the following verbs: click, choose, drag, enable, enter, type, go to, hold the pointer over, press, select, tap, turn on, and turn off.

rules.heading: HTML and semantic tagging
rules.text: Use HTML elements for the purposes that they were designed for.
rules.why: Semantic tagging conveys meaning, not just appearance.

rules.heading: HTML and semantic tagging
rules.text: When you give the title of a standalone work (such as a book or a movie), mark it with a cite element.

rules.heading: HTML and semantic tagging
rules.text: In situations where there are no semantically relevant HTML elements, use CSS or the few HTML elements that convey visual style without semantics.

rules.heading: Visual formatting
rules.text: If you want to achieve specific visual results, don't use HTML elements that convey different semantics.

rules.heading: Visual formatting
rules.text: Don't use frames or tables for layout; instead, use your site's CSS to lay out the page.

rules.heading: Visual formatting
rules.text: Don't use the heading elements (such as h1 and h2) to visually style text; use those elements only for hierarchically structured headings, and use CSS for visual style.

rules.heading: Visual formatting
rules.text: Don't use the em element to italicize something that isn't meant to be emphasized; instead, use the i element for non-emphasis italics.
rules.why: The em element indicates emphasis, not italics as such.

rules.heading: Visual formatting
rules.text: To bold a word that doesn't merit strong importance, use the b element, not the strong element.
rules.why: The strong element indicates strong importance, not bold as such.

rules.heading: Visual formatting
rules.text: Don't use the br element to adjust the spacing between lines; instead, use elements like p to semantically mark the text, and use CSS to adjust line spacing.
rules.why: br is only for line breaks that are part of content.

rules.heading: Visual formatting
rules.text: Don't use consecutive br elements to adjust the spacing between lines; use p elements and CSS.
rules.why: br is only for line breaks that are part of content.
rules.example:
First paragraph.
