not_applicable.reason: Introduction to the list of guidelines.

rules.heading: Example domains and names
rules.text: Don't use real domain names, email addresses, or people's names in your examples.
rules.why: Real data in examples can expose real people or organizations.

rules.heading: Example domains and names
rules.text: Don't reveal personally identifiable information (PII), such as domain names, email addresses, phone numbers, people's names, project names, or credit card numbers; provide imaginary (fictitious) examples or use placeholders, like USER_ID or EMAIL_ADDRESS.
rules.why: Protects privacy of real people.

rules.heading: Example domain names
rules.text: When you need a generic domain name in an example, use example.com, example.org, or example.net, or one of the domains Google owns for documentation: altostrat.com, examplepetstore.com, example-pet-store.com, myownpersonaldomain.com, my-own-personal-domain.com, or cymbalgroup.com.
rules.why: These domains are reserved for use in documentation.

rules.heading: Example domain names
rules.text: If you need an example domain name for an internationalized domain name, use one of the IDN Test TLDs and copy from the "URL of the test site" column.
rules.good: Hostnames that include non-ASCII characters are encoded using Punycode. For example, http://مثال.إختبار is encoded as xn--kgbechtv.

rules.heading: Example email addresses
rules.text: If you need a generic email address, use one of the listed example domain names and one of the listed example person names—for example, dana@example.com; generic addresses like support@example.net are OK.
rules.good: dana@example.com

rules.heading: Example email addresses
rules.text: Don't use person names, product names, or made-up names in email addresses.

rules.heading: Example person names
rules.text: When you need to include example given names, draw from the following list: Alex, Amal, Ariel, Bola, Charlie, Cruz, Dana, Dani, Hao, Ira, Izumi, Jie, Kai, Kalani, Kim, Kiran, Lee, Lucian, Luka, Mahan, Noam, Nur, Quinn, Raha, Rosario, Sasha, Tal, Taylor, Tristan, Yuri.

rules.heading: Example person surnames
rules.text: When you need to include example surnames, use an initial after the given first name—for example, Quinn N. or Dana A.
rules.good: Quinn N.

rules.heading: Further notes about example people
rules.text: Strive to include a variety of people in your examples, so that real readers with different jobs, cultural contexts, and backgrounds feel respected, valued, and welcomed.
rules.why: Your audience includes many different kinds of people.

rules.heading: Further notes about example people
rules.text: Use the gender-neutral singular pronouns they, their, and theirs whenever possible, and avoid specifying gender unless it is integral to the information you are communicating.

rules.heading: Further notes about example people
rules.text: Avoid examples that depend on a gender binary.

rules.heading: Further notes about example people
rules.text: If an example requires specifying gender, check that the names you have chosen do not carry a conflicting gender connotation in a given language or culture.

rules.heading: Further notes about example people
rules.text: Be mindful of assumptions and stereotypes that hypothetical examples might reinforce, such as job roles and levels (like executive) disproportionately assigned gendered personas, or job roles (like developer or engineer) disproportionately assigned particular ethnic personas.

rules.heading: Further notes about example people
rules.text: Don't use the Alice and Bob characters unless you're writing documentation that refers to a technical specification that uses those characters.

rules.heading: Further notes about example people
rules.text: If you use the Alice and Bob characters in a document, use only names from that cast of characters.

rules.heading: Example company names
rules.text: When you need a company name in an example, use Example Organization; to differentiate between two fictional companies, add a description, such as Enterprise Example Organization and Startup Example Organization.

rules.heading: Example phone numbers
rules.text: To show an example phone number, use a US number in the range 800‑555‑0100 through 800‑555‑0199, and never use a real phone number in examples.
rules.why: That range is reserved for use in examples and fiction.

rules.heading: Example phone numbers
rules.text: Use a phone number in the range 800‑555‑0100 through 800‑555‑0199 for examples.
rules.why: Never use a real phone number in examples.
rules.example: Call 650-253-0000 for support.

rules.heading: Example IP addresses
rules.text: When you need an IPv4 address in an example, such as in a log, use one of the RFC 5737 addresses reserved for documentation: 192.0.2.0 through 192.0.2.255, 198.51.100.0 through 198.51.100.255, or 203.0.113.0 through 203.0.113.255.
rules.why: These addresses are reserved for use in documentation.

rules.heading: Example IP addresses
rules.text: When you need an IPv6 address, use values from the RFC 3849 range, such as 2001:db8::, 2001:db8:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff, or 2001:db8:1:1:1:1:1:1.

rules.heading: Example IP addresses
rules.text: For IPv6 address ranges, use 2001:db8::/32.

rules.heading: Example street addresses
rules.text: Avoid using real street addresses in examples; instead, use one of these fictional addresses: 1800 Amphibious Blvd. Mountain View, CA 94045; Avenida da Pastelaria, 1903 Lisbon, 1229-076; or 8 Rue du Nom Fictif 341 Paris.

rules.heading: Example project names
rules.text: When you need an example project name, create a name that's meaningful or descriptive and applicable to the reader's environment.

rules.heading: Example project names
rules.text: Don't use unclear components like foo, bar, and baz in names.

rules.heading: Example project names
rules.text: When necessary, use an appended numbering scheme for project names, for example, production-1, production-2.
rules.good: staging, frontend-development, backend-development, production-1, production-2

rules.heading: Example project names
rules.text: Don't use unclear components like foo, bar, and baz in names.
rules.why: Unclear names aren't meaningful to readers.
rules.example: Create a project named foo.

rules.heading: Example service account IDs
rules.text: When you need a unique ID for a service account in an example, use the numeric ID 123456789012345678901.
rules.good: The allow policy shows the identifier deleted:serviceAccount:my-service-account@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com?uid=123456789012345678901.

rules.heading: Word list
rules.text: If there are multiple spellings in the Merriam-Webster word entry, use the first form listed, which is the most common spelling.
rules.bad: cancelled
rules.good: canceled
rules.why: The first listed form is the most common spelling.

rules.heading: Word list
rules.text: For a term marked "use with caution", avoid using the term when possible or use a more specific term; where appropriate, define the term or use it only once, as explained on the Jargon page.
rules.why: The term might be ambiguous or obscure.

rules.heading: Word list
rules.text: Don't use a term marked "don't use" in any case.
rules.why: Ambiguous, or offensive or non-inclusive association.

rules.heading: Word list
rules.text: If a term marked "don't use" appears in code, replace or write around the term.
rules.why: Ambiguous, or offensive or non-inclusive association.

rules.heading: Word list
rules.text: Use canceled, not cancelled, because Merriam-Webster lists canceled first.
rules.why: Merriam-Webster lists canceled first as the more common form.
rules.example: The job was cancelled before it finished.

rules.heading: Numbers and Symbols
rules.text: It's OK to use + with numbers in text, such as customer records with 300+ demographic attributes, except in formal contexts.
rules.good: customer records with 300+ demographic attributes

rules.heading: Numbers and Symbols
rules.text: Don't use & instead of and in headings, text, navigation, or tables of contents; use & only when referencing UI elements that use &, in table headings and diagram labels where space constraints require abbreviation, or for technical purposes in code.

rules.heading: Numbers and Symbols
rules.text: When referring to Google's 2-Step Verification, use initial caps; when referring to generic 2-step verification, use lowercase.

rules.heading: Numbers and Symbols
rules.text: Use either initial caps (2-Step Verification) or all lowercase (2-step verification), never mixed casing.
rules.why: Mixed casing matches neither the Google feature nor generic term.
rules.example: Turn on 2-Step verification for your account.

rules.heading: a and an
rules.text: Use a when the next word starts with a consonant sound, regardless of what letter it starts with.
rules.why: The article follows the sound, not the letter.

rules.heading: A/B testing
rules.text: Capitalize and use slash notation for A/B.
rules.example: Run a/b testing on the landing page.

rules.heading: abnormal
rules.text: Don't use abnormal to refer to a person; it's OK to use it to refer to a condition of a computer system.

rules.heading: abort
rules.text: Avoid abort in general usage; instead, use words like stop, exit, cancel, or end.
rules.why: In Linux, abort is a specific signal type.

rules.heading: about versus on
rules.text: When a cross-reference includes information that describes what the cross-reference links to, use about instead of on.
rules.bad: For more information on indexes, see Managing indexes.
rules.good: For more information about indexes, see Managing indexes.

rules.heading: above
rules.text: Don't use above for a range of version numbers; instead, use later.

rules.heading: above
rules.text: Don't use above to refer to a position in a document; instead, use earlier or preceding.

rules.heading: above
rules.text: Don't use above to refer to a position in the UI; instead, write instructions that avoid directional language.
rules.why: Directional language isn't accessible.

rules.heading: access (verb)
rules.text: Avoid access as a verb when you can; instead, use friendlier words like see, edit, find, use, or view.

rules.heading: access token
rules.text: Lowercase access token except at the beginning of a sentence, heading, or list item.
rules.example: Create an Access Token for the app.

rules.heading: account name
rules.text: Don't use account name; instead, use username.
rules.example: Enter your account name and password.

rules.heading: actionable
rules.text: Avoid actionable unless it's the clearest and simplest phrasing for your audience; instead, leave it out or replace it with a phrase like that you can act on or useful.

rules.heading: actionable
rules.text: Don't use actionable in the legal sense without consulting a lawyer.

rules.heading: action bar
rules.text: In Android documentation, don't use action bar; instead, use app bar.
rules.why: App bar replaced the former term action bar.

rules.heading: ad tech
rules.text: Write out ad tech on first mention: advertising technology (ad tech).

rules.heading: ad tech
rules.text: Don't use adtech or ad-tech; use ad tech.
rules.example: Measure your adtech spending.

rules.heading: address bar
rules.text: Use address bar to refer to the URL bar or the combined URL bar and search box in a browser; don't use omnibox.
rules.example: Type the URL in the omnibox.

rules.heading: ad hoc
rules.text: Use ad hoc only in database and analytics contexts to mean free-form or user-written; for other contexts, try to find a more specific English equivalent.

rules.heading: ad hoc
rules.text: Don't italicize ad hoc.

rules.heading: ad hoc
rules.text: Don't hyphenate ad hoc.
rules.example: Run an ad-hoc query.

rules.heading: admin
rules.text: Write out administrator unless admin is the name of a UI label or other element; it's OK to use admin in Android documentation.

rules.heading: administrator
rules.text: In Android documentation, don't use administrator; instead, use admin.

rules.heading: advertised route priority
rules.text: Don't shorten or use variations of advertised route priority or base advertised route priority; base advertised route priority is OK when discussing region-to-region costs.

rules.heading: agnostic
rules.text: Don't use agnostic; instead, use a more precise term like platform-independent.
rules.example: The library is platform agnostic.

rules.heading: AI
rules.text: You can use AI without spelling out artificial intelligence, but if you think your audience isn't familiar with the term, spell it out on first use.
rules.why: Most readers are familiar with the abbreviation AI.

rules.heading: aka
rules.text: Don't use aka; instead, write out also known as, or present an alternative term using parentheses or the word or.
rules.good: Geographic data, also known as geospatial data, is ...
rules.example: Geographic data, aka geospatial data, is used here.

rules.heading: all apps screen
rules.text: In Android documentation, lowercase all apps screen except at the beginning of a sentence, heading, or list item.
rules.bad: Open the All Apps screen.
rules.good: Open the all apps screen.

rules.heading: allowlist (verb), allowlisted, allowlisting
rules.text: Don't use allowlist as a verb; instead, rewrite to improve clarity. It's OK to use allowlist as a noun.

rules.heading: allowlist (verb), allowlisted, allowlisting
rules.text: Don't use allowlisted or allowlisting; rewrite to improve clarity.
rules.example: Make sure your IP address is allowlisted.

rules.heading: allows you to
rules.text: Don't use allows you to; instead, use lets you.
rules.example: This feature allows you to export data.

rules.heading: alpha
rules.text: Lowercase alpha except when it's part of a product name.
rules.good: PRODUCT_NAME is in alpha.

rules.heading: America, American
rules.text: Use America and American only to refer to the Americas or the American continent; to refer to the United States, use a more precise term like the US or the United States, and people in the US.

rules.heading: AM, PM
rules.text: Use all caps, no periods, and a space before AM and PM.
rules.why: Consistent with Material Design.
rules.example: The job runs at 9:00 am every day.

rules.heading: and/or
rules.text: Don't use and/or unless space is limited, such as in a table.

rules.heading: Android
rules.text: When referring to the operating system, capitalize Android.

rules.heading: Android-powered device
rules.text: Use Android-powered device, not Android device.
rules.example: Install the app on your Android device.

rules.heading: and so on
rules.text: Avoid using and so on whenever possible.
rules.example: Supported formats include CSV, JSON, and so on.

rules.heading: anti-pattern
rules.text: Avoid using anti-pattern, particularly as a standalone heading; instead, consider using a more specific and broadly understood term.
rules.bad: Avoid these five SQL anti-patterns.
rules.good: Avoid these five programming practices that make SQL queries inefficient.

rules.heading: API
rules.text: Use API to refer to either a web API or a language-specific API; don't use API when referring to a method or a class.
rules.bad: This resource has one API.
rules.good: This resource has one method.

rules.heading: API Console, APIs console, developer console, dev console, or Google API Console
rules.text: Don't use API Console, APIs console, developer console, dev console, or Google API Console; instead, refer to the Google APIs Explorer or to the Google Cloud console.
rules.avoid: API Console, APIs console, developer console, dev console
rules.example: Open the API Console and create a project.

rules.heading: API Console key
rules.text: In most contexts, use API key instead of API Console key; in Apps admin APIs, it's OK to use API Console key to distinguish from other API keys.

rules.heading: API key
rules.text: Use API key, not developer key or dev key.
rules.example: Copy your developer key into the request.

rules.heading: APIs Explorer
rules.text: Use APIs Explorer, not API explorer or other variants.
rules.avoid: API explorer, API Explorer, APIs explorer
rules.example: Try the method in the API explorer.

rules.heading: app
rules.text: In general, use app instead of application when referring to programs for end users, especially for mobile or web software; application is OK in enterprise contexts and in standard phrases such as application programming interface.

rules.heading: appendix
rules.text: Use the plural appendixes, not appendices.
rules.example: See the appendices for details.

rules.heading: as
rules.text: If you mean because, then use because instead of as.
rules.why: As is ambiguous; it can refer to time.

rules.heading: as of this writing
rules.text: Avoid as of this writing because this phrase is implied.
rules.bad: As of this writing, BigQuery doesn't support that function.
rules.good: BigQuery doesn't support that function.
rules.why: Can disclose strategy or imply future change.

rules.heading: as of this writing
rules.text: Avoid as of this writing.
rules.avoid: as of this writing, As of this writing
rules.example: As of this writing, BigQuery doesn't support that function.

rules.heading: authentication and authorization
rules.text: In general, use authenticated only to refer to users, and use authorized only to refer to requests that are sent by a client app on behalf of an authenticated user.

rules.heading: authentication and authorization
rules.text: When you want to use a preposition with authenticate, use against.

rules.heading: authN, authZ
rules.text: Don't use authN or authZ; instead, use authentication or authorization.
rules.example: Configure authN for the service.

rules.heading: autohealing
rules.text: Use autohealing, not auto-healing.
rules.example: Turn on auto-healing for the group.

rules.heading: auto mode VPC network
rules.text: Use auto mode VPC network, not auto mode network.
rules.example: Create an auto mode network in your project.

rules.heading: autopopulate
rules.text: Use autopopulate, not auto populate or auto-populate.
rules.example: The form fields auto-populate when you sign in.

rules.heading: autoscaling
rules.text: Use autoscaling, not auto-scaling.
rules.example: Enable auto-scaling for the cluster.

rules.heading: autotagging
rules.text: Use autotagging, not auto-tagging.
rules.example: Turn on auto-tagging in your account.

rules.heading: autoupdate
rules.text: Don't use autoupdate; instead, use automatically update.
rules.example: The app will autoupdate overnight.

rules.heading: -aware
rules.text: Avoid using -aware as a compound modifier, as in healthcare-aware; it's OK when it's part of a product name, such as Identity-Aware Proxy.

rules.heading: backend
rules.why: Google spells it as one word.
rules.example: Deploy the back-end service.

rules.heading: bar
rules.text: Avoid using bar when possible.
rules.why: Metasyntactic placeholder names are unclear.

rules.heading: baz
rules.text: Avoid using baz when possible.
rules.why: Metasyntactic placeholder names are unclear.

rules.heading: bare metal
rules.text: Lowercase bare metal except at the beginning of a sentence, heading, or list item.

rules.heading: bare metal
rules.text: Hyphenate bare metal when used as a compound modifier, such as bare-metal server.
rules.good: bare-metal server

rules.heading: bare metal
rules.text: Hyphenate bare-metal when used as a compound modifier.
rules.why: Compound modifiers are hyphenated.
rules.example: Create a bare metal server.

rules.heading: base64
rules.text: Lowercase base64 except at the beginning of a sentence, heading, or list item; otherwise, capitalize Base64 only if it's part of a formal name.

rules.heading: base64
rules.text: Write base64 in code font only if it's a string literal or otherwise quoted from code.

rules.heading: below
rules.text: Don't use below for a range of version numbers; instead, use earlier.

rules.heading: below
rules.text: Don't use below to refer to a position in a document; instead, use later or following.
rules.why: Directional language isn't accessible.

rules.heading: below
rules.text: Don't use below to refer to a position in the UI; instead, write instructions that avoid directional language.
rules.why: Directional language isn't accessible.

rules.heading: below
rules.text: It's OK to use below in set phrases such as below (the) average, below the mean, below zero, and in a non-directional way, such as when describing a hierarchy.

rules.heading: best effort
rules.text: Avoid best effort where possible; instead, use more specific wording, and after providing a description, you can add a phrase like "sometimes referred to as best effort."
rules.why: Specific wording is clearer.

rules.heading: beta
rules.text: Lowercase beta except when part of a product name.
rules.good: PRODUCT_NAME is currently in beta.

rules.heading: between versus among
rules.text: Use between when you're talking about two or more distinct things, and use among when you're talking about things that are part of a group or things that aren't distinct.
rules.bad: You can share services between multiple clients.
rules.good: You can share services among multiple clients.
rules.why: Between isn't interchangeable with among.

rules.heading: big-endian
rules.text: Hyphenate big-endian, and lowercase it except at the beginning of a sentence, heading, or list item.
rules.bad: The codebase assumes Big-endian byte ordering.
rules.good: The codebase assumes big-endian byte ordering.

rules.heading: big-endian
rules.why: Hyphenate and lowercase.
rules.example: The codebase assumes big endian byte ordering.

rules.heading: billing charges
rules.text: Don't use billing charges to mean charges that appear on a bill; instead, use billed charges, and use billing charges to describe the cost of creating the bill.

rules.heading: black-box
rules.text: Avoid using black-box, blackbox, or black box to describe monitoring and testing; for monitoring, use synthetic monitoring, and for testing, use opaque-box testing.
rules.why: A more precise term is clearer.

rules.heading: black-box
rules.avoid: black-box testing, blackbox testing, black box testing
rules.why: Use a more precise term.

rules.text: Use primitive with caution, and don't use primitive in a disparaging sense.

rules.heading: project
rules.text: Use Google Cloud project on first mention and in any context in which there might be ambiguity about what kind of project you're referring to.

rules.heading: proper, properly
rules.text: Avoid proper and properly, which are vague and can imply subjective judgments of correctness or superiority; instead, focus on describing the technical details.
rules.bad: Ensure the port is properly configured.
rules.good: Verify that the port is open and accepting connections.

rules.heading: pros
rules.text: Don't use pros; instead, use a more precise term, such as advantages.
rules.why: Use a more precise term, such as advantages.
rules.example: Consider the pros of each option.

rules.heading: quick, quickly
rules.text: Try eliminating quick or quickly from the sentence; what might be quick for you might not be quick for others.
rules.why: What might be quick for you might not be for others.

rules.heading: quota
rules.text: Where possible, use a more specific term than quota for API usage limits, such as usage limit.
rules.why: Quota means many different things to many different people.

rules.heading: quota
rules.text: In Google Cloud documentation, where quota is the standard term, use quota.
rules.why: Quota is the standard term in Google Cloud documentation.

rules.heading: RDP
rules.text: Don't use RDP as a verb; instead, use connect using RDP, or connect if it's clear from context that they're using RDP.

rules.heading: read-only
rules.text: Always hyphenate read-only; don't write read only.

rules.heading: recents screen
rules.text: In Android contexts, use recents screen instead of overview screen.

rules.heading: redline
rules.text: Don't use redline as a verb; instead, use precise terms appropriate to the context, such as tracking changes or priority lining.

rules.heading: regex
rules.text: Don't use regex. Instead, use regular expression.
rules.example: Enter a regex to filter the results.

rules.heading: rehost
rules.text: Use rehost to describe the migration of an app or workload with no changes or minimal changes to that app or workload.

rules.heading: rehost
rules.text: On first mention, associate rehost with lift and shift.
rules.good: You can use this reference architecture to efficiently rehost (lift and shift) on-premises applications to the cloud.

rules.heading: rehost
rules.text: Don't use the forklift approach.
rules.example: Migrate the app using the forklift approach.

rules.heading: repo
rules.text: Don't use repo. Instead, use repository.
rules.example: Clone the repo to your computer.

rules.heading: Representational State Transfer
rules.text: Don't use Representational State Transfer; refer to it as REST and don't explain what it stands for.
rules.why: The expansion is meaningless to people unfamiliar with REST.
rules.example: The API follows Representational State Transfer principles.

rules.heading: reservation, off the
rules.text: Don't use off the reservation.
rules.example: This configuration goes off the reservation.

rules.heading: resource record set
rules.text: Use resource record set, not resource recordset.
rules.example: Add a resource recordset to the zone.

rules.heading: retarded
rules.text: Don't use retarded. If you are referring to a system or component being slowed, use the word slowed.
rules.example: The process is retarded by network latency.

rules.heading: retriable, triable
rules.text: Don't use retriable or triable, unless a code item uses that spelling; outside of code font, write around the term.
rules.example: The request is retriable.

rules.heading: retryable, tryable
rules.text: Where possible, write around retryable and tryable; for example, write out you can try it again or can be tried again.
rules.example: The error is retryable.

rules.heading: review
rules.text: If you mean "read, potentially for the first time," then use read instead of review; use review only to mean "read critically, commenting on problems."
rules.bad: If you've never heard of OAuth, then review the OAuth documentation.

rules.heading: RFC
rules.text: When referencing an RFC specification, use a space between RFC and the number (for example, RFC 2318).
rules.example: For details, see RFC2318.

rules.heading: roll out
rules.text: Don't use roll out to mean a sudden or instantaneous launch; if you use roll out, define what you mean, and when possible use a more precise, non-figurative term like gradual, in stages, phases, or progressive.

rules.heading: RTFM
rules.text: Don't use RTFM. Instead, use a more precise phrase like "For more information, see ...."
rules.example: If you're stuck, RTFM.

rules.heading: runbook
rules.text: Use runbook, not run book.
rules.example: Follow the steps in the run book.

rules.heading: runtime, run time
rules.text: Use the noun runtime when referring to the environment in which software runs, such as a Ruby or Java runtime.
rules.good: The App Engine standard environment has two generations of runtime environments. The second-generation runtimes significantly improve the capabilities of App Engine.

rules.heading: runtime, run time
rules.text: Use the noun phrase run time when referring to the time during program execution when something occurs, as contrasted with compile time.
rules.good: The profiler collects data at run time, and the scheduler uses this data at compile time to improve performance for subsequent runs.

rules.heading: SaaS
rules.text: Write out on first mention: software as a service (SaaS).
rules.good: software as a service (SaaS)

rules.heading: sane
rules.text: Don't use sane; instead use a word like valid or sensible.
rules.example: Make sure that the input values are sane.

rules.heading: sanity check
rules.text: Don't use sanity check; instead, use a term like quick check, confidence check, preliminary check, or coherence check.
rules.example: Run a sanity check before you deploy.

rules.heading: SAP
rules.text: Write an SAP system, not a SAP system.
rules.bad: a SAP system
rules.good: an SAP system
rules.why: SAP is pronounced as individual letters.
rules.example: Connect to a SAP system.

rules.heading: scale
rules.text: Don't use scale alone to say that something is large or increasing.
rules.bad: The system performs better at scale.
rules.good: The system performs better at a larger scale.

rules.heading: scale
rules.text: Include supporting words to indicate magnitude or direction of change, such as scaling up or down, or scaling out or in.
rules.bad: The system scales quickly.
rules.good: The system scales up quickly, but it scales down more slowly.

rules.heading: screenshot (noun)
rules.text: Don't use screenshot as a verb; instead, use take a screenshot.
rules.bad: Screenshot the dialog.
rules.good: Take a screenshot of the dialog.

rules.heading: screenshot (noun)
rules.text: Use screenshot, not screen shot or screensnap.
rules.example: Take a screen shot of the dialog.

rules.heading: scroll
rules.text: If possible, instead of scroll, use a term that isn't specific to implementation.
rules.bad: scroll to the section
rules.good: go to the section

rules.heading: scroll
rules.text: If you use scroll, don't use directional language like scroll up.
rules.why: Directional language isn't accessible.
rules.example: Scroll up to the Settings section.

rules.heading: Search (as part of product name)
rules.text: Capitalize Search when referring to a product like Google Search.
rules.good: Google Search

rules.heading: Search Console
rules.text: Capitalize each word in Search Console.
rules.example: Verify your site in search console.

rules.heading: select
rules.text: Use select to describe choosing an item from among multiple options, selecting text, or marking a checkbox.
rules.bad: Check Automatically check for updates.
rules.good: Select Automatically check for updates.

rules.heading: service
rules.text: If the term services leads to ambiguity, then use the product names.

rules.heading: service level agreement
rules.text: Lowercase service level agreement when referring to service level agreements in general; use title case (Service Level Agreement) only when referring to a specific document.

rules.heading: service level agreement
rules.text: Abbreviate service level agreement, service level indicator, and service level objective as SLA, SLI, and SLO only after first use.
rules.term: service level agreement, service level indicator, service level objective

rules.heading: service level indicator
rules.text: Lowercase service level indicator and service level objective except at the beginning of a sentence, heading, or list item.
rules.term: service level indicator, service level objective

rules.heading: service level indicator
rules.text: Don't use title case for service level indicator or service level objective.
rules.avoid: Service Level Indicator, Service Level Objective
rules.example: Define a Service Level Objective for latency.

rules.heading: setup (noun or adjective), set up (verb)
rules.text: Use setup as a noun or adjective and set up as a verb.

rules.heading: sexy
rules.text: Don't use sexy; instead, use precise, positive words, such as fast, powerful, or elegant.
rules.example: The new dashboard is sexy.

rules.heading: SHA-1
rules.text: Use SHA-1, not SHA1, except in string literals/enums and in hyphenated phrases such as HSA-SHA1.
rules.example: The file is signed with SHA1.

rules.heading: shall
rules.text: Avoid shall except under advice from a lawyer.
rules.example: The user shall provide a valid key.

rules.heading: she, her, hers
rules.text: Don't use a gendered pronoun except for a specific individual of known gender.

rules.heading: she, her, hers
rules.text: Use they and their for the general singular pronoun.

rules.heading: sherpa
rules.text: If possible, use a more precise term than sherpa; for example, if you mean guide, use that term.

rules.heading: shift left
rules.text: Avoid using shift left to mean moving something earlier in time; instead, use a less figurative phrase, such as shift earlier or move to an earlier phase.
rules.why: Assumes the natural flow is left to right.

rules.heading: should, should be
rules.text: Generally avoid should, because it's ambiguous.
rules.why: Should is ambiguous by definition.

rules.heading: sign-in (noun or adjective), sign in (verb)
rules.text: Use sign-in and sign-out as nouns or adjectives, and sign in and sign out as verbs.
rules.term: sign-in (noun or adjective), sign in (verb), sign-out (noun or adjective), sign out (verb)

rules.heading: sign-in (noun or adjective), sign in (verb)
rules.text: Use sign in and sign out, not log in, signin, log out, or signout.
rules.avoid: log in, signin, log out, signout
rules.example: Log in to the console.

rules.heading: sign into
rules.text: Don't use sign into; instead, use sign in to.
rules.example: Sign into your account.

rules.heading: sign-on, sign on
rules.text: Don't use sign-on or sign on on its own; use the hyphenated version as part of single sign-on.
rules.good: single sign-on
rules.example: Configure sign-on for your users.

rules.heading: single sign-on (noun or adjective)
rules.text: Write single sign-on with a hyphen.
rules.good: single sign-on
rules.example: Enable single sign on for your domain.

rules.heading: simple, simply
rules.text: Try eliminating simple or simply from the sentence, because usually the same meaning can be conveyed without it.
rules.why: What's simple for you might not be for others.

rules.heading: since
rules.text: If you mean because, then use because instead of since.
rules.why: Since can refer to the passage of time.

rules.heading: single most
rules.text: Use single most, not singlemost.
rules.example: This is the singlemost important setting.

rules.heading: single pane of glass
rules.text: Avoid single pane of glass; it can almost always be replaced by single interface or unified interface.
rules.example: Monitor all clusters from a single pane of glass.

rules.heading: slave
rules.text: If you're replacing master and slave together, consider combinations such as primary/secondary, primary/replica, original/replica, controller/worker, initiator/responder, mixer/leaf, aggregator/collector, publisher/subscriber, leader/follower, and active/standby.

rules.heading: slave
rules.text: If the command or code that you're documenting uses the literal word slave, use it only in direct reference to the code item (formatted as code), make it clear what you're referring to, and use the new term thereafter.
rules.good: Invoke the secondary (slave) process directly when debugging issues between the primary and secondary processes.

rules.heading: slave
rules.text: Don't use slave; instead, use alternative terms appropriate to your domain, such as worker or replica.
rules.example: The master sends writes to the slave.

rules.heading: slice and dice
rules.text: Don't use the phrase slice and dice; instead, use specific terms appropriate to the task, such as segment data for analysis or break information into smaller parts.
rules.example: Use the report to slice and dice your data.

rules.heading: smartphone, smart phone
rules.text: Don't use smartphone or smart phone; instead, use mobile phone or phone, or mobile device if you're talking about more than phones.
rules.example: Open the app on your smartphone.

rules.heading: soon
rules.text: Avoid soon in timeless documentation.
rules.bad: This setting is optional for existing applications but will soon be required for all applications.
rules.good: This setting is optional.
rules.why: Can become outdated or disclose product strategy.

rules.heading: spin up
rules.text: Avoid using spin up unless you're referring to a hard disk; instead, use a less colloquial term like create or start.
rules.bad: spin up an instance
rules.good: create an instance

rules.heading: SQL
rules.text: Refer to a SQL, not an SQL.
rules.why: SQL is pronounced "sequel."
rules.example: Run an SQL query.

rules.heading: ssh and SSH
rules.text: Don't use ssh or SSH as a verb.
rules.bad: ssh into your remote shell.
rules.good: Connect to the instance by using SSH.
rules.why: SSH is a protocol; ssh is a utility.

rules.heading: ssh'ing
rules.text: Don't use ssh'ing.
rules.good: When you use ssh to log in ...
rules.example: After ssh'ing into the VM, run the script.

rules.heading: startup (noun or adjective), start up (verb)
rules.text: Use startup as a noun or adjective and start up as a verb.

rules.heading: static external IP address
rules.text: Don't use static IP address or external IP address to refer to static external IP addresses.

rules.heading: status bar
rules.text: Lowercase status bar except at the beginning of a sentence, heading, or list item.

rules.heading: status bar
rules.text: Use status bar, not statusbar or status-bar.
rules.example: Check the statusbar for errors.

rules.heading: STONITH, STOMITH
rules.text: Avoid STONITH and STOMITH; instead, explain the relevant feature, such as fence failed nodes.
rules.why: Avoid graphic or metaphorical language.
rules.example: Enable STONITH for the cluster.

rules.heading: style sheet
rules.text: Use style sheet or stylesheet consistently throughout a given document.

rules.heading: sub-command
rules.text: Use sub-command, not subcommand.
rules.example: Run the subcommand with the --help flag.

rules.heading: subnet
rules.text: Use subnet or subnetwork consistently throughout your document.

rules.heading: subtree
rules.text: Use subtree, not sub-tree.
rules.example: Copy the sub-tree to the new location.

rules.heading: subzone
rules.text: Use subzone, not sub-zone or sub zone.
rules.example: Create a sub-zone for the domain.

rules.heading: such as
rules.text: Use such as to introduce examples or draw comparisons.

rules.heading: such as
rules.text: Don't combine such as, like, or include with etc., so forth, or and more.
rules.why: These already introduce non-exhaustive lists.

rules.heading: surface
rules.text: Avoid surface as a transitive verb; instead, use a more specific term, such as make people aware of or expose.
rules.bad: To surface audit logs, you must configure the monitoring system.
rules.good: To make the audit logs available, you must configure the monitoring system.

rules.heading: tab
rules.text: When referring to the sub-pages of a console, use page instead of tab.

rules.heading: table name
rules.text: Set specific table names in code font.

rules.heading: table name
rules.text: Write table name as two words.
rules.example: Enter the tablename in the box.

rules.heading: tablet
rules.text: If you don't know whether it's a tablet or a phone, use device.

rules.heading: tap
rules.text: Use tap for on-screen and soft (capacitive) buttons.

rules.heading: tap
rules.text: Use tap instead of click when the environment is definitely a touch device.

rules.heading: tap
rules.text: For mechanical buttons, use press.

rules.heading: tarball
rules.text: Don't use tarball. Instead, use tar file.
rules.example: Download the tarball and extract it.

rules.heading: target
rules.text: Avoid using target as a verb when possible, especially in reference to people; use alternatives such as intended for, looking for, focused on, or interacting with.
rules.why: For some readers, target has aggressive connotations.

rules.heading: terminate
rules.text: Avoid using terminate as a synonym for stop; instead, use words like stop, exit, cancel, or end.

rules.heading: text box, textbox
rules.text: Use field instead of box.
rules.good: In the Instance field, specify a value less than 64 characters long.

rules.heading: text box, textbox
rules.text: Don't use text box or textbox. Instead, use box.
rules.avoid: Text box, text box, Textbox, textbox
rules.example: Enter your name in the text box.

rules.heading: then
rules.text: Include helper words like then in if...then statements.

rules.heading: they (singular)
rules.text: Use they as the preferred gender-neutral pronoun.
rules.good: A user enters their password, and then they insert their security key.

rules.heading: they (singular)
rules.text: Whether they is used as singular or plural, use the plural verb.
rules.good: A user enters their password, and then they insert their security key.

rules.heading: third party (noun), third-party (adjective)
rules.text: Spell as third party when used as a noun and as third-party when used as an adjective.

rules.heading: third party (noun), third-party (adjective)
rules.text: Avoid abbreviating to 3rd party or 3rd-party.
rules.example: Install a 3rd-party library.

rules.heading: this, that
rules.text: Where possible, put a noun after this or that for clarity.
rules.why: Otherwise readers may not know what noun you mean.

rules.heading: timeframe
rules.text: Avoid timeframe where possible, or use an alternative such as period, schedule, deadline, or when.

rules.heading: timeframe
rules.text: Write timeframe as one word, not time frame.
rules.example: Complete the migration within the time frame.

rules.heading: timeout (noun), time out (verb)
rules.text: Use timeout as a noun and time out as a verb.

rules.heading: timestamp
rules.text: Use timestamp, not time stamp.
rules.avoid: time stamps, time stamp, Time stamp
rules.example: Each entry includes a time stamp.

rules.heading: time to live
rules.text: Abbreviate time to live as TTL after first use.

rules.heading: time to live
rules.text: Use time to live, not time-to-live.
rules.use: time to live, Time to live
rules.example: Set the time-to-live for the record.

rules.heading: time zone (noun), time-zone (adjective)
rules.text: Spell as time zone when used as a noun and as time-zone when used as an adjective.

rules.heading: tl;dr
rules.text: Don't use tl;dr. Instead, use something like To summarize, or revise the sentence.
rules.example: tl;dr: restart the server.

rules.heading: toolkit
rules.text: Use toolkit, not tool-kit or tool kit.
rules.avoid: tool-kit, Tool-kit, tool kit, Tool kit
rules.example: Install the tool kit before you begin.

rules.heading: touch
rules.text: Don't use touch; instead, use tap, although touch & hold is OK to use.

rules.heading: "touch & hold"
rules.text: Use touch & hold, not touch and hold.
rules.avoid: touch and hold, Touch and hold
rules.example: Touch and hold the app icon.

rules.heading: touchscreen
rules.text: Use touchscreen, not touch screen.
rules.avoid: touch screens, touch screen, Touch screen
rules.example: The device has a touch screen.

rules.heading: traditional
rules.text: If possible, use a more precise term than traditional.
rules.bad: This tutorial explains how to migrate from a traditional data warehouse to BigQuery.
rules.good: This tutorial explains how to migrate from an on-premises data warehouse to BigQuery.

rules.heading: transpile
rules.text: Use transpile, not transcompile.
rules.example: Use Babel to transcompile your code.

rules.heading: tribal knowledge, tribal wisdom
rules.text: Don't use tribal knowledge or tribal wisdom; use a less figurative term for knowledge held by a group of people.
rules.avoid: tribal knowledge, tribal wisdom, Tribal knowledge, Tribal wisdom
rules.example: This process relies on tribal knowledge.

rules.heading: trojan
rules.text: Lowercase trojan when referring to malware.

rules.heading: turn on
rules.text: In procedures, use the appropriate label and action for the UI element that the user interacts with.
rules.good: In Settings, click the Magic mode toggle to the on position.

rules.heading: turn on
rules.text: For turning on or activating an option or feature, use turn on or enable consistently throughout your document.
rules.good: To turn on Magic Mode, follow these steps.

rules.heading: type
rules.text: In general, use enter instead of type for entering text.
rules.why: Text can also be pasted or spoken, not only typed.

rules.heading: typically
rules.text: Don't use typically as the first word in a sentence.
rules.why: Can leave the meaning open to misinterpretation.
rules.example: Typically, the job finishes in an hour.

rules.heading: UI
rules.text: Don't use UI generically to refer to a page or dashboard; use a more specific term like page or console.
rules.bad: In the Cloud Tasks UI
rules.good: On the Cloud Tasks page
rules.why: Specific terms tell readers exactly where to look.

rules.heading: UI
rules.text: If a specific term like page or console is unavailable, use web interface instead of UI.
rules.bad: In the Cloud Tasks UI
rules.good: In the Secure Source Manager web interface

rules.heading: unarchive
rules.text: Don't use unarchive, uncompress, untar, or unzip. Instead, use extract.
rules.example: To get the files, unzip the downloaded archive.

rules.heading: uncheck
rules.text: To refer to clearing a check mark from a checkbox, use clear, not deselect.
rules.bad: Deselect Automatically check for updates.
rules.good: Clear Automatically check for updates.

rules.heading: uncheck
rules.text: Don't use uncheck to refer to clearing a check mark from a checkbox. Instead, use clear.
rules.bad: Uncheck Automatically check for updates.
rules.good: Clear Automatically check for updates.
rules.example: Uncheck Automatically check for updates.

rules.heading: under
rules.text: Don't use under for a range of version numbers. Instead, use earlier.

rules.heading: under
rules.text: Don't use under to refer to a position in the UI.
rules.bad: Under Service account ID, enter a name.
rules.good: In the Service account ID field, enter a name.

rules.heading: Unicode
rules.text: Write Unicode, not UNICODE.
rules.example: The file uses UNICODE characters.

rules.heading: Unix-like
rules.text: Write Unix-like, not Unixlike or Unix like.
rules.example: Install the tool on a Unixlike system.

rules.heading: Unix epoch time
rules.text: Use Unix epoch time instead of Unix time or epoch time to refer to a point in time represented as a number of seconds since the Unix epoch.
rules.example: Timestamps are stored as Unix time.

rules.heading: unselect
rules.text: Don't use unselect. Instead, use clear for checkboxes, and deselect for other UI elements.
rules.why: Replacement depends on the UI element.
rules.example: To disable the option, unselect the checkbox.

rules.heading: unsighted
rules.text: Don't use unsighted.
rules.example: Screen readers help unsighted users.

rules.heading: US
rules.text: Use US as the abbreviation for United States; don't use U.S. or U.S.A.
rules.example: The service is available to U.S. customers.

rules.heading: user
rules.text: Use the word user only to refer to the user of the software that your reader is developing.

rules.heading: user
rules.text: Otherwise, address the reader as you and assume that they will complete the tasks that you're documenting.

rules.heading: user base
rules.text: Write user base, not userbase.
rules.example: The app has a large userbase.

rules.heading: using
rules.text: Where using might have more than one interpretation, use by using or that use instead to help clarify the logic of the sentence; it's OK to use using (or with) when misinterpretation is unlikely.
rules.bad: Filter the IAM roles using custom permissions.
rules.good: Remove the Compute Engine VMs by using the test tag.
rules.why: Ambiguous using obscures the logic of the sentence.

rules.heading: UTF
rules.text: Include the hyphen in the names of Unicode encodings, such as UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32.
rules.example: Save the file as UTF8.

rules.heading: utilize, utilization
rules.text: Don't use utilize when you mean use; it's OK to use utilize or utilization when referring to the quantity of a resource being used.
rules.bad: To distribute network traffic, utilize a load balancer.
rules.good: To distribute network traffic, use a load balancer.

rules.heading: v (abbreviating version)
rules.text: Use lowercase v when abbreviating version.
rules.example: Install V2.1 of the client library.

rules.heading: via
rules.text: Don't use via.
rules.example: Send the request via the API.

rules.heading: vice versa
rules.text: Don't use vice versa; write out the relationship explicitly, or use a more precise term like conversely to emphasize the reciprocal or contrasting relationship.
rules.bad: You can copy local files to the cloud and vice versa.
rules.good: You can upload local files to the cloud or download cloud files to your local environment.

rules.heading: vice versa
rules.text: Don't use vice versa.
rules.why: Write out the relationship explicitly.
rules.example: You can copy local files to the cloud and vice versa.

rules.heading: virtual machine (VM) instance
rules.text: Use virtual machine (VM) instance when first introducing virtual machines on a given page; for subsequent mentions, you can use VM instance or VM.

rules.heading: virtual machine (VM) instance
rules.text: On first mention of a Compute Engine VM, use Compute Engine instance and then use compute instance throughout the rest of the document.

rules.heading: virtual machine (VM) instance
rules.text: If you need to indicate other types of VMs, use VM, VM instance, or bare metal instance.

rules.heading: VLAN attachment
rules.text: Use VLAN attachment, not interconnect attachment (VLAN), Interconnect attachment, Cloud Interconnect attachment, or any variation thereof.
rules.avoid: Cloud Interconnect attachment, Interconnect attachment, interconnect attachment
rules.example: Create an Interconnect attachment for your connection.

rules.heading: voila
rules.text: Don't use voila.
rules.example: Click Save and voila, your changes are live.

rules.heading: voodoo
rules.text: Don't use voodoo; instead, use a term like mysterious, complicated, or nondeterministic.
rules.example: The caching logic is a bit of voodoo.

rules.heading: vs.
rules.text: Don't use vs. as an abbreviation for versus; instead, use the unabbreviated versus.
rules.example: Compare batch vs. streaming pipelines.

rules.heading: wake lock (noun), wake-lock (adjective)
rules.text: Spell as wake lock when used as a noun and as wake-lock when used as an adjective.

rules.heading: walkthrough
rules.text: Use walkthrough, not walk-through.
rules.example: Follow the walk-through to set up your project.

rules.heading: war room, warroom, war-room
rules.text: Don't use war room; use a more precise term to describe the activity or team, such as rapid response team, situation room, or incident-management team.
rules.avoid: war room, warroom, war-room, War room
rules.why: Use a more precise term for the activity or team.
rules.example: The team met in the war room during the outage.

rules.heading: warm
rules.text: When possible, avoid jargon like warm failover, warm standby, and warm spare; if you use one of these phrases, define it on first use and use it consistently throughout the document.

rules.heading: we
rules.text: Don't use we (or other first-person plural pronouns such as our or us) to address the reader who is performing the tasks that you're documenting; instead, use you. It's OK to use we to refer to the organization that's represented as the author of the document as long as the antecedent is clear.

rules.heading: web (lowercase)
rules.text: Write web in lowercase.

rules.heading: WebAssembly, Wasm
rules.text: Use the capitalization established in the WebAssembly specification: WebAssembly and Wasm.
rules.why: Capitalization established in the WebAssembly specification.
rules.example: Compile the module to WASM.

rules.heading: web application firewall (lowercase)
rules.text: Write web application firewall in lowercase.
rules.example: Configure a Web Application Firewall for your site.

rules.heading: webmaster, web master
rules.text: Don't use webmaster; use a more precise term to describe the specific role, such as website owner, website administrator, web content manager, or owner of a site.
rules.avoid: webmaster, web master, Webmaster, Web master
rules.why: Use a more precise term for the specific role.
rules.example: Contact your webmaster for access.

rules.heading: web server
rules.text: Use web server, not webserver.
rules.example: Restart the webserver after you change the configuration.

rules.heading: while
rules.text: Don't use while to indicate a contrast; instead, use a more precise term, such as although. It's OK to use while to refer to a period of time.

rules.heading: white-box
rules.text: Avoid using white-box, whitebox, or white box to describe monitoring and testing; for monitoring, use introspective monitoring, and for testing, use clear-box testing.
rules.avoid: white-box, whitebox, white box, White-box, Whitebox, White box
rules.why: Use introspective monitoring or clear-box testing instead.
rules.example: Run white-box tests against the service.

rules.heading: white glove, white-glove, whiteglove
rules.text: Avoid using white glove; instead use terms like high-touch, premium, or platinum-level.
rules.avoid: white glove, white-glove, whiteglove, White glove, White-glove
rules.why: Use high-touch, premium, or platinum-level instead.
rules.example: We offer white-glove onboarding for enterprise customers.

rules.heading: whitehat, white hat, white-hat
rules.text: Don't use whitehat; instead, use precise terms for the kind of compliance, such as legal, ethical, or following the rules.
rules.avoid: whitehat, white hat, white-hat, Whitehat, White hat, White-hat
rules.why: Use precise terms like legal or ethical.
rules.example: Use only white-hat SEO techniques.

rules.heading: white label, whitelabel, white-label
rules.text: Don't use white label; instead, use a more precise term for your context, such as unbranded, unlabeled, or blank label.
rules.avoid: white label, whitelabel, white-label, White label, Whitelabel, White-label
rules.why: Use unbranded, unlabeled, or blank label.
rules.example: Resellers can offer a white-label version of the app.

rules.heading: whitelist, white list, white-list
rules.text: Don't use whitelist, whitelisted, whitelisting, or their variants; see the blacklist entry.
rules.avoid: whitelist, white list, white-list, whitelisted, white listed, white-listed, whitelisting, white listing, white-listing, Whitelist, White list, White-list, Whitelisted, Whitelisting
rules.why: See the blacklist entry.
rules.example: Add the IP address to the whitelist.

rules.heading: whitepaper
rules.text: When possible, use a more precise term than whitepaper; if you must use the term whitepaper, also use descriptive terms to provide context.
rules.why: Whitepaper has a variety of meanings in various contexts.

rules.heading: whitepaper
rules.text: Use whitepaper, not white paper.
rules.example: Download the white paper to learn more.

rules.heading: whitespace
rules.text: Use whitespace, not white space.
rules.example: Remove trailing white space from each line.

rules.heading: wildcard
rules.text: Use wildcard, not wild card.
rules.example: Use an asterisk as a wild card.

rules.heading: will
rules.text: Avoid will; this applies equally to its past tense, would. Use present tense.

rules.heading: wish
rules.text: Don't use wish; instead, use a word like want or need.
rules.why: Use want or need instead.
rules.example: If you wish to continue, click Next.

rules.heading: with
rules.text: Don't use with when expressing ownership.
rules.bad: A handset with 2 GB of RAM.
rules.good: A handset that has 2 GB of RAM.

rules.heading: with
rules.text: Don't use with when expressing use.
rules.bad: Debug this tool with the debugging tool.
rules.good: Use the debugging tool to debug.

rules.heading: workload
rules.text: Where possible, use a more precise term than workload to describe what you mean.
rules.why: Workload can mean software, resources, or physical components.

rules.heading: workload
rules.text: If you use the term workload, define your meaning on first use as you normally would with jargon and other ambiguous terms.

rules.heading: World Wide Web
rules.text: Don't use World Wide Web; instead, use web.
rules.example: The page is available on the World Wide Web.

rules.heading: would
rules.text: Avoid using would; instead, use can where possible.

rules.heading: ymmv
rules.text: Don't use ymmv. Instead, use something like your results might vary.
rules.why: Abbreviation is informal and unclear to many readers.
rules.example: Performance gains depend on your workload, so YMMV.

rules.heading: you
rules.text: Use you instead of user to address the reader of your document.
rules.why: Address the reader directly in second person.

rules.heading: zippy
rules.text: Don't use zippy to refer to expander arrows, unless you're specifically referring to the Zippy widget in Closure.

rule.heading: lock screen
rule.text: In Android contexts, write lock screen as two words; not lockscreen or lock-screen.

rule.text: Don't use tap & hold or tap and hold; use touch & hold.
